articles.title: Revised Biosynthetic Pathway of Alnumycin Involves a Complex Interplay of Redox Reactions, Stereoisomerization, and an Atypical DUF6081 Isomerase
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Alnumycin A is an antimicrobial natural product distinguished by an unusual 1,3-dioxane moiety attached to an aromatic polyketide core. While previous studies had established that d-ribose serves as the precursor to the 1,3-dioxane and its attachment to the aromatic ring system is catalyzed by a C-glycoside synthase, less is known about its subsequent transformation. Aln6 is a member of the domain of unknown function (DUF) 6081 protein family and was previously annotated as a cofactor-free oxidase. Herein, Aln6 is shown to catalyze a redox-neutral isomerization that converts the ribose moiety to a fused furan-dioxolane via an unprecedented rearrangement mechanism. Aln4 subsequently catalyzes an NADPH-dependent reductive ring-opening of the furan, setting the stage for nonenzymatic rearrangement of the dioxolane that produces the 1,3-dioxane structure and explains the stereochemical diversity of alnumycin A observed in vivo. Together, these findings not only revise the established view of the late-stage biosynthesis of alnumycin A but also redefine the chemistry of Aln6, expanding the catalytic repertoire of the DUF6081 family beyond canonical oxidative reactions.

articles.title: A Triboelectric Nanogenerator-Based Self-Powered Embodied Flow Perception System for Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles
Contact-Electrification Activated Immunoadjuvant with Intrinsic Tumoricidal Activity for Colorectal Cancer Immunotherapy
Light-Induced Néel Vector Reversal in 2D van der Waals Antiferromagnets
articles.abstract: Antiferromagnetic spintronics promises ultrafast device performance, yet the essential Néel vector reversal is hindered by its intrinsic immunity to external magnetic fields. Here, we propose a mechanism for deterministic Néel vector reversal in 2D van der Waals antiferromagnets enabled by ultrafast laser pulses. The core physics involves light-induced asymmetric interlayer demagnetization, which drives the antiferromagnet into a transient ferrimagnetic state with a finite net moment. This transient symmetry breaking allows the Néel vector to be controlled by an external magnetic field. We identify that the intrinsic structural and electronic asymmetries and spin–orbit-coupling mediated spin flips are essential for this process. Using first-principles calculations and real-time time-dependent density functional theory, we further demonstrate this mechanism in bilayer NiICl and YI2. Our work establishes a general strategy for the optical manipulation of 2D antiferromagnetic order.

articles.title: Molecular and Nanoscale Control of Exciton Transfer in TADF-Sensitized Fluorescence
articles.abstract: TADF-sensitized fluorescence (TSF), also known as hyperfluorescence, combines efficient triplet exciton harvesting with the narrowband emission of fluorescent emitters. Yet, its performance depends on the interplay between exciton conversion, energy transfer, and molecular organization across different length scales. Herein, we review recent progress in nanoscale exciton-transfer engineering for TSF, with emphasis on molecular excited-state dynamics, sensitizer-dopant spatial control, diversified energy-transfer pathways, and interlayer sensitization. These approaches regulate exciton conversion and lifetime, balance Förster and Dexter energy transfer, and control exciton distribution within emissive layers and across interfaces. We also discuss emerging directions including kinetic matching, spatial organization, and multiscale modeling for understanding the links between molecular structure, energy-transfer dynamics, and device performance. This Mini-Review provides profound insights into transforming random blend systems into controllable nanoscale exciton-transfer networks, paving the way for efficient narrowband TSF OLEDs.

articles.title: A Porphyrinic Metal–Organic Framework Platform for Red-Light Photoredox Catalysis
articles.abstract: Low-energy photoredox catalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for promoting mild, chemoselective transformations through radical intermediates. While various red-light-absorbing photocatalysts, including molecular porphyrins, have enabled diverse synthetic transformations, these processes operate almost exclusively under homogeneous conditions in organic solvents. Here, we demonstrate that integrating a photoactive porphyrin as the organic linker in a metal–organic framework (MOF) affords an air- and aqueous-compatible, heterogeneous photoredox catalyst. Using porphyrinic zirconium MOFs such as PCN-224, we enable a range of bond-forming reactions, including Giese additions, C(sp2)–H alkylations, C(sp2)–H arylations, formal cycloadditions, and radical polymerizations under mild red-light irradiation. While preserving the intrinsic reactivity of molecular porphyrins, heterogenization provides practical advantages including efficient photocatalysis independent of catalyst solubility and reaction medium, structural tunability, high turnover number (TON), and easy catalyst recovery and reuse. Mechanistic studies indicate that radical generation occurs predominantly within the framework pores.

articles.title: Aldehyde or Carboxylic Acid: Defining the Selectivity of Electrochemical Oxidation of Aliphatic Alcohols by Tuning the Surface Phase of NiO(OH)
articles.abstract: Nickel oxyhydroxide (NiO(OH)) is the catalytically active species during electrochemical alcohol oxidation at nickel electrodes. Herein, we demonstrate that the adopted phase structure of NiO(OH) (β- and γ-NiO(OH)) can dramatically influence the catalytic properties of nickel electrodes. We show that β-NiO(OH) oxidizes aliphatic alcohols preferentially to aldehydes and that carboxylates are formed at γ-NiO(OH). By combining the effect of the NiO(OH) phase with reagent effects (electrolyte pH, alcohol concentration, and trace amounts of Fe), we achieve aldehyde formation with ∼90% selectivity or carboxylate formation with ∼85% selectivity. Furthermore, we perform an in situ Raman spectroelectrochemical study to elucidate the reaction conditions that favor the formation of β- and γ-NiO(OH) phases, respectively. Freshly deposited nickel electrodes form γ-NiO(OH) phases upon oxidation, whereas an electrochemical conditioning protocol can be employed to transform γ- to β-NiO(OH). Finally, we show that the efficiency of this transformation depends on the precise reaction conditions and the precursor used. Hence, we showcase that the exact surface structure of the phase formed in situ on top of transition metal (oxides) affects the product distribution of electrochemical reactions. Moreover, we highlight how the “history” of these catalysts affects their performance via an intricate interplay among the reaction environment, pre-treatment, and surface structure.

articles.title: Discovery of Racemization Organocatalysts and Biocatalysts for Ketoreductase-Catalyzed Dynamic Reductive Kinetic Resolution
articles.abstract: Cyclic α-halo ketones and vicinal halohydrins serve as essential synthetic intermediates or structural motifs for a variety of pharmaceuticals. Ketoreductase-catalyzed dynamic reductive kinetic resolution (DYRKR) of cyclic α-halo ketones is an attractive strategy for the synthesis of chiral cyclic vicinal halohydrins. However, we found that the spontaneous racemization of the α-halo groups of 3-bromo-chroman-4-ones and 2-bromo-1-tetralones was less efficient than the ketoreductase-catalyzed reduction of the more reactive enantiomers, resulting in a low conversion and poor (dia)stereoselectivity. To address this challenge, two classes of racemization catalysts were identified: prolinol-derived organocatalysts and racemase-based biocatalysts, both of which could accelerate the racemization of cyclic α-halo ketones. Consequently, combining these catalysts with ketoreductases improved both the conversion and product (dia)stereoselectivity of the DYRKR. Based on the discovery of racemization catalysts, this work provides an efficient strategy for biocatalytic dynamic kinetic resolution and an operationally simple route for the synthesis of chiral cyclic vicinal halohydrins.

articles.title: Covalent-Bond Engineering Stabilizes Layered Oxide Cathodes for Sodium-Ion Batteries
articles.abstract: Developing practicable layered oxide cathodes remains a critical challenge for sodium-ion batteries. Here, by systematically varying Cu contents to tune TM–O covalency in Nay[CuxFe3/9Mn(6/9–x)]O2, we show that an optimal degree of covalency simultaneously boosts energy density and structural resilience. The optimized Na7/9[Cu2/9Fe3/9Mn4/9]O2 delivers 131.6 mAh g–1 at 0.1 C and retains 80% capacity after 500 cycles at 0.5 C. Mechanistically, the enhanced Cu–O covalency converts trivalent Cu from a conventional d8 to a heavily mixed d9L configuration, delocalizing holes across the extended TM–O network, enlarging polaron size, and “flattening the ripple” of local lattice distortions. Side-by-side comparison with an ionic Ni analogue confirms the suppressed cation migration and polarization. Crucially, the covalency-driven stabilization is not unbounded–excessive covalency rigidifies the lattice, defining a covalency threshold for optimal performance. These findings establish covalency modulation within a defined threshold as a predictive design principle for durable layered oxide cathodes.

articles.title: Electrochemical Capture and Accumulation of Uranium Using a Layered Uvanite Electrode
articles.abstract: Extracting uranyl ions (UO22+) from uranium mining leachates can enhance national uranium security and mitigate the environmental impact of nuclear energy. Conventional techniques such as ion exchange and iron-based reductive precipitation have notable limitations. This study reports that the uvanite (U2V6O21) electrode, a layered uranium-vanadium oxide, enables potentiodynamic decoupling of UO22+ and proton intercalation/deintercalation, as well as proton-induced UO22+/UO3 precipitation and dissolution reactions. Building on a comprehensive understanding of charge-transfer and transport mechanisms, we found that potentiodynamic modulation enables selective capture of uranium species using a uvanite electrode. By allowing competing cations to deintercalate at lower potentials and preventing proton deintercalation, UO3 dissolution is inhibited, achieving a high UO3 recovery capacity of 515 mg/g at 10 times the competing cation concentration. The new electrochemistry of the uvanite electrode helps develop cost-effective, sustainable battery electrodes for critical ion extraction from water.

articles.title: Implications for CO2 Reduction: Methanol Formation by Reaction of Benzimidazole Hydrides with Inorganic Oxide Materials
Light-Driven Hydrogenation–Dehydrogenation of Toluene–Methylcyclohexane by Plasmonic Photocatalysis
articles.abstract: The development of an efficient and reversible hydrogen storage and transport system is crucial for a sustainable hydrogen economy. Liquid organic hydrogen carriers (LOHCs) offer a potential solution due to their high hydrogen storage density and ease of transport, but conventional thermal approaches for the hydrogenation and dehydrogenation of LOHCs remain heavily reliant on harsh operating conditions. Here, we demonstrate a plasmonic photocatalysis approach for toluene hydrogenation to methylcyclohexane and methylcyclohexane dehydrogenation to toluene under substantially milder conditions. We observe changes in reaction orders and substantial reductions in activation barriers by 0.34 and 1.11 eV for toluene hydrogenation and methylcyclohexane dehydrogenation, respectively, as compared to thermocatalysis due to the role of hot carriers. Both reactions exhibit high activity, stability (>70 h), and excellent selectivity (>95%), offering a sustainable pathway for on-demand hydrogen storage and release.

articles.title: When Literature Data Can Mislead Artificial Intelligence in Materials Discovery
Dislocation Arrays Hosting Topological Bound States in Epitaxial Tetragonal FeSe Films
articles.abstract: Topological defects in real space can host robust, localized quantum states for quantum information processing and sensing, yet deterministic control over their formation in crystalline materials remains challenging. Here, we show that symmetry-mismatched epitaxy of tetragonal FeSe films on SrTiO3(111) naturally generates networks of screw dislocations and tilt grain boundaries composed of periodic arrays of edge dislocations. Low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy measurements reveal localized electronic states pinned to these dislocation cores. Combined with first-principles calculations, we identify these states as topological bound states arising from the interplay between the real-space topological invariant of the defect, the Burgers vector, and the nontrivial electronic topology of FeSe. Our work demonstrates symmetry mismatch epitaxy as a scalable route toward template topological defect networks and their associated quantum states in solid-state materials.

articles.title: In Situ Nanoscale Visualization of Stripping-Induced Failure Behavior in Aqueous Zinc Batteries
articles.abstract: Aqueous zinc batteries (AZBs) show great promise for large-scale energy storage due to their low cost, intrinsic safety, and environmental compatibility. However, their practical deployment is hindered by dendrite formation, residual zinc (Zn) accumulation, and limited cycle life. Recent studies have identified the stripping process as a critical factor governing battery longevity, yet the underlying failure mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, leveraging a fourth-generation synchrotron radiation source, we employed in situ nanoscale X-ray microscopy to visualize the morphological evolution from planar to mossy Zn during cycling at 50 mA cm–2. Combining observations of the entire cycling process with optical flow analysis of the stripping process on different substrates at 1 mA cm–2, we categorize the origins of residual Zn into four distinct pathways: (i) dendrites formed during plating; (ii) dendrites generated by crystallographically selective stripping; (iii) bulky Zn that loses electrical contact during stripping; and (iv) Zn fragments resulting from inward dissolution. Ex-situ XRD and DFT calculations further confirm the preferential dissolution of Zn(100) and Zn(101) over Zn(002). These findings highlight the critical role of the stripping process in AZB failure and demonstrate that minimizing local variations in dissolution behavior through kinetic modulation is one of the keys to achieving complete dissolution and enhancing Zn reversibility.

articles.title: Molecular Single-Photon Emitters across Chemical Space: Substrate Effects and Design Principles
articles.abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are an emerging molecular platform for single-photon emitters, but predictive design strategies across chemical space have been lacking. Here we establish two general principles governing PAH/hBN emitters. The zero-phonon-line energy is molecule-controlled and robust to the substrate environment, whereas the Huang–Rhys (HR) factor is environment-governed and exhibits two distinct regimes. Pristine hBN modestly enhances HR through soft interfacial modes. In contrast, the NB antisite defect, introduced to immobilize the molecules, produces a molecule-specific HR response that cannot be predicted from gas-phase or pristine-hBN data alone. Strikingly, the defect can either partially restore the HR factor toward its intrinsic gas-phase value or amplify it by up to 3.7×, depending on the molecule. This positions defect engineering as a tunable design knob for vibronic coupling in molecule/hBN emitters. Combining high-throughput hybrid density functional theory (DFT) screening of 662 PAHs identifies 47 gas-phase candidates with low HR factors and high radiative rates spanning the near-infrared to ultraviolet. Among five representative candidates explicitly tested on NB@hBN, two retain HR factors below unity in gas-phase, pristine hBN, and defect-bound environments. However, no PAH simultaneously exhibits favorable single-photon-emitter properties and an excited-state singlet–triplet splitting below 0.5 eV, suggesting that PAH-based spin–photon interfaces will require further molecular design. All data are released through the open MolExDB platform.

articles.title: Nanozyme-Catalyzed Lateral Flow Assay for the Simultaneous Detection of RNA and Protein Biomarkers
articles.abstract: Molecular diagnostics have advanced rapidly over the past decade, driven by the demand for accessible and scalable testing solutions. However, current assays often focus on single biomolecule types, limiting their ability to capture the multifactorial nature of disease. Integrating distinct molecular readouts─such as transcriptomic and proteomic biomarkers─could provide richer diagnostic information and improve clinical decision-making. Here, we present MOSAIC (Multiplexed Orthogonal Sensing Assay Integrated with CRISPRZyme), a unified lateral flow assay that enables simultaneous detection of RNA and protein biomarkers using a shared nanozyme-catalyzed readout. The assay combines CRISPR/Cas13a-mediated RNA detection and antibody-based protein detection, with assay components optimized through antibody conjugation tuning, blocking agent optimization, and probe loading calibration to achieve balanced and cross-talk-free performance. Using cardiovascular disease as a model, the platform successfully detects NTproBNP and LIPCAR long noncoding RNA simultaneously from the same sample. The assay was further optimized for spiked human plasma, incorporating tailored pretreatment and recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) to maintain RNA stability and performance in complex biofluids. Extending its versatility, the same assay design was adapted to detect SARS-CoV-2 biomarkers, the spike (S) protein and ORF1ab gene, in pooled human saliva. To enable standardized interpretation of multiplexed readouts, we additionally developed a machine-learning-assisted computational workflow that automates strip localization, signal extraction, and calibration curve construction. Together, these results demonstrate a modular, paper-based diagnostic platform that unites transcriptomic and proteomic analyses within one assay architecture, offering a practical step toward accessible and multiplexed molecular diagnostics across diverse disease contexts.

articles.title: Rapid-Mixing In Situ X-ray Diffraction Reveals Precursor-Reorganization Signatures in Additive-Free Zeolitic Imidazolate Framework-8 Nanoparticle Formation
articles.abstract: Controlling particle size and phase purity in solution-processed metal–organic frameworks requires understanding how disordered precursors evolve before they crystallize into the final framework. However, capturing this precursor-to-crystal conversion remains a key challenge. Here, we couple a central-collision-type microreactor with time-resolved in situ X-ray diffraction to track the additive-free formation of zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (ZIF-8) in water–methanol cosolvents, achieving 5 s temporal resolution after submillisecond micromixing. The setup directly captures crystal appearance, apparent crystallization kinetics, and subsequent lattice relaxation. Crystallization is fastest at 40–50 vol % methanol, where Bragg reflections appear earliest and grow most rapidly. Water-rich media approach a competing phase boundary between ZIF-8 and layered zeolitic imidazolate framework-L (ZIF-L) and yield a predominantly amorphous product at the water-rich extreme, whereas methanol-rich media form pure ZIF-8 more slowly. After crystallinity emerges, the apparent lattice constant contracts, indicating that the earliest Bragg-detectable domains undergo lattice relaxation as growth proceeds. Strikingly, raising the total reactant concentration at a fixed metal-to-linker ratio delays crystal appearance and yields larger particles, contrary to the behavior typically expected in a nucleation-dominated system. We propose that concentration-dependent precursor accumulation, coarsening, and interconnection, coupled to metal–ligand network reorganization, link these contrasting trends.

articles.title: Single-Atom Nanoisland with Dual-Nanoconfinement Effects for Cascade Self-Amplified Synergistic Antitumor Therapy via Redox/Metabolism Disruption
articles.abstract: Enzyodynamic therapy (EDT) represents a promising cancer therapeutic modality; however, its efficacy is constrained by the catalytic activity of nanozymes and intrinsic tumor-adaptive defense mechanisms. Leveraging the atomic–nano structure and nanoconfined effect of single-atom nanoislands (SANIs), a SANI-based nanozyme (CPH) is elaborately constructed through vapor filling and spatially confined reduction/growth of metal species, featuring ultrasmall Pt nanoislands with embedded Ce single atoms confined within the channels of hollow carbon spheres. CPH exhibits multienzymatic activities resembling those of oxidase, catalase, peroxidase, glucose oxidase, glutathione peroxidase, and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide oxidase, sustaining a self-reinforcing catalytic cascade that disrupts redox homeostasis and blocks energy metabolism. This process facilitates H2O2 self-supplementation while alleviating hypoxia and elicits reactive oxygen species storm and lipid peroxidation, thereby establishing an apoptosis/ferroptosis dual-pathway therapeutic strategy. Mechanism investigation reveals that the enhanced catalytic properties can be ascribed to the favorable shift of the d-band center and synergistic effects among multiactive centers after Ce single-atom embedding. Concurrently, the nanoconfined photothermal effect facilitates heat concentration while minimizing thermal dissipation, further augmenting the catalytic efficiency and enabling synergistic mild-photothermal therapy (mild-PTT)/EDT synergistic therapy. This study provides a proof of concept of SANI-based nanozymes as efficient therapeutic tools toward tumor ablation.

articles.title: Universal In-Plane Confined Growth of Mesoporous Metal–Organic Framework Crystalline Heterostructures
articles.abstract: Constructing mesoporous MOF heterostructures on conductive two-dimensional hosts remains challenging because interfacial contact and pore accessibility are rarely optimized simultaneously. Herein, we report a universal in-plane confined growth strategy for mesoporous UiO-66-NH2/MXene heterostructures featuring continuous interfacial contact and vertically accessible mesochannels. In contrast to conventional particle-on-sheet hybrids, the resulting architecture enables improved electrolyte penetration, shortened Zn2+ transport pathways, and efficient interfacial electron transfer. By regulating micellar assembly at the interface, an optimal mesostructural regime is identified in which ion accessibility and structural confinement are best balanced. Consequently, the optimized heterostructure delivers a high energy density of 163.9 Wh kg–1, excellent rate capability (∼68% retention over a 50-fold current increase), and ∼100% capacity retention over 50,000 cycles. Kinetic analyses and ex situ studies further show that the interfacial mesoporous architecture suppresses diffusion limitations and preserves structural integrity during Zn2+ storage. Moreover, the assembly concept shows transferability across substrates of different dimensionalities, highlighting its broader utility for constructing mesoporous crystalline heterostructures. This work provides an effective route to mesoporous MOF heterostructures and a generalizable design principle for hybrid crystalline electrodes.

articles.title: 3D Observations of Grain Growth in Textured and Untextured Undoped Alumina
Energetic Role of Adaptive Mg Sublattice in Size-Mismatched Mg2(Si, Sn) Thermoelectric Meta-phases
Pencil glide, crystal rotation, and non-Schmid slip behavior in MoReW single crystals during tensile deformation
Boron‐Oxygen Covalent Fusion Enables Narrowband Deep‐Red CP‐OLEDs Based on BODIPY Emitters
articles.abstract: Realizing solution-processable deep-red circularly polarized organic light-emitting diodes (CP-OLEDs) with both intense CP and high color purity remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report the first solution-processed narrowband deep-red circularly polarized hyperfluorescence OLEDs based on a helically chiral boron-dipyrromethene emitter. Intramolecular boron–oxygen (B–O) covalent fusion simultaneously regulates molecular conjugation and conformational rigidity, thereby suppressing excited-state structural relaxation and vibronic coupling while preserving efficient deep-red emission. As a result, BDP-BO exhibits deep-red emission at 654 nm with a high photoluminescence quantum yield of 71% and an ultranarrow emission bandwidth of 34 nm (0.10 eV). The corresponding P- and M-enantiomers display excellent chiroptical activity, with a luminescence dissymmetry factor (|g lum|) up to 3.54 × 10−3 and a circularly polarized luminescence brightness (B CPL) of 49 M−1 cm−1. Exploiting these merits, the M-BDP-BO-based device delivers deep-red electroluminescence (EL) within the National Television System Committee color gamut, a maximum external quantum efficiency of 2.6%, and a large EL dissymmetry factor (|g EL|) of 5.49 × 10−3. This work establishes B–O covalent fusion as an effective strategy for simultaneously regulating molecular conjugation and conformational rigidity, providing a versatile platform for high-performance solution-processed deep-red CP-OLEDs.

articles.title: Fluorinated Fullerene Derivatives for Thermally Stable Perovskite Solar Cells
articles.abstract: PCBM (phenyl‐C61‐butyric acid methyl ester) is one of the most used electron transport layers (ETLs) in perovskite solar cells (PSCs). However, PCBM tends to self‐aggregate during the thermal aging process, disrupting film continuity and limiting device lifetime. To address this issue, we synthesized new fluorinated phenyl fullerene derivatives, FPCPB and 5FPCPB, forming a composite fullerene ETL by blending with PCBM. We found that fullerene self‐aggregation was suppressed through the synergistic effects of weak interactions, such as π–π conjugation between phenyl and fluorophenyl groups and C─H···F van der Waals interactions, and the constrained molecular conformation induced by intermolecular steric hindrance, thereby markedly improving film uniformity and thermal stability, reducing defect‐state density, and suppressing ion migration. In addition, the energy level alignment between perovskite and ETL is optimized, enhancing electron transport. Ultimately, 5FPCPB, having more compatible energy levels and stronger conjugation effects than FPCPB, achieved a 26.42% power conversion efficiency (PCE), with improved operational and thermal stability (T90 under light = 1200 h; T95 under 85°C > 700 h). The fullerene co‐doping strategy opens a new pathway for achieving high‐performance and thermally stable perovskite devices.

articles.title: Guest Transition Metals in Host Keplerate Nanocapsules as Supramolecular Inorganic Functional Mimics of Monooxygenase Enzymes
articles.abstract: Advanced design of supramolecules can mimic enzyme complexes. Methane monooxygenases have several subparts, hydroxylases active for alkane oxidation, and complexes and channels that regulate electron, proton, substrate, and product access to the active site. The replication of a hydroxylase active site with inclusion of regulatory functionalities within a porous Keplerate nanocapsule host was undertaken. A Cu active site guest within a Keplerate cavity was prepared by an assembly reaction using a histidine surrogate as binding site for CuII. The guest–host assembly enables transfer of protons and electrons and enables substrate and product diffusion to and from an active site into confined space. Characterization of the guest–host complex was by NMR, XPS, infrared, and Raman spectroscopies. Cyclic voltammetry was used to identify possible hydroxylase reactivity, followed by controlled potential electrolysis to verify hydrocarbon oxygenation. Substrate scope, optimal cathodic potential, and the number of metal sites needed were surveyed. Comparison of substrate reactivity revealed that their access to the active site was rate determining. Kinetics of a “dummy” substrate and product diffusion was measured by Guest Exchange Saturation Transfer 19F NMR. These guest–host Keplerate nanocapsules represent an initial foray into the mimicking of a complicated metalloenzyme complex in an inorganic synthetic system.

articles.title: Mechanistic Insights Into the Solid‐State Redox Reactions: Role of Organic Piezoelectric Materials
articles.abstract: Mechanochemistry has gained tremendous recent attention because it combines sustainability with the ability to access unique reaction pathways and materials while offering practical advantages for efficient and scalable chemical synthesis. However, predicting solid‐state transformations from mechanical energy remains a formidable challenge, as the current mechanistic models are insufficient. While solid‐state electrocatalytic reactions in the presence of inorganic piezoelectric materials have been demonstrated recently, the ability of piezoelectric organic solids, which possess an order of magnitude lower piezoelectric coefficients, remain completely unexplored. Here, using different crystalline forms, we demonstrate that under ball‐milling, non‐centrosymmetric organic crystals generate piezoelectric potentials that are sufficient to drive a range of redox bond‐forming reactions, including C─B, C─S, C─Se, C─C, and C─P couplings. To further evaluate the role of piezoelectricity, we compared chemically identical crystal forms of a compound, differing only in symmetry: Non‐centrosymmetric crystals are highly reactive, whereas centrosymmetric counterparts remain largely inert. These findings reveal crystal symmetry as a previously unrecognized determinant of chemical function and identify organic piezoelectric solids as active energy‐transduction media for chemical synthesis. More broadly, this work provides a framework for designing self‐powered chemical systems that directly couple mechanical energy harvesting with molecular transformation.

articles.title: Porphyrin Integration Enhances Bipolar Redox Accessibility for High‐Rate Sodium‐Based Dual‐Ion Storage
articles.abstract: Closing the gap between theoretical multielectron capacity and practical accessibility remains the central bottleneck for high-energy organic batteries. Herein, we report a molecular design strategy that integrates a porphyrin motif into a sulfur-rich conjugated polymer (BTTP) to align electronic structure, state-dependent ion interactions, and electrochemical kinetics across the bipolar window. Despite possessing a lower theoretical capacity than its reference counterpart (BTB), BTTP achieves an exceptional theoretical capacity utilization of 94.2% (delivering 477 mAh g−1 at 0.5 A g−1, compared to only 53.5% and 351 mAh g−1 for BTB). Electrokinetic analyses, including GITT and DRT, confirm accelerated apparent ion diffusion and reduced polarization limitations, enabling BTTP to retain 166 mAh g−1 at an ultrahigh current density of 20 A g−1 over 25 000 cycles. Operando/ex situ spectroscopy and theoretical calculations elucidate that the dual pyrrolic/imino nitrogen sites in porphyrin and the sulfur-rich backbone cooperatively provide potential-dependent coordination environments for PF6 − anions and Na+ cations. This work suggests that molecular regulation of complementary ion-interaction environments within multi-active-unit frameworks, rather than simply increasing the number of redox units, is important for enhancing rate capability and capacity utilization.

articles.title: π‐Extended Bisallyls Through Valence Isomerism: From Transient Diradicals to Persistent Anions
articles.abstract: Bisallyl diradicals are central intermediates in allene dimerization, yet they are normally too short‐lived to observe under thermal conditions. Here, π‐extension of Staudinger‐type allene dimers weakens the central cyclobutane bond sufficiently to make reversible ring opening accessible near room temperature. Variable‐temperature NMR spectroscopy and ROESY exchange correlations reveal repeated cleavage and reformation of this bond, with activation free energies of 15.77 and 13.79 kcal mol−1 for the Staudinger dimer and its π‐expanded analogue, respectively. Calculations reproduce this trend and identify low‐population open‐shell singlet bisallyls as the intermediates, while explaining the absence of neutral‐state EPR signals. Reduction reverses the relative stability of the closed and open valence isomers. Voltammetry and chemical reduction support a sequence of ring‐opened radical‐anion, dianion, and tetraanion states. The dianion is characterized by NMR spectroscopy and x‐ray diffraction, while spectroscopy and calculations reveal progressive bond redistribution from mixed‐valence allyl‐radical/allyl‐anion character to two allyl‐anion units and, finally, four fluorenyl‐anion‐like termini. These results connect hidden neutral diradicals with persistent reduced bisallyl frameworks through charge‐controlled covalent‐bond reorganization.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Generative Science of Food Formulation
articles.journal: Annual Review of Food Science and Technology
articles.abstract: Food formulation requires balancing taste, nutrition, sustainability, and cost. Traditionally, new foods have emerged through empirical experimentation, expert intuition, and iterative refinement. Now, artificial intelligence (AI) offers the opportunity to accelerate this process. Yet despite rapid advances across food science, most AI applications remain isolated prediction and optimization tasks rather than parts of a broader scientific approach. Here we integrate these emerging technologies into a unified framework—the generative science of food formulation—in which digital food representations enable AI to predict, discover, generate, organize, simulate, and optimize. We illustrate this approach through sustainability and nutrition, where generative AI transforms environmental and nutritional metrics from post hoc evaluation criteria into explicit design objectives. Finally, we identify the data, models, benchmarks, and automation that will establish computational food design as a rigorous scientific discipline. Together, these advances have the potential to transform food formulation from an empirical discipline into a generative science.

articles.title: In Sync with the Kidney: Reciprocal Regulation of Renal Circadian Rhythms
articles.abstract: Circadian rhythms regulate the time of day at which various physiological processes take place, including the functions of the kidney. This regulation is made possible by key transcriptional regulators: the core molecular circadian clock, which mediates expression of clock-controlled genes on a 24-h cycle. The present landscape of circadian rhythm research in the kidney spans impacts on the clinical level as well as in basic research, where its role in individual kidney cell types, disease states, and the impacts of environmental stressors is being studied. Recent research has also identified sex differences, cross talk between various tissues, and immune signaling as important considerations for understanding the circadian clocks within the kidney. This review synthesizes the current knowledge of circadian rhythms of the kidney in regard to these issues and stresses the importance of time of day in research as well as in patient health.

articles.title: Probiotics for Human Health: Mechanisms, Clinical Evidence, Risks, and Next-Generation Microbial Therapeutics
articles.abstract: Probiotics are widely used live microbial supplements intended to promote human health, yet their clinical benefits remain inconsistent and often strain-specific. Most currently available probiotics are derived from Lactobacillus , Bifidobacterium , and Saccharomyces species originally isolated from fermented foods or human microbiota. Preclinical studies suggest that these organisms may influence host physiology through several mechanisms, including antimicrobial activity, toxin inhibition, strengthening of intestinal barrier function, modulation of immune responses, and signaling along the gut–brain axis. However, translation of these mechanisms into consistent clinical benefit has been limited by heterogeneity in probiotic strains, dosing, and study design. Emerging evidence also highlights potential unintended consequences of probiotic use, including rare infections in vulnerable patients, alterations of microbiome recovery after antibiotics, and possible interactions with host metabolism or medications. Recent advances in microbiome research have supported the development of next-generation probiotics and engineered microbial therapeutics, representing a shift toward more targeted and mechanistically informed live microbial therapies.

articles.title: Stalled Capillary Blood Flow in the Brain: New Measurement Tools Unveil a Critical Role in Neurological Diseases
articles.abstract: Flow disturbances in the smallest blood vessels of the brain, the capillaries, have long been considered a potential cause of brain dysfunction. However, owing to the technological challenge of studying blood flow in three-dimensional capillary networks, elucidating the incidence, causes, and consequences of capillary obstructions has been difficult. Advances in optical microscopes for in vivo imaging, primarily high-spatiotemporal-resolution optical coherence tomography and two-photon microscopy, have recently enabled detailed studies of these capillary stalling events in both healthy and diseased mice. In this review, we describe these imaging approaches to quantify capillary stalling, identifying strengths and weaknesses of different methods. We then review recent findings on the incidence, molecular and cellular causes, and physiological and neurological consequences of capillary stalling across multiple mouse models of brain disease, including Alzheimer's disease, stroke, and traumatic brain injury. We conclude by suggesting necessary next steps in instrumentation and analysis for studying capillary stalling, as well as how to address key unanswered questions about underlying mechanisms for capillary stalling in the brain and how this phenomenon may impact disease progression and cognitive function.

articles.title: Influence of particle size and metal–support interactions on nitroarene reductive amination over Pd/TiO 2 catalysts
articles.abstract: Pd/TiO 2 catalysts enable mild reductive amination of aromatic and bio-based aldehydes. Particle size control and SMSI enhance amine selectivity, boost turnover frequency nearly 200-fold, and support reuse.

articles.title: CRISPR mutagenesis of the MYC locus reveals a druggable ultraconserved RNA element
articles.abstract: CRISPR tiling mutagenesis of the 10-kb human MYC locus mapped the fitness landscape of an entire human gene at base-pair resolution. This unbiased interrogation revealed that 67% of functionally essential base pairs are noncoding. An ultraconserved RNA regulatory element was identified that controls MYC localization and can be therapeutically targeted to suppress cancer cell growth in patient-derived tumor organoids.

articles.title: 5-Azacytidine incorporation into mRNAs disrupts translation and induces ribosome collisions
articles.abstract: 5-Azacytidine (5-AzaC) is a cytidine analog chemotherapeutic widely used to treat myeloid malignancies. Although its activity is primarily attributed to DNA hypomethylation, the majority of 5-AzaC is incorporated into RNA, where its functional consequences are less understood. Here, we show that 5-AzaC treatment of cells leads to inhibition of protein synthesis. Ribo-seq, Disome-seq, and RNA-seq in treated cells exhibit a time-dependent C-to-G conversion in mRNAs. These conversion events are enriched within footprint positions corresponding to the A-site of monosomes or stalled leading ribosomes in a disome complex. Footprints are accumulated at sites with C-rich codons in the A-site, with particular emphasis on the second codon position. Consistent with disome-mediated signaling, 5-AzaC activates ZAK- and GCN2-dependent stress responses. Furthermore, loss of the ribosome-associated quality control factor, ZNF598, sensitizes cells to 5-AzaC. These findings suggest that translation disruption represents an additional layer of 5-AzaC's mechanism of action, alongside its known DNA-mediated effects.

articles.title: A hierarchical regulatory cascade programs chlamydospore formation in the nematode-trapping fungus Arthrobotrys flagrans
articles.abstract: Chlamydospores provide durable stress tolerance for fungal survival and enable shelf-stable biocontrol agents, yet their genetic regulation in fungi remains poorly understood. Here, using the nematode-trapping fungus Arthrobotrys flagrans as a model, we define a hierarchical regulatory cascade for chlamydospore formation. LaeA mediates H3K9 monomethylation to license this developmental program. Furthermore, we identify VeA and Ste12 as LaeA partners, and the importin KapA as a nuclear gatekeeper. This upstream module activates VosA/VelB, which induces AbaA/StuA to control the effectors ChsG, McdD, and McdD-modified glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins for chlamydospore cell wall biogenesis. The expression levels of regulators within this regulatory cascade (LaeA/VeA/Ste12-VosA/VelB-StuA/AbaA-ChsG and McdD) determine chlamydospore yield and convert environmental cues into differentiation. This framework guides strain engineering for high-yield chlamydospore production and suggests a regulatory paradigm potentially conserved across fungi.

articles.title: A single-cell atlas of pediatric undifferentiated recurrent fever reveals candidate immune regulators
articles.abstract: Children with periodic fever syndromes not attributable to infections, rheumatic disorders, malignancies, or known monogenic autoinflammatory conditions are classified as "syndrome of undifferentiated recurrent fever" (SURF). To date, treatment remains empirical, often resulting in only a partial response, underscoring the unmet clinical need for new therapeutic strategies. To advance the molecular understanding of SURF, we generated a large-scale single-cell RNA-seq immune atlas of 29 SURF patients with more than 200,000 cells. Comparison of patients with three healthy cohorts revealed large-scale metabolic shifts together with a distinct cytokine signature already observable during afebrile periods. This indicates that afebrile SURF cannot be considered a less inflammatory resting state but rather as a distinct homeostatic state. Furthermore, our analysis suggests an NAMPT-mediated autocrine feedback loop connecting the metabolic dysregulations with the pro-inflammatory phenotype in monocytes. This study offers insights into the SURF immunopathology and generates testable hypotheses to guide future therapies.

articles.title: Clearing perivascular light chain-derived amyloid to counteract aging-associated decline in liver regeneration
articles.abstract: Aging impairs organ regeneration, with insufficient angiogenesis as a key contributor. Here, we show that the endothelial immunoproteasome subunit PSMB8 is upregulated in aged mouse livers after partial hepatectomy. Endothelial PSMB8 deletion or PR-957 inhibition promotes angiogenesis and rescues liver regeneration. diGly proteomics identifies TAZ (transcriptional co-activator with PDZ-binding motif) as a ubiquitin-dependent immunoproteasome substrate, and TAZ activation restores aged liver regeneration. Aging triggers the infiltration of CD38+IGLC1+ IgM B cells and aberrant perivascular light chain-derived amyloid deposition in the liver. Recombinant light chain-derived amyloid fibrils directly induce PSMB8 expression in vitro. Anselamimab-mediated light chain-derived amyloid clearance mitigates immunoproteasome overactivation and restores regeneration. Single-cell RNA sequencing confirms that anselamimab reverses aging-induced endothelial marker loss and inflammatory gene upregulation. Our findings establish a pathway linking perivascular light chain-derived amyloid deposition to regenerative decline via endothelial immunoproteasome activation, suggesting amyloid clearance as a promising therapeutic strategy for aging-associated decline in liver regeneration.

articles.title: Exosome secretion is required for Sonic Hedgehog dispersal and signal gradient formation in the embryonic limb bud mesenchyme
articles.abstract: Carrier-assisted diffusion and cytoneme transport help disperse Hedgehog morphogens across diverse embryonic tissues, yet their relative contributions to patterning mesenchymal tissues remain poorly understood. Here, we combine signaling assays with quantitative microscopy to establish exosome secretion as a major mechanism for Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) dispersal. Using a synchronous release system to visualize Shh trafficking, we demonstrate that Shh traffics through the exosome biogenesis pathway in limb bud mesenchymal cells. Shh-bound exosomes diffuse through extracellular space and also bind and travel along cytonemes, providing two alternative modes of transport. We show that exosome secretion is essential to establish short-range Shh signaling gradients in vitro and contributes to shaping Shh protein gradients in the limb bud in vivo. We propose that exosome-based Shh secretion, combined with different modes of extracellular transport, provides a tunable mechanism to sculpt Shh gradients across different length and time scales.

articles.title: Hyperosmotic stress induces rewiring of 3D chromatin interactions
articles.abstract: Cells continually face environmental stressors that challenge homeostasis, yet how three-dimensional (3D) chromatin structure contributes to these stress responses remains unclear under hyperosmotic conditions. To investigate this, we map 3D chromatin structure, its molecular drivers, and transcriptional outcomes during sorbitol-induced hyperosmotic stress. Within 1 hour of sorbitol treatment, pre-existing loops and domains collapse, while several hundred de novo sorbitol-induced loops emerge. These loops are punctate, longer-range, and transient. 3D chromatin structure largely returns to baseline conditions by 24 hours. Loop reorganization is consistent across cell types and hyperosmotic stimuli. Sorbitol-induced loops require cohesin but not CTCF, and anchors are enriched at active promoters harboring GC-rich transcription factor motifs. Genes at these anchors show delayed activation following loop formation, consistent with loops acting upstream of transcription. Together, hyperosmotic stress triggers rapid, reversible, CTCF-independent chromatin reorganization that correlates with transcriptional adaptation.

articles.title: Intermittent fasting enhances muscle regeneration via an EDA2R-NIK-myomixer axis
Plagl2 reprograms adult mouse retinal Müller glia for proliferation and injury-enhanced neurogenic competence
articles.abstract: Müller glia (MG) in the adult mammalian retina have long been recognized as a potential endogenous source for the regeneration of lost retinal neurons. However, existing MG reprogramming strategies yield an incomplete regenerative response by favoring either proliferation or neurogenic differentiation. Here, we show that the zinc-finger transcription factor gene Plagl2, previously shown to reactivate quiescent neural stem cells, is sufficient to reprogram adult mouse MG into a progenitor-like state with coupled proliferative and neurogenic competence. Using histology, time-lapse imaging, and single-cell transcriptomics, we find that Plagl2 drives regulated rounds of MG cell cycle re-entry, while N-methyl-D-aspartate-induced retinal injury further promotes the acquisition of neurogenic competence biased toward inner nuclear layer neuronal identities. These findings indicate that Plagl2 regulates mammalian MG reprogramming, and supports a broader approach to tissue regeneration through the adaptation of reprogramming modules across distinct cell types.

articles.title: Programmed bacterial lysis in vivo alters host immune responses and microbial pathogenesis
articles.abstract: Vibrio cholerae injects toxic type VI secretion system (T6SS) effectors to lyse sensitive intestinal commensals, but how this bacterial antagonism enhances mucosal host immune responses and its pathogenicity remains unknown. To mimic T6SS-mediated killing, we engineered V. cholerae lysis strains by using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) to knockdown essential genes in peptidoglycan biogenesis or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) transport. Our results indicate that controlled bacterial lysis in vivo leads to divergent mucosal immune responses that directly modulate colonization and pathogenicity of a bystander, non-lysing V. cholerae ΔT6SS strain. Mass spectrometric analysis of the lysis debris revealed proinflammatory muropeptides correlating with these changes. We confirmed that oral co-administration of a synthetic peptidoglycan-derived metabolite with a V. cholerae ΔT6SS mutant, but not the wild type, shows dramatic enhancement of disease symptoms. These findings show that intestinal exposure to discrete bacterial cell wall metabolites can differentially modulate host innate immune responses and consequently bacterial pathogenesis.

articles.title: Tau-driven hyperexcitability of locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons underlies sleep fragmentation and cognitive decline in mice
articles.abstract: Early sleep disruption is a hallmark of preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD), but its underlying mechanisms are unclear. The locus coeruleus (LC) dopamine-β-hydroxylase noradrenergic (LCDBH) neurons are vulnerable to early tau pathology in AD. Using P301S transgenic mice and cell-type-specific tau overexpression models, we show that pathological tau accumulation selectively increases the intrinsic excitability of LCDBH neurons. Tau-induced neuronal hyperactivity disrupts sleep homeostasis, reduces non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and slow-wave activity, increases sleep fragmentation and microarousals, and delays both anesthetic induction and sleep onset. Furthermore, tau overexpression in LCDBH neurons leads to significant recognition memory deficits. Notably, optogenetic suppression of LCDBH-tau neuronal activity reverses sleep disturbances and rescues cognitive dysfunction. Our findings demonstrate that tau-driven hyperexcitability of LCDBH neurons is a core driver of early sleep and cognitive impairments in AD, providing a mechanistic insight and potential target for preclinical AD treatment.

articles.title: Temporal shifts in post-asthmatic immune responses define tumor outcomes via strain-specific monocyte reprogramming
articles.abstract: Epidemiological evidence linking asthma to lung cancer risk remains contradictory, presenting asthma as either a risk factor or a protective condition. We hypothesize that this heterogeneity stems from the temporal dynamics of inflammatory response and host genetic background. Using ovalbumin (OVA)-induced asthma models, we identify a temporal shift in immune effectors driving post-asthmatic tumorigenesis. During acute airway inflammation, eosinophil infiltration accelerates tumor growth across mouse strains. Following resolution, however, tumorigenic outcomes in recovery diverge along genetic lines. Prior asthma reshapes chromatin landscapes of bone marrow myeloid progenitors, establishing innate immune memory that differentially programs monocytes across strains. In C57BL/6 mice, trained monocytes adopt oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), acquiring a suppressive, tissue-remodeling phenotype that promotes tumor progression. Conversely, BALB/c-trained monocytes utilize glycolysis to maintain a pro-phagocytic state, enabling tumor clearance. These findings delineate a biphasic mechanism wherein temporal shifts in post-asthmatic immune responses define tumor outcomes via strain-specific monocyte metabolic reprogramming.

articles.title: The YAP/TAZ-Tgfbr2-stiffness feedback loop governs divergent cell fates of muscle-resident mesenchymal progenitors
articles.abstract: Mesenchymal progenitors are essential for muscle regeneration, but also contribute to fat accumulation and fibrosis. Several extrinsic and intrinsic factors regulating adipogenic or fibrogenic differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors have been identified. However, it remains unclear how different cues are integrated to determine cell fate. Here, we demonstrate that interstitial stiffness and the mechanosensitive hippo pathway regulate mesenchymal progenitor cell fate. Fat accumulation model reduced interstitial stiffness and nuclear YAP/TAZ-positive mesenchymal progenitors compared with a regeneration model, whereas YAP/TAZ deficiency in mesenchymal progenitors enhanced fat deposition. Mechanistically, YAP/TAZ induced expression of the anti-adipogenic genes Aldh1a2 and Wnt5a, and the pro-fibrogenic gene Tgfbr2, which mediates TGF-β binding. Loss of Tgfbr2 in mesenchymal progenitors reduced transient collagen deposition, decreased stiffness, and increased fat accumulation during regeneration. We propose a stiffness-YAP/TAZ-Tgfbr2-collagen regulatory loop governing mesenchymal progenitor cell fate and highlight its importance for optimal muscle regeneration.

articles.title: eHLAstic reveals an extended canonical and non-canonical HLA-E immunopeptidome in human cancers
articles.abstract: HLA-E is a non-classical MHC class I molecule with restricted polymorphism, offering a putative path to broadly applicable off-the-shelf therapies. Yet, the wider HLA-E peptide repertoire remains poorly defined and is largely assumed restricted to signal peptide-derived sequences. We developed eHLAstic, a dedicated HLA-E-binding predictor, that improved the precision of HLA-E ligand discovery almost 3-fold compared with existing approaches. Using eHLAstic and orthogonal biochemical validation, we report 30 previously unrecognized canonical and non-canonical HLA-E-associated peptides, including six cancer-restricted ligands detected in acute lymphoblastic and myeloid leukemia but not healthy blood or bone marrow cells. Most identified ligands were shared across individuals with diverse HLA backgrounds and were detected across hematological and solid cancers. All but one non-canonical ligands were detected exclusively in cancer-associated samples and not in healthy tissues. These findings redefine the HLA-E ligandome and uncover canonical and non-canonical HLA-E ligands with potential for immune recognition and therapeutic targeting.

Perivascular macrophages restrict CXCR4-dependent accumulation of stem-like CD8+ T cells in tumors and limit chemotherapy efficacy
articles.abstract: Cheung et al. show that HO-1 expressed by PvTAMs restricts the post-chemotherapy accumulation of stem-like CD8+ T cells in the TME. These cells enter tumors through a CXCR4-dependent pathway associated with chemotherapy-expanded CXCL12+ PvCAFs. Once within the TME, they differentiate into anti-tumor effectors, contributing to durable anti-tumor immunity.

articles.title: Annulation reactions by intramolecular cross-electrophile coupling
articles.abstract: Intramolecular cross-electrophile coupling (iXEC) offers a unified strategy for building semisaturated rings directly from simple dielectrophiles. This work establishes conditions that generate persistent nickel intermediates capable of rapid radical capture through solvent-controlled activation of aryl and alkyl electrophiles. The approach enables efficient access to heteroaromatic, spirocyclic, and macrocyclic compounds under mild conditions, thus providing a broadly applicable platform for pharmaceuticals and natural products where arrays of diverse ring systems can be synthesized from a single core.

articles.title: Atom transfer radical polymerization for sustainable processes and materials
articles.abstract: Atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) combines increasingly sustainable polymerization processes with precise macromolecular engineering to create materials with extended lifetimes, improved circularity, and advanced functions for energy technologies. This perspective discusses recent advances and future opportunities for greener, scalable ATRP processes and the design of high-performance polymeric materials that integrate functionality and sustainability.

articles.title: Cellular protein delivery through cell-penetrating peptide-mediated water pores driven by membrane potential
articles.abstract: Combining quantitative live-cell imaging, electrophysiology, and atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, we establish a mechanism by which CPP additives drive the direct translocation of proteins across cellular membranes through membrane potential-dependent water pores. This framework provides a basis for intracellular delivery of protein therapeutics to expand access to intracellular, previously undruggable targets.

articles.title: Photocatalytic therapy via cross-coupling hydrogen evolution in cancer cells
articles.abstract: Zhou et al. develop an oxygen-independent photocatalytic strategy that converts glutathione to its oxidized form while generating hydrogen in cancer cells, thereby disrupting the intracellular redox balance. This catalytic redox remodeling induces ferroptosis and antitumor immune activation, establishing an oxygen-independent mode of photocatalytic cancer therapy.

articles.title: Predicting battery stability from electron-ion transport mismatch
articles.abstract: A battery stability prediction model covering LIBs, SIBs, and ZIBs has been proposed. The electron-ion transport mismatch is identified as a key determinant of battery stability. A linear correlation between the battery stability and the electron-ion transport mismatch has been revealed: the closer the transport rates of electrons and ions, the more stable the battery. The battery stability could be predicted rapidly from the electron-ion mismatch, with no need for time-consuming long-term cycling.

articles.title: Atomic-Scale Origin of Spatially Heterogeneous Insertion in Hollandite-Type MnO2
articles.abstract: Hollandite-type α-MnO2 is a prototypical tunnel-structured host for rechargeable batteries, yet the atomic-scale mechanisms governing multivalent-ion insertion remain poorly understood. Here, we reveal how guest-ion species dictate electrochemical reaction pathways through distinct occupation modes within the one-dimensional tunnels of α-MnO2. By combining electrochemical analyses, atomic-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy, and soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we directly correlate reaction kinetics with guest-ion configurations and the accompanying structural and electronic responses of the host framework. Electrochemical measurements reveal substantial diffusion-controlled contributions for both Na+ and Mg2+, whereas Ca2+ exhibits predominantly surface-controlled behavior. Atomic-resolution imaging demonstrates that, despite their comparable macroscopic kinetic contributions, Na+ and Mg2+ exhibit distinctly different microscopic insertion modes: Na+ homogeneously occupies the tunnel-center sites throughout the particles, whereas Mg2+ occupies both tunnel-center and off-center sites, with pronounced near-surface enrichment accompanied by local tunnel distortion. In contrast, the Ca2+ reaction is largely confined to the near-surface region, with no clearly detectable occupation of the internal tunnel sites. Soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy further reveals spatially heterogeneous Mn reduction, with more pronounced reduction near the structurally less constrained particle surface. These results establish a direct relationship between guest-ion occupation modes, electrochemical reaction pathways, and the resulting structural evolution, providing an atomic-scale design principle for engineering tunnel-type host materials for multivalent-ion insertion.

articles.title: Electronic Structure Perspective on Cation and Anion Redox in Li2FeS2
articles.abstract: Multielectron redox in Li2FeS2 involves both cation and anion contributions. While prior studies have investigated this process experimentally, questions remain about the Fe-to-S redox transition, persulfide formation, and incomplete delithiation. Here, we revisit the electrochemistry of Li2FeS2 using density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Initial Fe oxidation is shown to proceed via increased Fe−S covalency driven by ligand-to-metal rehybridization. This accounts for only ∼60% of the Fe capacity, after which phase separation into Li1.5FeS2 and Li0.5FeS2 induces a shift to S oxidation. We identify nonbonding S 3p orbitals as redox-active centers. To track their evolution during delithiation, we isolate the localized nonbonding states by subtracting the bonding and antibonding contributions from the total electronic densities of states. These orbitals undergo S-to-Fe rehybridization, progressive oxidation, and eventual reorganization into persulfide bonds. At high states of charge, Li vacancies enable FeS4 tilting and facilitate S−S bond formation. Further delithiation beyond Li0.5FeS2 would require unstable S hole formation or conversion to pyrite FeS2, explaining why it is challenging to fully delithiate this material. These findings offer insights into the interplay of cation and anion redox, guiding the design of high-capacity sulfide cathodes.

articles.title: Microenvironment-Responsive Polyaniline− Gelatin Conductive Hydrogel Promotes Infected Diabetic Wound Healing by Modulating Skin-Resident Cells Behavior
articles.abstract: Diabetic wound healing is severely impaired by persistent inflammation, bacterial infection, impaired angiogenesis, and especially disrupted bioelectrical signaling. Conductive hydrogels can help restore local bioelectrical signal transmission and provide an attractive strategy for intractable wound healing by modulating the behaviors of bioelectrically responsive skin-resident cells. Here, we developed a glucose/pH-responsive polyaniline− gelatin conductive hydrogel (HGP@D) based on double dynamic covalent crosslinking of the imine bond and boronic ester bond for promoting the Staphylococcus aureus-infected full-thickness diabetic wound healing. The HGP@D hydrogel had strong mechanical property, great tissue adhesive strength, glucose/pH dual-responsive drug release behavior, alongside robust broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, and potent intracellular antioxidation. The HGP@D hydrogel restored local bioelectrical signaling and created an anti-inflammatory wound microenvironment, thereby modulating the behaviors of skin-resident cells involved in diabetic wound repair, including fibroblast migration, macrophage M2-like polarization, and endothelial angiogenic activity. Mechanistic analyses suggested that the HGP@D hydrogel promoted infected diabetic wound healing through two Ca2+-associated regulatory axes: the Ca2+/CaMKKβ/AMPK/NF-κB axis for inflammatory regulation and the Ca2+/PI3K/Akt/mTOR/HIF-1α/VEGF axis for angiogenesis and tissue reconstruction. Overall, HGP@D provides a promising clinical therapeutic strategy for the advanced healing of diabetic wounds and other non-healing wounds by integrating glucose/pH-responsive microenvironment regulation with bioelectrical modulation.

articles.title: Predator Becomes Prey: Records of Intraguild Predation Between Velvet Worms (Onychophora) and Arthropods (Arthropoda) With an Expanded Review of Predation on Velvet Worms
articles.abstract: From 3954 citizen‐science observations screened, we report novel cases of predation by omnivorous arthropods on velvet worms, including the first confirmed records for harvestmen and a cave wētā. Using photographic evidence derived from citizen‐science observations, we document multiple predation events involving harvestmen (Opiliones: Cranaidae and Triaenonychidae) and a cave wētā (Orthoptera: Rhaphidophoridae), encompassing both intraguild predation and higher‐order opportunistic predation within cryptic terrestrial habitats. These interactions represent previously undocumented trophic links between phylogenetically distant lineages and expand the known repertoire of omnivorous arthropods as predators of onychophorans. Our findings document a previously unrecorded vulnerability in Onychophora, a group traditionally regarded as specialized predators defended by an adhesive slime system, and underscore the trophic flexibility of arthropod predators operating within leaf‐litter and subterranean ecosystems. Collectively, these observations document previously unrecorded trophic links in cryptic environments and illustrate the value of natural history data and citizen‐science platforms for detecting rarely documented interactions.

Co-producing ‘nature’: autonomous grazing in the Dutch Room for the River programme
articles.abstract: Conservation biology has traditionally sought to justify public investment made specifically for biodiversity. I explore an alternative proposition: whether biodiversity can be co-produced through investments that society already undertakes for other public purposes. Using the Dutch Room for the River programme as a case study, I examine how autonomous grazing contributes to the long-term management and functional improvement of restored river wetlands created primarily to improve flood safety. Rather than evaluating autonomous grazing as a restoration philosophy, I analyse it as a management technology operating within contractual hydraulic boundary conditions defined by the national river management authority. This study demonstrates that self-organising groups of large herbivores can maintain floodplain vegetation within prescribed hydraulic limits whilst contributing to wetland functions and reducing the need for repeated mechanical intervention. Nationally standardised Dutch cost estimates indicate that vegetation management based predominantly on autonomous grazing costs approximately one quarter as much as management relying largely on repeated mowing and biomass removal. Biodiversity therefore emerges not as the primary objective of public investment, but as a valuable co-produced public good arising from the management of an engineered landscape. This study also illustrates the practical application of the Ecosystem Approach adopted under the Convention on Biological Diversity. Indeed, a clearly defined societal choice (flood protection) can be achieved through management that allows self-organising ecological processes to contribute simultaneously to economic efficiency, wetland functioning and biodiversity. It demonstrates that biodiversity need not always justify public investment, but can instead emerge as a valuable co-produced public good.

articles.title: The price of adulthood: ontogenetic patterns of mandibular wear in a drywood termite
articles.abstract: IntroductionIn eusocial insects, the division of labor often entails significant mechanical costs for working individuals. In one-piece nesting termites, such as the Chilean endemic drywood termite, Neotermes chilensis, the colony's labor is performed by totipotent immatures that inhabit and consume structurally sound wood. This translates directly into severe mandibular wear. While the intense wood-processing activity of immatures has traditionally been viewed as an altruistic behavior that benefits the colony, recent evolutionary frameworks suggest it may represent a selfish developmental cost, the mechanical "price of adulthood", to fuel their own ontogeny into winged reproductives (alates). Conversely, alates, which can no longer molt to renew cuticular structures, must preserve their mandibles to excavate a nuptial chamber and found a new colony.MethodsTo investigate this, we quantified structural wear using a Mandibular Wear Index (MWI) and high-resolution scanning electron microscopy (SEM) across different developmental stages and sexes of N. chilensis (N = 147). To rule out size-related allometric artifacts, absolute mandibular dimensions were evaluated using an interactive Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) log -log model and estimated marginal means at a standardized common size (512.4 µm).ResultsOur results revealed no sexual dimorphism in wear but highly significant differences among castes that persisted independently of absolute mandibular size. Nymphs exhibited the most severe mandibular wear, consistent with their feeding activity to sustain energetic developmental demands. In stark contrast, swarmed alates possessed the sharpest, least worn mandibles. Primary reproductives and pseudergates displayed intermediate levels of wear.DiscussionThese findings reveal a caste-specific balance between mandibular wear in working immatures and preservation of mandibular structure in adult dispersers.

articles.title: Tumor-to-dendritic cell reprogramming induces immunogenic lymphoid structures across cancers
articles.abstract: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) support effective cancer immunity but remain difficult to induce experimentally. Ascic, Chatelain, et al. establish tumor-to-cDC1 reprogramming as a strategy to generate immunogenic TLSs across multiple cancers, uncovering how localized migratory cDC1 and CD40-dependent T cell interactions coordinate local and systemic cellular and humoral immunity.

articles.title: Why sulfur stays present but inaccessible in practical lithium-sulfur pouch cells
articles.abstract: Sulfur can remain physically present in a lithium-sulfur pouch cell while becoming electrochemically inaccessible. This perspective links local electrolyte availability and the transport of lithium ions and soluble sulfur species to sulfur conversion, lithium-metal degradation, and variations in pressure and temperature. Two qualitative diagnostic questions and a staged validation protocol guide regional failure analysis and the translation of laboratory strategies into practical cells.
