articles.title: CARTnet: Template-guided B-cell Epitope Prediction with Contact-aware Attention
articles.abstract: B-cell epitope prediction remains challenging due to the limited availability of experimentally characterized data and the incomplete understanding of antibody-antigen recognition. Here, we present CARTnet, a novel contact-aware deep learning framework that integrates multimodal features and template-derived epitope information. CARTnet demonstrated superior performance when compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods across most evaluation metrics on both the internal and external test datasets. In particular, CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.243 on the internal test set, compared with 0.220 for DiscoTope-3, 0.140 for BepiPred-2, and 0.198 for BepiPred-3. This improvement was also observed on the external test set, where CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.267, compared with 0.192, 0.111, and 0.215 for DiscoTope-3, BepiPred-2, and BepiPred-3, respectively, supporting its generalizability. CARTnet also supports template-guided prediction, in which limited prior epitope information can improve the identification of additional epitope residues; a single template residue increased the AUPRC of the template-based variant from 0.225 to 0.403 on the internal test set. Furthermore, we demonstrated that epitope information from closely related viruses can be transferred across the genus Alphavirus to improve epitope prediction accuracy. These results establish CARTnet as an accurate framework for both de novo and template-guided B-cell epitope prediction.

articles.title: Can the Human Plastisphere Account for the Rise of Type 1 Diabetes: A Computational Molecular Mimicry Study
articles.abstract: An increased incidence of childhood type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) has been widely documented, but its pathophysiological origins are poorly understood. The post-World War II expansion of the plastics industry in the United States and elsewhere coincides with a marked increase in T1DM incidence; however, no pathophysiological mechanism has been proposed that could justify such a temporal correlation. Here, we leverage recent advances in artificial intelligence and protein structure prediction and binding to show that molecular mimicry is a plausible pathophysiological mechanism for plastic fragments to induce onset of T1DM for individuals with certain HLA haplotypes. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.

articles.title: CloneVI: A deep generative model for deciphering the relationships between cell state and mitochondrial genotype
articles.abstract: Cellular diversity arises from both genetic lineages and non-genetic regulation of cell states, and knowing which cell states are tied to lineages is central to understanding how clones shape disease. Single-cell multi-omics technologies measure mitochondrial DNA mutations together with gene expression or chromatin accessibility in the same cells, but clones are usually inferred from mutations alone, making such clones difficult to identify. We developed CloneVI, a deep generative model that infers clonal structure from a latent cell state derived from gene expression or chromatin accessibility. It estimates the clonal probability of each cell from this cell state, together with the allele frequency of each clone by reconstructing the observed mutation counts. In simulated data, CloneVI recovered the ground-truth clonal structure in both single-clone and mixed-clone cell populations. In clonal hematopoiesis single-cell RNA-seq data with enriched mitochondrial transcripts, the inferred clones were associated with specific mitochondrial DNA mutations, and some of them showed high expression of a T-cell receptor variable-region gene. In chronic lymphocytic leukemia mitochondrial single-cell ATAC-seq data, CloneVI separated populations with different heteroplasmy levels and identified increased PAX9 accessibility. In a multi-donor ovarian tumor cohort, CloneVI captured mutant-cell populations enriched in particular cell states, and a differential test weighted by the clonal probability revealed the transcription factor activity of the cell state in which the mutant cells concentrated. CloneVI thus identifies populations defined by mitochondrial DNA mutations and associated with cell states in single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data. CloneVI is available at https://github.com/TaichiHIBI/cloneVI.

articles.title: Comparative Transcriptomic Analysis of Gene Expression Patterns in Neutrophils from Rheumatoid Arthritis and COVID-19
articles.abstract: Background: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disorder characterised by chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation, and neutrophils play a key role in its progression. COVID-19 also involves neutrophil hyperactivation that contributes to severe immune responses. Emerging evidence links COVID-19 to increased incidence or exacerbation of RA, potentially through overlapping immune mechanisms. Objective: To compare neutrophil transcriptomic profiles in RA and COVID-19 and identify shared immune pathways and disease-specific features. Methods: Publicly available neutrophil RNA-seq count data from the Gene Expression Omnibus were analysed: RA versus healthy controls (GSE116899) and COVID-19 versus healthy controls (GSE212041). A second COVID-19 comparison (severe versus convalescent) was assembled from GSE272381 and GSE227116. Differential expression was analysed with DESeq2, pathway enrichment with fgsea (Hallmark gene sets) and topGO (Gene Ontology biological process and molecular function). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were compared between diseases by direction of change. Results: In RA neutrophils, 11,355 DEGs were identified, of which 90 had an absolute log2 fold change of at least 2 with p<0.05 (70 upregulated, 20 downregulated). Twenty-four Hallmark gene sets were positively enriched at adjusted p<0.05, led by interferon alpha and interferon gamma responses, and Gene Ontology analysis highlighted type I interferon, antiviral and double-stranded RNA terms. In COVID-19 neutrophils, 420 DEGs were identified (37 upregulated, 383 downregulated), and no Hallmark gene set reached adjusted p<0.05. Of the 90 RA DEGs, 46 changed in the same direction in COVID-19 without reaching significance, and 27 changed significantly in the opposite direction, including CAMK1G, SIGLEC1, OAS1 and OAS3. In the second COVID-19 comparison, several of these genes, including OAS1, OAS3 and SIGLEC1, changed in the same direction as in RA. Conclusions: RA neutrophils show a transcriptional programme enriched for interferon and antiviral-response pathways. Part of the RA signature is shared with COVID-19 neutrophils, while a subset of genes diverges, and this divergence depended on the COVID-19 comparison used. These findings are hypothesis-generating and provide candidate genes for experimental validation.

articles.title: Cross-cancer knowledge transfer for lymph node metastasis prediction: Applicability of an axillary lymph node-based deep learning model
articles.abstract: Evaluation of lymph node (LN) metastasis is critical for cancer staging and treatment planning. Since radiologic hallmarks of metastatic LNs are shared across primary cancers, a computed tomography (CT)-based deep learning (DL) classifier developed from one anatomy may transfer to others. This study built a DenseNet-121 ensemble model using clinical-implication-applied preprocessing and evaluated its cross-anatomical generalizability to LNs from diverse primary cancers. A DenseNet-121 ensemble model combining fixed-size cropping (FSC) and adjustable square cropping (ASC) was trained from ImageNet initialization on an axillary lymph node (ALN) dataset (n = 1,128 from 523 breast cancer patients). The model utilized clinical-implication-applied perinodal cropping with bicubic filtering and standardized resizing. To test cross-anatomical generalizability, an external dataset of 256 CT images across four anatomical regions was evaluated: cervical, mediastinal, upper-abdominal, and lower-abdominal LNs. Perinodal free margins were systematically varied from 10% to 40% to optimize the balance between context preservation and surround interference. Bicubic filtering and standardized resizing yielded the highest internal performance on the original ALN dataset (FSC-ASC ensemble area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.958, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.920–0.987 at 40% margin). The model demonstrated site-dependent, above-chance generalizability across all external regions. Cervical LNs achieved the highest performance at a 40% margin (AUROC 0.939, 95% CI 0.875–0.989). Mediastinal LNs peaked at a 10% margin (AUROC 0.796, 95% CI 0.672–0.903), with wider margins degrading performance due to adjacent structural interference. Upper-abdominal and lower-abdominal LNs reached optimal performance at a 30% margin (AUROC 0.814 for upper; AUROC 0.917 for lower). A single ALN-trained DL model can accurately predict LN metastasis across cervical, mediastinal, and abdominal stations through site-specific perinodal margin tuning. These findings support the feasibility of cross-cancer knowledge transfer and the clinical utility of generalizable backbones for pan-cancer nodal assessment. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.

articles.title: Deep Recovery of Effective Migration Surfaces
articles.abstract: The isolation-by-distance (IBD) principle describes the tendency for genetic relatedness to decline with geographic distance. Although the existence IBD has long been documented in natural populations, recent analyses of spatially referenced genotype data have shown that the strength of this relationship can vary across a landscape due to geographic barriers, habitat compatibility, or other factors. Effective migration surfaces (EMS) have emerged as a popular exploratory tool for visualizing spatial patterns in IBD. However, fitting likelihood-based EMS models is often computationally demanding, requiring repeated large-scale matrix calculations. Here, we introduce Deep Recovery of Effective Migration Surfaces (dreems), a graph neural network for amortized inference of effective migration surfaces. dreems maps genetic covariance and sampling locations directly to an effective migration surface, while simultaneously providing predictive uncertainty estimates. Once trained, the network accommodates different graph sizes and sampling designs without needing to re-train. Across independent coalescent simulations that were not seen during training, dreems has roughly 10-30% lower estimation error compared to a state-of-the-art likelihood-based method, with the largest gains observed under sparse sampling designs that are commonly encountered in practice. Reanalysis of several published datasets recovers spatial patterns that are broadly consistent with earlier likelihood-based estimates, while reducing computation time by orders of magnitude. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. National Institute of General Medical Sciences, https://ror.org/04q48ey07, R35GM151145, R35GM137919

articles.title: Deterministic DNA-first discovery reveals recurrent genomic architectures
articles.abstract: Genome mining typically begins with known genes or protein families, which can make systems defined primarily by genomic organization difficult to detect. We developed a DNA-first framework combining asymmetric-covariance natural-vector representations with generic positional recurrence, joining separately calibrated signals through genomic coordinates. In benchmarks of array-associated reverse transcriptase (ART) loci, the target-free mathematical arm localized seven of eight predeclared loci, including all seven with exact-array coordinates. Dual-arm signals occurred in none of three non-array RT controls and in one of five UG27 systems, indicating selectivity within these small control sets. A separate profile-guided search of 6.12 Gb identified five candidate array-associated RT-like systems. In an independent 54.38-Gb evaluation of this profile-guided arm, structural compatibility was 24/32 under a historical-rule mirror, 12/32 after novelty-only selection, and 0/17 for architecture-selected complete ORFs; the two 32-member panels shared six exact sequences. Together, these results suggest that mathematical features of raw DNA can complement protein-directed searches in nominating genomic architectures for experimental RNA-to-DNA studies.

articles.title: Direct NMR evidence for transient binding of the vesicular SNARE protein synaptobrevin-2/VAMP2 to the α-synuclein C-terminus
articles.abstract: The protein α-synuclein (α-syn) plays a central role in several neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's disease; however, its physiological function remains enigmatic. We provide direct evidence by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, microscale thermophoresis (MST), and biolayer interferometry (BLI) measurements that the α-synuclein C-terminus binds to the vesicular SNARE (soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor) protein synaptobrevin-2 (syb-2), also known as VAMP2 (vesicle-associated membrane protein). The observed dissociation constant (Kd) in the 10 - 50 micromolar range falls within the estimated concentration range of α-synuclein in neurons, while local concentrations may be substantially higher. NMR chemical shift perturbation (CSP) and paramagnetic relaxation enhancement (PRE) experiments mapped the binding site with residue-specific resolution to the α-synuclein C-terminus (V118 - E137) and to the synaptobrevin-2 SNARE motif/linker domain interface (region A82 - K87), and also affected the synaptobrevin-2 N-terminus (M1 - S2). NMR CSPs and PREs indicate a transient interaction in the fast exchange (μs-ms) regime. These transient weak binding interactions are characteristic of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and allow both proteins to engage in multiple binding interactions, thereby enabling α-synuclein to play a regulatory role upstream of or during neuronal exocytosis. While the exact physiological role of α-synuclein remains debated, the involvement of its pathological form in several neurodegenerative diseases (dubbed synucleinopathies) is well established. Our data suggest a direct link between proteins involved in neurodegeneration and neuronal exocytosis.

articles.title: Disentangling Context-Specific Alzheimer's Disease Progression Signatures through an Explainable AI Framework
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression involves stage-dependent transcriptional changes that are often masked by dominant cellular and biological variation. Here, we present ADVISE (Alzheimer's Disease Variational Isolation of Signal Embeddings), an interpretable deep generative framework designed to disentangle Braak stage-associated transcriptional signals from background biological variation through separate latent representations. Using explainable AI, ADVISE prioritizes genes and pathways contributing to the disease-specific representation. Applying ADVISE to large-scale single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from the human prefrontal cortex, we identify shared and context-specific signatures of AD progression across global, sex-specific, and cell-type-specific analyses, revealing convergent molecular programs involving synaptic transmission, HSF1-associated proteostatic stress responses, and SLIT/ROBO axon guidance. Notably, ADVISE prioritizes ROBO2 as a progression-associated candidate in excitatory neurons. Experimental validation using CRISPR activation in hiPSC-derived excitatory neurons demonstrates that ROBO2 activation reduces the phosphorylated Tau-to-total Tau ratio. ADVISE thus reveals context-dependent molecular signatures of AD progression and bridges human single-cell discoveries with experimental validation of candidate regulators of AD pathology. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.

articles.title: Disulfide Crosslink Density is a Key Determinant in the Formation, Dynamics, and Maturation of Cysteine-rich Designer Biomolecular Condensates.
articles.abstract: Biomolecular condensates form through weak, multivalent, non-covalent interactions, but the role of covalent crosslinks in shaping their assembly and material properties remains poorly understood. We previously showed that disulfide bonds between cysteines in designer phase-separating peptides (PSPs) act as redox-reversible crosslinks that lower the saturation concentration (Csat) and help maintain condensate fluidity. Here, we ask which sequence features govern this behavior. We built two peptide libraries: one varying the inter-cysteine spacer length (2-10 residues) and one varying cysteine density (0-33%). Inter-cysteine spacers tuned condensate properties only modestly. Longer inter-cysteine lengths raised Csat from 300 to 900 μM, showed greater fluidity (as assessed by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) recovery rate, and resisted loss of fluidity during maturation; all inter-cysteine length variants dissolved and reformed reversibly over three redox cycles. Cysteine density, in contrast, was the dominant control parameter. Increasing cysteine density lowered Csat about 60-fold (1.5 mM to 25 μM) and reduced the fluidity by an order of magnitude. Its effect on fluidity was non-monotonic: condensates with up to ~14% cysteine density stayed liquid-like for 10 days, whereas those with 21-33% cysteine density in the peptide showed slower coalescence. Condensates with the highest densities also resisted dissolution under reducing conditions and showed sharply reduced uptake of a protein cargo (eGFP; ~60% to ~9%) and a small molecule (TMR, ~70% to ~45%), consistent with smaller mesh size. Together, these results identify disulfide crosslink density as a key lever for programming condensate assembly, viscoelasticity, redox responsiveness, and porosity. The results offer key design principles both for understanding cysteine-rich disordered proteins in biomolecular condensates and for engineering redox-responsive biomaterials.

articles.title: Electrostatic control of conformational dynamics drives proton translocation in respiratory Complex I
articles.abstract: Complex I is a large membrane protein that transduces redox energy into a proton motive force across a biological membrane, powering cellular respiration. Yet, despite significant experimental and computational efforts, its long-range proton translocation mechanism remains poorly understood. Here, we combine nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and site-directed mutagenesis experiments with multiscale classical and hybrid quantum/classical (QM/MM) simulations to probe how conformational dynamics is linked to proton transfer reactions in the terminal antiporter module (Nqo12/NuoL/ND5) of Complex I. We show that protonation of a conserved proton-loading site (Lys329/His241Nqo12) in the terminal antiporter-like module gives rise to conformational changes that result in opening of the proton pathway. We further show that this protonation reaction is controlled by buried ion-pairs that modulate the barrier for proton translocation by intrinsic electric field effects. On a general level, our combined findings reveal how bioenergetic machines combine conformational dynamics with hydration transitions to establish efficient redox-driven proton pumps. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. articles.title: Error-Controlled Discovery of Protein Interactions via Conformal Calibration
articles.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are powerful predictors of protein interactions, but strong benchmark performance does not ensure reliable discoveries. We introduce PPI-Caliper, a model-agnostic framework that adapts conformal calibration to select interactions at user-specified false discovery rate (FDR) levels using held-out labels without retraining the predictor. Across five species, two PLM-based predictors, and two human training-data versions for each predictor, PPI-Caliper keeps empirical FDR at or below the target level under in-distribution calibration. Under distribution shift, transferred thresholds tend to become conservative when predictive performance improves, but can fail to control FDR when performance deteriorates. PPI-Caliper connects pre-trained interaction scores to explicit error targets and demonstrates why reliable biological discovery requires evaluating calibration alongside predictive accuracy.

articles.title: Evaluating the Identifiability of Temporal Delay and Response Attenuation in Endometrial Decidualization
articles.abstract: Endometriosis is associated with impaired endometrial decidualization, yet conventional differential expres-sion analyses cannot readily distinguish delayed transcriptional activation from reduced response amplitude.These mechanisms may produce similar expression differences at individual time points while implying distinct biological interpretations. Establishing when they can be distinguished is therefore a computational identifiability problem.We implement an identifiability-aware analysis of temporal displacement and amplitude attenuation in longitudinal transcriptomic responses. The approach combines reference trajectories, constrained amplitude-only and amplitude-plus-delay models, analytical examples of observational equivalence, and simulation-based assessments of mechanism distinguishability. Held-out time-point evaluation and culture-level sensitivity analyses examine the stability of model-dependent conclusions.In GSE246591, a candidate-delay-dependent dynamic-range filter excluded 30.9 - 38.3% of initially dynamic features under a hypothetical 24-hour shift across four endometrial stromal cultures. A two-component diagnostic separating retained dynamic range from affine shape similarity revealed that small projection residuals can arise from either loss of observable dynamics or similarity of response shapes. These findings demonstrate why a single separation statistic may be insufficient for interpreting temporal identifiability.Complementary independent in vivo analyses provided biological context. In GSE51981, an endometrial progesterone-response-associated transcriptional score was reduced in endometriosis samples (phase-model estimate 0.155, 95% CI 0.222 to 0.088). GSE6364 showed a directionally consistent but statistically inconclusive difference (0.033, 95% CI 0.068 to 0.002). Neither observation independently establishes a temporal delay.Together, these results support selection-aware evaluation of temporal transcriptomic responses, distin-guishing structural ambiguity and loss of dynamic signal from evidence of a biological timing change.

articles.title: Evolution of Vesicle Shape Parameters Based on A Deep-Learning Based Image Analysis Framework Over Extended Time Periods
articles.abstract: A precise analysis of shape instabilities in cell-sized membrane compartments requires thorough quantification of the shape dynamics of individual components over extended periods. Herein, we have used phase-contrast microscopy to image giant unilamellar membrane vesicles (GUVs), which are widely used as model systems for cellular structures. GUVs were prepared in the fluid lamellar phase of 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine with and without cholesterol dissolved within a potato starch solution. The morphological changes and budding dynamics of individual GUVs with different chemical compositions were quantified using a deep-learning based image analysis framework over extended time periods, by using phase-contrast micrographs as input data. This automated framework integrates contour-based detection of the mother vesicle with precise segmentation of daughter compartments, thereby enabling explicit identification and tracking of mother and daughter vesicles at high temporal resolution. These findings further facilitate the measurement of the temporal evolution of vesicle morphometrics including area, and local membrane curvature during budding, that can be used as an input to develop computational models aimed at elucidating curvature-driven membrane remodeling in complex soft materials.

articles.title: Evolutionary and acclimatory shifts in ion transporter gene expression across salinity transitions in the copepod Eurytemora carolleeae
articles.abstract: Many aquatic invaders are crossing biogeographic boundaries from saline to freshwater habitats. This transition often requires acclimation or evolution of physiological mechanisms to maintain internal ionic homeostasis. Populations of the copepod Eurytemora affinis complex have repeatedly invaded freshwater environments from saline habitats over the past century, providing an ideal model for investigating rapid adaptation to salinity change. Prior studies have found that ion transport-related genes form the largest functional categories of genes under selection and show evolutionary shifts in gene expression across saline to freshwater transitions in the E. affinis complex. In this study, focusing on the top targets of selection, we investigated evolutionary and acclimatory shifts in gene expression for 19 ion transport-related genes for populations of E. carolleeae (Atlantic clade of the E. affinis complex). Using a quantitative real-time PCR approach, we compared gene expression between ancestral saline and derived freshwater populations through a common garden reaction norm experiment and a laboratory natural selection experiment. We found that different ion transport-related gene paralogs within expanded gene families showed divergent patterns of expression in response to salinity change, consistent with specialization. For instance, Na+/K+-ATPase subunit α paralog 1 ( NKA-α-1 ) and Na+,K+,2Cl− cotransporter paralog 3 ( NKCC-3 ) exhibited the evolution of increased expression in the freshwater population across all conditions, relative to the saline population. In contrast, Na+/H+ antiporter paralog 7 ( NHA-7 ) and NHA-5 showed evolution of elevated expression in the saline population under low salinity relative to the freshwater population. Several genes also showed evolutionary differences in plasticity between saline and freshwater populations, such that saline populations retained phenotypic plasticity, whereas freshwater populations were comparatively canalized. In the laboratory natural selection experiment imposing salinity decline, evolutionary responses of the paralogs NKCC-3 , NHA-5 , and NHA-7 in the saline selection line largely recapitulated the evolutionary shifts observed in the natural populations. On the other hand, expression patterns of the ion transporters in the freshwater selection line showed little response during salinity increase, suggesting canalization. Together, these results reveal evolutionary and acclimatory divergence in gene expression among paralogs, suggesting the evolution of functional divergence among them. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. U.S. National Science Foundation, https://ror.org/021nxhr62, IOS-2412790, DEB-2055356, OCE-1658517, PRFB 2409904 Agence Nationale de la Recherche, ANR-19-MPGA-0004

articles.title: Facilitating the identification of cryo-EM hit matter in drug discovery with Astex-Faro
articles.abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is emerging as a tool for large-scale ligand screening and fragment-based drug discovery, generating extensive collections of reconstructions. At the same time, the systematic inspection of local density variations remains challenging, particularly when identifying weak or partially occupied features. Here, we present Astex-Faro, a statistical framework that defines an expected specimen state from a reference ensemble and identifies significant structural deviations in a target map through comparison against this reference. Furthermore, the method allows the enhancement of weak or poorly resolved features, enabling the recovery of signals that would otherwise be difficult to interpret. Fourier Shell Coherence (FSCoh) is introduced as a metric that quantifies consistency across reconstruction ensembles. We show that Astex-Faro reliably detects subtle structural features and improves their interpretability across datasets spanning a broad range of experimental challenges, from highly homogeneous specimens to membrane proteins, low-occupancy ligands and fragment-screening experiments. Together, these developments provide a practical framework for cryo-EM screening, increasing confidence in hit identification and reducing the risk of missed binding events.

articles.title: Floral scent diversity and evolution in deceptive Cypripedium, and post-pollination effects on floral scent and its biosynthesis in C. henryi
articles.abstract: Background and Aims: Floral scent is a primary driver of pollinator attraction and reproductive isolation in deceptive orchids. Yet, little is known about the variation and evolution of scent in a phylogenetic framework and how pollination affects the biosynthesis and emission of scents in these lineages. This study characterizes scent diversity across Cypripedium, a genus of deceptive orchids, examines phylogenetic constraints, and investigates post-pollination effects on scent composition in one of the species. Methods: Floral volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were sampled from 31 Cypripedium taxa using dynamic headspace techniques, and analysed by gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (GC/MS). Uni- and multivariate methods were used to analyse intra- and interspecific scent variation and test for phylogenetic signal in floral scent. Post-pollination effects on scent composition were experimentally tested in C. henryi using four pollination treatments, combined with RNA-seq analyses of floral tissues to examine transcriptional responses in VOC biosynthetic pathways. Key results: We detected 258 floral VOCs, revealing a high chemical diversity dominated by terpenoids, aliphatics, and aromatic compounds. Floral scent composition was highly species-specific, and closely related taxa often shared only few compounds. Scent composition differed among pollination groups, but these groups explained only a limited proportion of overall scent variation. We detected a significant but weak phylogenetic signal, suggesting limited evolutionary constraint in floral scent. Pollination had limited effect on C. henryis floral scent and volatile biosynthesis gene expression, despite a significant decrease in total scent emission after pollinium deposition. Transcriptional changes predominantly occurred in the petals rather than the labellum and staminode. Conclusion: Floral scent evolution in Cypripedium is characterized by high chemical diversity, and a weak phylogenetic constraint, consistent with variable selection in food-deceptive systems. The pollination study further suggests the absence of a strong, directed post-pollination effect on the floral scent of C. henryi. Keywords: Cypripedium; deceptive pollination; floral scent; volatile organic compounds (VOCs); phylogenetic signal; linalool; post-pollination effects; transcriptome profiles; differential gene expression; floral organs ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.

articles.title: Functional analysis of small-molecule and protein binding domains using monomeric streptavidin-based two-component biosensors
articles.abstract: Protein biosensors are important analytical and diagnostic tools that convert molecular recognition into measurable activity. Most common two-component biosensors require two non-competing recognition domains, yet binding affinity and specificity alone do not reliably predict their compatibility with the rest of the biosensor. We report a modular platform that exploits monomeric streptavidin (mSA2) as a surrogate recognition domain, enabling rapid functional evaluation of candidate binders in the context of biosensor scaffold without requiring a second ligand-specific binding protein. We established a chromatography-free protocol for recovering functional mSA2-based biosensor components from Escherichia coli. Using biotinylated small molecules methotrexate and vitamin D3, as well as heart failure protein biomarkers galectin-3 and S100A7 we demonstrate ligand-dependent reporter biosensor activation. The developed platform provides a scalable approach for rapid binder evaluation and biosensor prototyping, streamlining biosensor development using binding domains generated by directed evolution or computational protein design. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. ARC Centre of Excellence in Synthetic Biology, https://ror.org/01p2zg436, CE200100029 ARC Linkage Project, LP200200916 NHMRC Investigator grant, APP2033951 CSIRO BioFoundry, 178477198

articles.title: Functional genomic characterization of anti-phage defense systems in vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium
articles.abstract: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a significant public health threat, demonstrating high rates of antibiotic resistance and frequently causing hospital-acquired infections. Bacteriophages (phages) are a promising adjunctive therapy to reduce bacterial load and manage VREfm infections. Many bacteria encode anti-phage defense systems--groups of genes that can counteract phage infection--but these systems have not been characterized in VREfm. Here we explored the diversity of anti-phage defense systems within clinical VREfm isolate genomes and examined their impact on phage susceptibility. We first used two available bioinformatic tools (DefenseFinder and PADLOC) to identify putative anti-phage defense systems in 21 hybrid-assembled VREfm clinical isolate genomes, and observed that most anti-phage defense systems were located on plasmids, defense islands, and prophages. Combining this information with functional testing of phage susceptibility did not reveal robust associations between specific defense systems and resistance to four VREfm-targeting lytic phages. Due to inherent limitations of phage susceptibility testing, we next developed an assay to assess phage survival after co-incubation with bacteria, and identified over two dozen genes associated with phage killing, including a potentially novel defense island. Lastly, we attempted to functionally validate 10 candidate anti-phage defense systems, only four of which were ultimately tested in enterococci. Expression of one of these candidates, AbiE, decreased bacterial susceptibility to two Enterococcus-targeting phages. As VREfm-targeting phage therapy becomes more widely available, identification of genes contributing to phage resistance can aid in streamlining the provision of phages to patients who could benefit from this new therapeutic modality.

articles.title: Hazard Structure and Repair Kinetics: A 2x2 Classification that Resolves the Stochastic-Death / Individual-Tolerance Dilemma
articles.abstract: The two variants of GUTS (General Unified Threshold model of Survival), stochastic death and individual tolerance, disagree about no-effect concentrations under time-variable exposure, and no standard test separates them. Each variant fixes two independent choices, which form a 2x2 classification: whether the hazard accumulates while damage exceeds a threshold (cumulative) or is set by the highest damage reached (peak-based), and whether repair is proportional or saturating. Calibration fit cannot choose: each structure fits by adjusting its own damage recovery, the cumulative one faster in twelve of fourteen compounds. For two identical pulses separated by complete recovery, the cumulative hazard predicts equal survival through both whatever the parameters, so a carry-over ratio (second-to-first survival) above one excludes it; in Gammarus pulex fourteen of fifteen ratios are at or above one, seven significantly. The peak-based hazard predicts the ratio's maximum, approached as intervals lengthen in five of six compounds. For organophosphates, whose recovery outlasts the published pulse intervals, the one test on measured damage favours the peak-based hazard: diazinon-exposed Daphnia magna stopped being immobilised once acetylcholinesterase, still inhibited, began to recover. The peak-based hazard is the appropriate default for toxicokinetic-toxicodynamic risk assessment of narcotics and uncouplers, and provisionally of organophosphates.

articles.title: HiFiTaxa: a reproducible analysis pipeline for full length 16S rRNA gene and ITS amplicon sequencing from PacBio reads
articles.abstract: Long-read amplicon sequencing profiles communities at high resolution, but taxonomic accuracy depends on the reference, classifier and the parameters used. Here, we present HiFiTaxa, a reproducible, single command Nextflow pipeline for PacBio HiFi 16S rRNA gene and fungal ITS amplicons. It builds versioned references from current GTDB and UNITE releases and supports Bayesian lowest common ancestor (BLCA) and naive Bayes (NB) classifiers and the read level profilers Emu (16S rRNA gene) and EMITS (ITS). We benchmarked them on mock communities and on holdouts with 10% of GTDB or UNITE databases sequences withheld. On the 16S rRNA gene mock of 20 species, BLCA detected all 20 species and reported two false positives, NB detected 17 and reported none, and Emu detected all 20 and reported eight. In the GTDB holdout, for taxa represented in the reference, BLCA reached 80.0% species level accuracy against 48.1% for the exact matching species step of NB. However, NB produced fewer incorrect assignments for taxa absent from the reference. On fungal ITS, BLCA had slightly higher holdout accuracy at species level(54.7%) against 52.2% for NB. NB was more conservative for novel taxa, and EMITS detected the most mock species. HiFiTaxa therefore offers a single reproducible workflow that uses current GTDB and UNITE releases and enables users to choose between different classifier algorithms depending on their needs.

articles.title: High-density environmental DNA metabarcoding reveals fine-scale three-dimensional structure of a fish community in a semi-closed bay
articles.abstract: Coastal fish assemblages are influenced by environmental heterogeneity across horizontal and vertical dimensions, yet their fine-scale three-dimensional structure remains poorly understood. We investigated spatial variation in fish assemblages using environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding at 100 stations across three depth layers (300 samples) in Maizuru Bay, a semi-enclosed coastal bay in Japan. Concurrent hydrographic measurements were used to examine associations between fish assemblage composition and environmental conditions. We detected 216 fish species, with mean species richness decreasing from 28.4 at the surface to 16.4 at the bottom. Thirty-three species were detected exclusively below the surface. Fish assemblage composition differed significantly among depth layers and exhibited pronounced horizontal turnover along the bay axis. Although depth, geographic position, and measured environmental variables were associated with assemblage composition, they collectively explained only 13.0% of the variation. The independent contribution of spatial position (2.9%) exceeded those of depth (0.8%) and measured environmental variables (0.9%). These findings demonstrate substantial three-dimensional heterogeneity in coastal fish assemblages that cannot be fully explained by conventional hydrographic measurements. Our study highlights the importance of integrating horizontal and vertical sampling to characterize coastal fish biodiversity and improve marine ecosystem monitoring.

articles.title: High-fat diet promotes exhaustion-associated T-cell remodeling across vascular and lymphoid tissues in atherosclerosis-prone mice
articles.abstract: Background: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease driven by lipid accumulation and immune dysregulation. How chronic dietary lipid exposure reshapes T-cell states across vascular and lymphoid tissues, and whether these changes resolve after dietary normalization, remains incompletely defined. This study examined diet-associated T-cell remodeling and the contribution of macrophage-mediated stimulation. Methods: ApoE-deficient mice received a vegetarian diet (VD) or high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 or 24 weeks; a dietary reversal group received HFD for 12 weeks followed by VD for 12 weeks. CD45-positive cells from aorta, blood, spleen, lymph nodes, and bone marrow underwent single-cell RNA sequencing with matched T-cell receptor sequencing. T cell states were annotated using canonical markers, and exhaustion- and naive-associated programs were quantified using UCell scores. Analysis assessed T-cell composition, clonal expansion, and predicted macrophage-T cell communication, with splenic flow-cytometric validation. Results: HFD was associated with enrichment of exhaustion-associated states, with the highest exhaustion scores in the aorta. At 24 weeks, the pooled exhausted-cell proportion was 15.7% under HFD versus 10.6% under VD. Dietary reversal restored this proportion to 10.6%, while residual transcriptional changes persisted in a tissue-dependent manner. Flow cytometry corroborated increased inhibitory receptor expression and co-expression. Aortic macrophages exhibited inflammatory and antigen-presentation programs alongside increased predicted communication with T cells. Aortic T-cell activation and clonal expansion accompanied these changes, and clonotype size correlated with exhaustion score (Spearman correlation coefficient = 0.57, p = 0.029). Conclusion: Chronic HFD is associated with multicompartment T-cell remodeling, with prominent vascular exhaustion-associated programs and tissue-dependent recovery after dietary normalization. These findings suggest that dietary lipid exposure may leave a durable adaptive immune imprint across organs during atherosclerosis.

articles.title: High-throughput, single-cell-encoded colony imaging reveals infection-linked heterogeneity
articles.abstract: Phenotypic heterogeneity within bacterial populations shapes adaptation, antibiotic tolerance, and infection dynamics, yet colony-level quantification remains difficult at scale and on dark/selective media. We present HeteroTyper, an automated, high-throughput time-lapse platform that measures colony phenotypes across >100 plates per run on both transparent and dark media. HeteroTyper includes a ready-to-use computational pipeline that can be deployed on common plate-imaging setups and across agar types, delivering appearance times as a proxy for lag times, growth trajectories, colony size, intensity, and morphology from routine image series. Automated counts closely matched manual counts, supporting accuracy and scalability. Using Yersinia pseudotuberculosis as a model, HeteroTyper resolves phenotypic heterogeneity in vitro, with early and late phases showing broader appearance time distributions than mid-log phases. It also reveals organ-specific heterogeneity in vivo, with mesenteric lymph node isolates displaying the broadest appearance time distributions compared to spleen and liver. Appearance time was negatively associated with final colony size and intensity, linking growth initiation to downstream colony outcomes. Together, these distribution-level measurements indicate that bacterial adaptation during infection is compartmentalized by tissue microenvironments and prior history, and establish HeteroTyper as a practical, generalizable route to quantify infection-relevant phenotypic diversity on solid media at routine, high throughput. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.

articles.title: Intestinal molecular siphoning by engineered bacterial spores for non-systemic treatment of nicotine addiction
articles.abstract: Eradicating toxic small molecules from the body typically requires the administrations of therapeutic agents for systemic circulation and tissue distribution, resulting in inevitable adverse events from off-target effects. Here, we propose a intestinal molecular siphoning approach for treating diseases caused by toxic substances, in which enzymatic degradation of a toxic substance in the intestinal lumen serves as a driving force for the diffusion of the toxic substance from blood to gut, and continuous elimination of the toxic substance in the gut could effectively ease substance dependence. Using nicotine as a model substance, a live bacterial system was constructed by displaying a trypsin-resistant nicotine oxidase on the surface of Bacillus subtilis spores, and encapsulating in enteric-coated microspheres for gastric protection and targeted intestinal release. After oral treatments with the live bacterial system in mice, peak concentrations of nicotine in blood and brain were remarkably reduced compared to controls. Moreover, the live bacterial system could effectively attenuate nicotine addiction by suppressing dopamine reward surges to reverse withdrawal hyperalgesia, preventing the upregulation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and alleviating anxiety-like behaviors. These findings show the potential of intestinal molecular siphoning as a target-independent therapeutic strategy for lowering circulating toxic substances through non-systemic enzyme reprogramming.

articles.title: Isolation of functional endogenous clathrin-coated vesicles and in vitro reconstitution of pure clathrin cages
articles.abstract: Clathrin-coated vesicles (CCVs) mediate key endocytic trafficking events, and dysfunction of CCVs is linked to multiple human diseases. Conventional centrifugation-based purification protocols can enrich endogenous CCVs but fail to eliminate intraluminal smooth vesicles (SVs) and co-isolated exosomes; these lipid contaminants reduce sample homogeneity and hinder high-resolution structural and proteomic analysis. Here, we present an integrated workflow to isolate biologically active endogenous CCVs from porcine brain and reconstitute homogeneous, SV-free clathrin cages. Crude CCVs are first enriched by differential and sucrose density gradient centrifugation to deplete the majority of exosomes. Clathrin cages are then depolymerized under alkaline conditions, allowing separation of soluble clathrin and adaptor proteins from SVs and residual lipid contaminants via ultracentrifugation. Purified coat proteins are reassembled in vitro into uniform clathrin cages. Functional assays confirm that purified CCVs retain Auxilin-Hsc70-dependent uncoating activity, and the enclosed SVs carry active vATPase proton pumps. This approach produces well-defined samples suitable for cryo-electron microscopy and mass spectrometry-based investigation of clathrin assembly and disassembly. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. National Natural Science Foundation of China, 32301014 Shandong Provincial Natural Science Foundation, ZR2022QC213

articles.title: LRCQ: phenome-wide heritability enrichment of genomic loci from GWAS summary statistics
articles.abstract: Some genetic variants are associated with many traits, but a variant's GWAS statistics are also inflated by the effects of variants in LD with it and by confounding shared by all variants in a study. Existing measures of per-variant pleiotropy, such as counts of significant associations or multi-trait association tests, do not separate these sources. Stratified LD score regression separates them for one trait at a time and only through predefined annotations. We present LRCQ (LD score regression on {chi}2 across many GWAS), which estimates for each locus its phenome-wide heritability enrichment: the variance of its causal effects across a set of traits, relative to an average locus. LRCQ regresses squared Z-scores from 30 or more GWAS jointly on squared LD, with per-trait LDSC intercepts and heritabilities fitted in earlier stages. Its pooled least-squares solution has a closed form whose cost does not grow with the number of traits. Its standard errors account for sample overlap and genetic correlation between GWAS. Squared Z-scores identify enrichment at the resolution of LD clumps, not single SNPs, so LRCQ reports clump-level estimates ("omni-loci"). These estimates can be aggregated over any functional annotation or gene set chosen after the analysis. In simulations with real UK Biobank LD and 30 to 1,000 traits, LRCQ was unbiased for its clump-level estimand. When GWAS share samples its test statistics are strongly right-skewed: normal-reference p-values were up to 10-fold anti-conservative at P < 0.001, and skewness-corrected p-values from the exact third cumulant restored type-I error and FDR control. Model-based standard errors were calibrated once the enrichment estimates plugged into them kept the polygenic background. It ranked enriched loci better than mean {chi}2, LD-normalised {chi}2, multi-trait omnibus tests and significant-association counts in 13 of 16 scenarios. Its main vulnerability was a misspecified LDSC intercept. Applied to 444 Pan-UK Biobank European-ancestry GWAS, LRCQ found strongly non-uniform phenome-wide enrichment: the SD of true clump-mean enrichment was 8.3, against a genome mean of 1. It identified 70 omni-loci (99 LD clumps) at FDR 5%, including CRP, CETP, APOB, AKTIP, SMOX, the SHBG region, CASZ1 and HNF1A. These ranked only moderately with mean {chi}2 and poorly with counts of significant associations. Gene-level phenome-wide enrichment rose with loss-of-function constraint. Phenome-wide heritability was 3-5-fold enriched in coding, conserved, 5' UTR and promoter sequence, and depleted in repressed chromatin. LRCQ turns hundreds of biobank GWAS into an LD-corrected map of where phenome-wide genetic variance lies, and complements its companion method LRCP, which estimates genetic-effect correlations between loci.

articles.title: Life on leaves left a lasting mark on the Methylobacterium core genome
articles.abstract: The extent to which core genomes reflect strictly vertical inheritance remains debated, particularly in ecologically diverse bacterial lineages. Here, we investigate the evolution of the core genome of Methylobacterium, a major leaf-associated bacterial genus, to assess how evolutionary signals vary across genes and whether they relate to functions involved in adaptation to life at the surface of plant leaves (the phyllosphere). Identifying 1,099 protein-coding core genes across 293 genomes, we combined gene tree comparisons, phylogenetic network reconstruction, nucleotide polymorphism patterns, and functional enrichment analyses. We found that most core genes show some deviation from the consensus phylogenetic tree. However, this discordance is not randomly distributed. Across all analytical approaches, genes showing the strongest deviations are consistently associated with functions linked to life in the phyllosphere, including anoxygenic photosynthesis, protection against UV and osmotic stress. These genes are often grouped into conserved clusters in the genome. In particular, a large cluster involved in anoxygenic photosynthesis, including bacteriochlorophyll and carotenoid biosynthesis, shows strong variation in its evolutionary history and organization across lineages, despite maintaining a conserved core structure. Similar patterns of phylogenetic incongruence and gene organization are observed across related Hyphomicrobiales inhabiting the phyllosphere, suggesting that these functions extend beyond Methylobacterium. Together, these results indicate that evolutionary heterogeneity within the core genome is concentrated in genes involved in key ecological functions. While alternative explanations cannot be excluded, these patterns are consistent with horizontal gene transfer contributing to the diversification of traits important for survival and adaptation in phyllosphere bacterial communities.

articles.title: Long read sequencing reveals changes in measured isoform structure and abundance due to RNA processing
articles.abstract: Oxford Nanopore Technology enables direct RNA sequencing without reverse transcription (RT) and cDNA sequencing without PCR amplification, allowing investigation of how RNA preparation protocols bias sequencing data. PCR amplification is known to introduce biases related to expression levels, transcript lengths, and GC content. However, biases introduced by RT have been described more recently and their quantification remains more elusive. Using seven cell line datasets from SG-NEx, we compared nanopore sequencing of direct RNA, direct cDNA, and PCR-amplified cDNA. We identified hundreds of differentially expressed genes and isoforms between protocols, indicating significant changes in observed expression. Differentially expressed isoforms displayed expected amplification biases, and further we observed decreased PCR counts associated with higher m6A methylation levels on native RNA. We also found differential transcript usage in hundreds of genes across cell lines, showing substantial changes in measured isoform proportions between protocols. Analysis of structural differences between isoforms that switch dominance revealed that while some events involve simple RNA fragmentation, most involve complex structural differences including novel junctions (e.g. exon skipping, intron retention). Compared to non-DTU genes, inserted introns (exitrons) were significantly more common after RT and amplification. Furthermore, visualisation of raw coverage data proved crucial for qualitative validation of experimental findings.

articles.title: Lung Epithelial TLR7 is a Factor in Viral Replication and Pathogenesis
articles.abstract: Respiratory virus infections are the leading causes of morbidity and mortality of infants and the elderly worldwide. Currently it is not known how Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) vaccination of infants can cause enhancement of RSV disease, highlighting gaps in our understanding about how viruses like RSV interact with the immune system. Here we address this and show that ERK MAP kinase signaling from Toll-like Receptor-7 (TLR7) detection of RSV and influenza, but not human parainfluenza virus type 3 (HPIV3), infections in bronchial epithelial cells (BECs) drives replication of the viruses. Virus infection is detected by pattern recognition receptors like TLR7 that bind to single stranded RNA (ssRNA) viral replication intermediates in late endosomes. Here we report that TLR7 is expressed in BECs and detects RSV ssRNA, causing ERK MAP kinase signaling. RSV and influenza use this detection and signaling in BECs to drive its replication and infection, a mechanism that counters TLR7s role in antiviral defence. Experimental blockade of TLR7 binding or downstream signalling through ERK MAP kinase decreased RSV and influenza replication, but had no effect on HPIV3. RSV viral loads in mouse and human females were higher compared to males, consistent with higher sex-dependent expression of the TLR7 gene from two copies of the X chromosome in females. In a TLR7 gain of function mouse model there was a significant enhancement of RSV replication and RSV eosinophilic and Th2 disease markers like interleukin-5 (IL-5). In summary, TLR7 is expressed in human lung BECs in the lungs where it acts as a factor in RSV and influenza replication and disease pathogenesis. We propose that this is a major factor in determining the sex-disparity of viral disease.

articles.title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
articles.abstract: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Office of Readiness and Response, 5D30124C20202 Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, Independent Research and Development Program

articles.title: Missing by design: why genomic metadata must be captured at submission, not recovered from the literature
articles.abstract: Plant and metazoan genome assemblies are being deposited in the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC) archives at an accelerating rate, but the biological context needed to interpret them, such as ploidy, cultivar, and subgenome structure, is often missing from the record: these attributes are optional in most submission checklists and, when supplied, are entered as free text. We describe the gap in three layers. Ploidy varies within a species and cannot be inferred from taxonomy; chromosome-naming conventions differ between assemblies of the same crop; and that inconsistency is concentrated in species named by subgenome and is not associated with the size of the research community, which points to the lack of a shared convention. As a case study, we built a pipeline that recovers these attributes from the publications linked to an assembly. On a benchmark of 82 assemblies, its current version reported one wrong ploidy, and across 1,059 plant assemblies an earlier, less strict version found the ploidy in a publication for about half; for nearly a third, it found a publication but no statement of ploidy in it. Recovery from the literature can annotate assemblies already deposited but cannot stop new ones from arriving incomplete. We therefore propose that ploidy, cultivar, and subgenome structure be captured at submission as mandatory, controlled-vocabulary attributes, building on existing INSDC and Genomic Standards Consortium checklists. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. Google Summer of Code

articles.title: MoALE1, an ART-like effector, contributes to rice blast virulence through host immune suppression
articles.abstract: Rice blast, caused by the hemibiotrophic fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, is one of the most destructive diseases affecting rice production worldwide. During infection, M. oryzae secretes effector proteins that suppress host immunity and facilitate colonization. Here, we characterized MoALE1, a predicted effector that is structurally similar to members of the heat-labile enterotoxin/cholera toxin family. Using a yeast secretion trap assay, we demonstrated that MoALE1 contains a functional signal peptide. A MoALE1-GFP fusion localized to the biotrophic interfacial complex, indicating that MoALE1 is a cytoplasmic effector. Expression analyses revealed that MoALE1 is expressed during biotrophy, from 16 to 48 h post-inoculation. Transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana showed that MoALE1 suppresses BAX-mediated cell death, suggesting a role in host immune suppression. To investigate its contribution to pathogenicity, a{Delta} moale1 mutant was generated and evaluated in rice infection assays. Deletion of MoALE1 significantly reduced disease severity but did not affect fungal growth, stress tolerance, sporulation, appressorium development, host penetration, or early invasive growth. In contrast, infection by the {Delta}moale1 mutant resulted in enhanced host H2O2 accumulation and increased expression of ROS-associated defense genes. Together, these findings identify MoALE1 as a biotrophy-associated cytoplasmic effector that promotes rice blast pathogenicity by suppressing host immune responses and provide new insight into the function of ADP-ribosyltransferase (ART)-like effector candidates in M. oryzae .

articles.title: Multispecies transport shapes electrochemical environments in perforated cells
articles.abstract: Cells maintain asymmetric electrochemical environments across selectively permeable plasma membranes. Ion channels on plasma membranes redistribute small ions, whereas large openings such as gasdermin pores allow both ions and proteins to cross the membrane, generating a multispecies transport regime. The transport of charged ions and proteins shapes electrochemical environments, leading to osmolarity changes, which in turn promotes water influx and cell swelling. Although biologists have observed the phenotypic progression from pore formation to cell swelling for decades, the molecular transport events underlying this progression remain elusive. To elucidate how pore formation drives downstream cellular effects, we establish quantitative multispecies transport frameworks to investigate gasdermin-perforated cells. We start by developing a reductionist model and benchmarking it against analytical Donnan predictions. We then explore three-dimensional geometries containing individual pores or pore clusters that form either simultaneously or sequentially. We reveal that ion-protein timescale separation generates non-canonical Donnan-like states, pore and cargo properties tune local transport, pore clustering modulates osmotic gradients, and sequential pore formation produces feedback-dependent dynamics. This work deepens our mechanistic understanding of cellular responses to membrane damage and informs the therapeutic design of pore-forming proteins with tunable cellular effects. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. articles.title: NORMA 3.0: aesthetic and group-aware visualization and analysis of annotated biological networks
articles.abstract: Interpreting a biological network often rests on the relationship between its connectivity and the functional groups annotated on it, such as pathways, complexes, or enriched terms. For example, whether a group forms a cohesive module, how groups overlap, and which proteins connect them. These relationships are often hard to assess visually when groups are numerous or overlap, and most tools represent membership only by node color. NORMA 3.0 is a complete client-side rewrite of its predecessors, delineating and laying out groups with convex hulls, bubble sets, or fog clouds. Multi-group nodes are rendered as pies and directed, and parallel edges retain their evidence channels. Eighteen 2D and nine 3D layouts are scored by silhouette width, outline intrusion and overlap, and benchmarked for group separation and run time. The implementation also includes edge bundling, network importers for six databases, 21 topological measures, group-level and enrichment statistics, comparison of up to ten networks, export of high-resolution images, and an Application Programming Interface. Availability and implementation: NORMA 3.0 is freely available at https://normaviz.org. The source code is available at https://github.com/PavlopoulosLab/NORMA.

articles.title: Naturalistic recall preserves temporal specificity despite cortical feature reorganization
articles.abstract: Although sensory input arrives in a largely continuous stream, recall is temporally compressed, discontinuous, and often structured as events. However, the temporal specificity of recall-related neural activity within events, and the separation and cortical organization of recalled features relative to perception, remain poorly characterized. We analyzed functional MRI data recorded during viewing and free recall of an episode of Sherlock. A data-driven alignment between viewing and recall data identified neural recapitulation of corresponding narrative events and revealed information that distinguished moments within events, particularly in the association cortex. Features ranging from low-level visual to semantic information predicted recall reinstatement. However, differences in predictive performance among feature levels became smaller during recall, and their organization along the cortical sensory-to-association gradient reversed relative to viewing. Thus, temporal specificity within events can be preserved despite substantial reorganization of feature representations across the cortex during recall.

articles.title: Non-equilibrium cyclic conformations of DNA under electrokinetic confinement
articles.abstract: Classic nanofluidic devices harness geometric confinement to modulate single polymer conformation and control chain dynamics. While classic nanofluidic devices have given rise to a range of applications, they are fundamentally limited by the static nature of their construction, which restricts real time control over molecular conformations. The reversible electrokinetic confinement (RECON) technique enables time-dependent control of DNA conformations in nanowells via dynamic modulation of field-induced confinement. Here, we demonstrate that applying dynamically varying confinement using stochastic and periodic signals can drive the confined polymer to access a range of non-equilibrium states, with the distinct configurations quantified via their radius of gyration tensor. For periodic driving, the device allows controlled cycling across conformational states, with distinct hysteresis observed in the shape anisotropy modulation. We quantify the interplay between the driving frequency, driving amplitude, and resulting hysteresis. Overall, our results establish RECON as a platform for active manipulation of single molecules, opening new avenues for studying non-equilibrium polymer physics and developing high-throughput, dynamically tunable nanofluidic devices. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. Fonds de Recherche du Québec  Nature et Technologies, https://ror.org/00b9f9778, 320394

articles.title: Omics-scale decoding of protein N-glycosylation using protein language model embeddings
articles.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) learn rich sequence semantics from vast volume of protein sequences, yet the information encoded in their high-dimensional embeddings remains largely a black box, posing an interpretability challenge. Here we show that semantic features learned by pLMs can be decoded to reveal biologically meaningful signals using coevolutionary analysis without downstream supervised-training. Building on this insight, we developed MaskNGly, a zero-shot framework that identifies protein N-glycosylation sites directly from PLM-embeddings while achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised predictors. MaskNGly is computationally efficient and intrinsically transferable, enabling omics-scale characterization of protein glycosylation landscape. Applied across proteomes, it reveals that canonical N-X-S/T motifs gain higher glycosylation propensities with increasing organismal complexity and that glycosylation preferentially occurs at structured, solvent-exposed regions. Mutations altering high-scoring motifs are more frequently disease-associated. The framework also captures signatures of glycosylation-mediated protein allostery. These results establish an interpretable and scalable route to study glycobiology from pLM-embeddings.

articles.title: Optimiser Repairs for Living-Cell Self-Driving Laboratories: Performance and Redundancy under Experimental Constraints
articles.abstract: Living-cell self-driving laboratories must optimise experiments despite delayed readouts, changing responses and limited sample availability. In simulations, we evaluate when optimiser repairs improve closed-loop performance and when platform constraints make them redundant, separating consumption of a sample from permanent loss of the ability to repeat its condition. We prove that exclusions and confirmation requests produce exactly the baseline trajectory when they act only on conditions already forbidden by the platform, share the same posterior and selection procedure, and release infeasible requested slots. This result covers the evaluated pending-exclusion, previous-batch and confirmation rules under permanent condition retirement; it does not cover arbitrary selection interventions. We then conduct 33,900 simulated policy runs with 200-300 paired campaign seeds per setting. A public PBMC reference supports characterisation of the target-label readout, while condition-response landscapes remain synthetic. Across 27 landscape, assay-size and kernel settings, previous-batch exclusion changes final normalised performance by -0.004 to +0.283, with positive differences surviving Holm adjustment in 13 settings. Effects are small on the rugged landscape. Permanent retirement can be harmful under noisy rugged responses. All three subsumed interventions reproduce every saved baseline event on 200 of 200 paired seeds. These results establish the importance of explicit availability constraints and evaluation across experimental regimes when assessing optimiser repairs. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.

articles.title: PLATE: a global atlas of food metaplasmidomes
articles.abstract: Plasmids play a central role in the acquisition and spread of genes underlying important traits in food-associated microorganisms. Although shotgun metagenomics has greatly expanded opportunities to study food microbiomes, their plasmid diversity remains largely uncharacterized. Here, we present the Plasmid Atlas of Food Ecosystems (PLATE), a curated global resource of food metaplasmidomes. Built from 4,690 food metagenomes spanning 55 countries and 17 categories, PLATE comprises a broad catalog (bPLATE) of 3,904,895 putative plasmid contigs (PPCs) and a refined catalog (rPLATE) of 213,474 PPCs, corresponding to 181,871 unique sequences. Both catalogs are complemented by curated sample metadata, host predictions, taxonomic assignments, and functional annotations covering antimicrobial resistance (AMR), protein families and KEGG orthologs, CRISPR-Cas systems, carbohydrate-active enzymes, and bioactive peptides. We demonstrate PLATE's utility through a case study of AMR genes detected on PPCs from food microbiomes. PLATE is freely accessible and enables users to interactively search for and download sequences, annotations, and associated metadata. By organizing plasmid-associated sequence diversity and functional potential across food ecosystems, PLATE provides a foundation for analyses of food metaplasmidomes.

articles.title: Cancer cells differentially modulate mitochondrial respiration to alter redox state and enable biomass synthesis in nutrient-limited environments
articles.abstract: The cell NAD+/NADH ratio can constrain biomass synthesis and influence proliferation in nutrient-limited environments. However, which cell processes regulate the NAD+/NADH ratio is not known. Here, we find that some cancer cells elevate the NAD+/NADH ratio in response to serine deprivation by increasing mitochondrial respiration. Cancer cells that elevate mitochondrial respiration have higher serine production and proliferation in serine-limiting conditions than cells with no mitochondrial respiration response, independent of serine synthesis enzyme expression. Increases in mitochondrial respiration and the NAD+/NADH ratio promote serine synthesis regardless of whether serine is environmentally limiting. Lipid deprivation can increase the NAD+/NADH ratio via mitochondrial respiration in some cells, including cells that do not increase respiration following serine deprivation. Thus, in cancer cells where lipid depletion raises the NAD+/NADH ratio, proliferation in serine-depleted environments improves when lipids are also depleted. Taken together, these data suggest that changes in mitochondrial respiration in response to nutrient deprivation can influence the NAD+/NADH ratio in a cell-specific manner to impact oxidative biomass synthesis and proliferation. Given the complexity of tumor microenvironments, this work provides a metabolic framework for understanding how levels of more than one environmental nutrient affect cancer cell proliferation.

articles.title: Estimating bone marrow adiposity from head MRI and identifying its genetic architecture
articles.abstract: Bone marrow (BM) adiposity changes radically through the lifespan, but this phenomenon is poorly characterized and understood in humans. Large datasets of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of the head have been collected to study the human brain, but also contain unexploited information about other organs. We developed an artificial neural network that localizes calvarial BM in T1-weighted MRI head scans, enabling us to study its composition in several large MRI datasets, and to model sex-dimorphic age trajectories, including the effect of menopause. We revealed high heritability in single-nucleotide polymorphism and twin data, and identified 41 genetic loci significantly associated with the trait, including six sex-specific loci. Integrating mapped genes with existing BM single-cell RNA-sequencing data revealed patterns of adipogenic lineage differentiation and lipid loading. Finally, we identified significant genetic correlations with several human traits, including cognitive ability and Parkinson’s disease, which is intriguing in light of the recently discovered channels that link calvarial BM to the meninges.

articles.title: Expression of concern: Insect metamorphosis is regulated differently between sexes by members of a microRNA cluster
Targeting tankyrase scaffolding in the β-catenin destruction complex by PROTAC overcomes the limitation of catalytic inhibitors in colorectal cancer
articles.abstract: Aberrant WNT/β-catenin signaling drives tumorigenesis and metastasis in cancer. Although enzymatic inhibitors of tankyrase (TNKS) effectively block AXIN degradation and stabilize the β-catenin destruction complex (DC), they have demonstrated limited efficacy in various colorectal cancer (CRC) models. Here, we demonstrate that, unexpectedly, the induction of AXIN puncta represents a major barrier to achieving therapeutic efficacy. Mechanistically, catalytic inhibition of TNKS prevents TNKS turnover and drives its accumulation in the DC, wherein the scaffolding function of TNKS induces AXIN puncta formation, rigidifies the DC, and impedes β-catenin turnover. Chemically induced degradation of TNKS overcomes this limitation by stabilizing AXIN without puncta formation, providing a deeper suppression of the WNT/β-catenin pathway activity and the proliferation of CRC cells harboring dysfunctional APC mutations. Collectively, these findings provide an explanation for the unsatisfactory outcomes of drugging the WNT/β-catenin signaling pathway by TNKS inhibitors and highlight TNKS degradation as a promising approach to treat WNT/β-catenin-driven CRC.

articles.title: A Global Atlas of Immune Alleles Reveals Health-Relevant Variation Across Groups
articles.abstract: Immune allele frequencies inform disease association mapping, pharmacogenomic guidance, and vaccine design, yet such data are missing for most of the world's groups. Here we present the Global Atlas of Immune Alleles (GAIA), applying benchmarked genotyping tools across the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA), Immunoglobulin Heavy Chain Constant (IGHC), and Fc Gamma Receptor (FCGR) loci to whole-genome sequencing data from 20,248 individuals, oversampling sub-Saharan African, Island Southeast Asian, and Pacific groups. Despite representing fewer than 0.5% of observations in the Allele Frequency Net Database, GAIA expands the database's catalogue by 38%, demonstrating that representation matters more than sample size. We identify HLA alleles at group-specific frequencies that challenge pharmacogenomic screening recommendations and document disease-risk alleles common in groups lacking clinical guidance. Finally, we introduce majority allelic diversity (MAD-X), which counts the alleles required for X% of individuals in a group to carry at least one, and show that reaching 90% HLA-B coverage for vaccine design requires up to 2.7 times more alleles in underrepresented groups than in those of Northwest European ancestry.

articles.title: A Multilevel Framework for Evaluating the Impact of Monoclonal Antibodies Against Respiratory Syncytial Virus in Daycare and Households
articles.abstract: Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) reduce the risk of severe disease caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) among immunized infants. The potential of these products to indirectly protect unimmunized contacts remains incompletely understood. This uncertainty is, in part, due to our limited understanding of how mAbs may influence population-level RSV transmission. Here, we develop a multiscale simulation framework that integrates RSV transmission dynamics across households and daycare centers to explore the characteristics of the population that could influence the strength of indirect effects of infant mAb immunization. The framework incorporates individual-level heterogeneity in age and time-varying infectiousness, as well as demographic variation in household composition and contact patterns, to capture realistic transmission pathways across close-contact networks. Using a virtual population informed by U.S. household characteristics, we show that infant immunization would only be expected to provide modest indirect protection to toddlers, and the magnitude of these effects depends on contact structure and intervention coverage. Our findings demonstrate the importance of integrating fine-scale transmission networks into evaluations of RSV prevention strategies and provide a generalizable framework for assessing population-level impacts of interventions against respiratory pathogens.
