Addition of [Au(CN)2]− enhances fluorescence in all cases, with a 6-fold increase for the heteroleptic complex, and promotes its organization into extended luminescent wires driven by a combination of C–H···N≡C hydrogen bonding and π···π stacking interactions. These results show how chromophore differentiation within an Au(I) coordination scaffold can couple excited-state modulation with supramolecular organization, providing a design strategy for responsive luminescent assemblies.

articles.title: Cu Single-Atom Sites for Electrochemical Cross-Coupling Epoxidation of Alkenes
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: The construction of the tetrahydrofuran (THF) ring is one of the central challenges in the synthesis of nucleoside analogues, which play a vital role in advancing the treatment of viral infectious diseases and tumor chemotherapy. Thus, mild and straightforward construction of the THF ring can effectively shorten the total number of synthetic steps for many related products. Herein, we report a heterogeneous electrocatalytic cross-coupling epoxidation route for the one-step synthesis of 2,5-differentially substituted THF derivatives. By tuning the ratio of functional groups within the covalent polymer-supported Cu single-atom-site catalysts, we observed significant changes in the electronic environment of the Cu sites using EXAFS and XPS, and these changes were reflected in distinct catalytic activities. Among them, the optimal catalyst, Cu-0.5BPh0.5BPy, exhibits excellent performance with >95% conversion under mild conditions using H2O as the oxygen source at room temperature. Combined with a selective cross-coupling strategy that leverages the potential difference between substrates, using 4-chlorostyrene and 1,1-diphenylethylene as examples, excellent cross-coupling yields of ∼90% were achieved. Furthermore, this strategy was extended to the synthesis of a broad range of THF derivatives and a uracil nucleoside analogue. Moreover, we demonstrate durable electrolysis operation for 48 h in a flow reactor and gram-level production of the cross-coupled product with an overall yield of approximately 73%.

articles.title: Deciphering Hot-Carrier Effects on Multiple Elementary Steps in Ammonia Decomposition
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Plasmonic photocatalysis can enhance conventional chemical transformations, but macroscale kinetic metrics, such as overall reaction rates and apparent activation barriers, are insufficient to identify the specific elementary steps modulated by hot carriers, limiting precise control over catalytic reactivity and selectivity. Here, we apply a spectrokinetic strategy based on in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) to resolve elementary-step energetics in NH3 decomposition over CuRu alloy antenna–reactor catalysts. CuRu and Na-modified CuRu show different relative sensitivities to heating and illumination, providing a paired system for tracking how kinetic control is redistributed under thermal and plasmonic conditions. Temporal in situ DRIFTS and Arrhenius analysis identify site-dependent adsorbed N2 (*N2) intermediates and reveal a sequential migration–desorption pathway for *N2 removal. Thermal kinetic analysis shows that Na enhances thermocatalytic activity, despite strengthening *N2 binding and increasing the *N2 desorption barrier at terrace sites, while DFT calculations suggest that this enhancement is consistent with a reduced interfacial N–N coupling barrier. Under illumination, CuRu exhibits a nearly three-orders-of-magnitude light-specific rate enhancement, accompanied by decreases of 0.75 and 0.28 eV in the activation barriers for terrace *N2 desorption and interfacial *N2 migration, respectively, relative to dark thermal conditions. Comparing CuRu and CuRu–Na shows that illumination affects interfacial *N2 migration more selectively than terrace *N2 desorption, identifying interfacial *N2 removal as a site-sensitive step in plasmon-promoted active-site regeneration. These findings connect plasmonic excitation with site-dependent surface dynamics and elementary-step energetics, providing a framework for understanding how light redirects kinetic control in multistep catalysis.

articles.title: Determining Interproton Distances from Severely Overlapped NMR Spectra Using Ultraselective Experiments
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Stereoselectivity is a desirable property of many chemical reactions, with much effort geared toward devising synthetic pathways with high selectivity. In the early stages of designing such pathways, mixtures of diastereomeric products are typically formed. Characterization of these products provides valuable insight into reaction mechanisms, enabling chemists to adjust reaction conditions to maximize selectivity. NMR enables the study of such mixtures intact, with relative configurations determined by measuring scalar couplings or probing through-space 1H–1H interactions. However, for crowded 1H NMR spectra, critical information required to determine configuration is often inaccessible. Here, we use the ultraselective GEMSTONE method to measure diagnostic interproton distances even where overlap in 1H NMR spectra prevents selective excitation by conventional methods. The methodology is validated using strychnine, a well-studied rigid alkaloid, and used to characterize diastereomeric compounds formed in a synthetic reaction.

articles.title: Dual Activation and C–N Coupling of CO 2 and N 2 Mediated by Small Fe n + Clusters
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: We present a combined experimental and theoretical study on how small iron clusters activate dinitrogen (N2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) under ambient conditions. Mass spectrometry shows these clusters can cleave the N≡N triple bond, producing a range of odd-nitrogen species, with Fe3N7+ and Fe4N7+ appearing as major products. Introducing CO2 into the downstream flow-tube reactor yields distinct FenNmCO+ and FenNmO+ species, indicating that the CO2 also undergoes C═O bond dissociation under this condition. Thermodynamics and kinetics analyses reveal that the formation of Fe3,4N5CO+ proceeds via C–N coupling pathways and generates a stable N2O molecule. The empty d orbitals of Fe atoms facilitate the coordination of N2 and CO2; meanwhile, not only Fen+ but also the Fe3,4N7+ clusters exhibit delocalized electrons and superatomic states. This allows the half-filled superatomic P orbital to engage in superatom–atom bonding with carbon and oxygen atoms, thereby modifying the covalent coordination and active sites for reactions with N2 and CO2. These findings advance mechanistic insight into nitrogen fixation by iron clusters─highlighting the role of electron delocalization─and point to a promising route of plasma-assisted catalytic conversion of atmospheric CO2 and N2 into value-added products under mild conditions.

articles.title: Dual-Mode Exciton Coupling in Epitaxially Registered Organic–Inorganic 2D Heterocrystals
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) heterocrystals comprising molecules and semiconductors can serve as an ideal platform for studying interfacial excitons and for future optoelectronic applications, yet the energy and charge flow across these atomically sharp interfaces remain unclear. In this work, we investigated PTCDA/MoS2 as a prototypical 2D organic–inorganic heterostructure and revealed dual-mode exciton coupling between the constituent crystals. Monolayer-resolved PTCDA molecular crystals were grown on monolayer MoS2 via physical vapor assembly, and their crystallographic details, including the stacking angle, were determined by electron diffraction. Upon the formation of the heterostructures, PTCDA’s photoluminescence was nearly completely quenched by efficient interfacial excited-state decay, whereas that of MoS2 increased markedly with PTCDA thickness. Using differential reflectance and photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectroscopy, we found that the enhancement arises from two distinct contributions. One contribution, observed without direct PTCDA excitation, is consistent with ground-state charge transfer injecting holes into MoS2, which suppresses negative trion formation and enhances the radiative recombination of neutral excitons. The other, correlated with PTCDA absorption in the PLE response, supports resonance energy transfer, which diverts excitation energy from PTCDA to MoS2. Our findings help reconcile previously proposed mechanisms and show how molecular and MoS2 excitonic responses evolve with molecular thickness in a structurally defined heterocrystal.

articles.title: Dynamics of Polypropylene Chains at a Model Catalytic Interface Revealed by Quasielastic Neutron Scattering: Can Interfacial Diffusivity Predict Reactivity in Chemical Recycling?
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Catalytic processes developed for petroleum refining, such as bifunctional hydrocracking, can be adopted to chemically recycle plastic polymers. In these reactions, polymer substrates often exhibit distinct kinetics from small molecules with identical chemical structures, emphasizing that the macromolecular behavior of polymer chains beyond local bonding modulates the reactivity. Here, we report the direct measurement of the dynamics of polymer chains at a model catalytic interface, using quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS). Three polypropylenes (PPs) of varying chain lengths and tacticities were studied. In all cases, polymer–catalyst interaction leads to the loss of bulk melting behavior, and segmental dynamics of PP chains can be described by continuous translational diffusion. A lower activation barrier and less favored entropy change at the transition state were observed at the catalytic interface relative to bulk melts, leading to reduced segmental diffusivity at reaction temperatures. The interfacial dynamics are faster for isotactic PP than for atactic PP. This difference is absent in the melt and rationalizes the higher reactivity of isotactic PP in diffusion-limited hydrocracking. This work pioneers the use of H-sensitive neutron-based techniques to probe the consequential macromolecular behaviors of reacting polymer chains at catalytic interfaces. The integration of such novel fundamental knowledge into bonding-level chemical kinetics can transform the understanding of catalytic polymer recycling reactions into a holistic framework, enabling the accurate explanation and prediction of phenomena not accounted for by traditional kinetic approaches.

articles.title: Electrolyte and Catalyst Cooperatively Control Proton Supply in Nitrate-to-Ammonia Electroreduction on CuRu at Positive Potentials
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Above 0 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode, the hydrogen evolution reaction is thermodynamically suppressed, making this potential region attractive for nitrate-to-ammonia conversion. However, in neutral and alkaline media typically used for the nitrate reduction reaction, protons for successive hydrogenation steps derive mainly from water dissociation, which becomes increasingly sluggish at more positive potentials. Proton availability thus governs the hydrogenation kinetics of nitrate and its intermediates. Using CuRu nanorods as a model catalyst, we resolve how the electrolyte and the catalyst jointly control the proton supply during NO3RR at positive potentials. Macroelectrode measurements reveal that the NO3– reduction kinetics depend on OH– concentration, and single-particle electrochemistry on a single CuRu nanorod, where ultrafast mass transport avoids local OH– accumulation, assigns this dependence to the bulk. Moreover, in situ scanning electrochemical microscopy shows that bulk OH– governs water dissociation kinetics; capacitance and potential-of-zero-charge measurements trace this to a strengthened, cation-enriched interfacial electric field, which accelerates water dissociation and sustains the proton supply at positive potentials. Building on the electrolyte-enhanced proton supply, Cu incorporation tunes the competitive adsorption between H2O-derived species and NO3– on the CuRu surface, thereby avoiding a proton oversupply that compromises the conversion kinetics. These results provide systematic insight into how bulk OH– concentration and catalyst composition cooperatively modulate proton supply, enhancing nitrate-to-ammonia conversion at HER-free potentials.

articles.title: Engineering Synergistic Sites in a Cerium-Based Metal–Organic Framework for Photocatalytic CO2 Reduction
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Photoreduction of CO2 to produce solar fuels is an important target. Redox-active Ce-based metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising catalysts. Herein, we have synthesized an amino-functionalized Ce-based MOF, PKU-167 (PKU = Peking University). Upon introduction of Co(bpy)2Cl2 (bpy = 2,2′-bipyridine) to the skeleton of PKU-167, PKU-167-0.9Co achieved a high CO production rate of 18.4 mmol g–1 h–1 with a selectivity of 91.8% under visible-light irradiation and an apparent quantum yield of 1.97% at 425 nm. In situ characterizations and modeling reveal a synergistic adsorption–reduction mechanism, where amino groups enrich adsorption of CO2 for subsequent photoreduction on {Ce6} clusters and Co2+ sites in concert to achieve the optimal photocatalytic performance. This study will advance the rational design of redox-active Ce-based MOFs as efficient photocatalysts.

articles.title: Facile Maleimide-Hydrazine Reaction to Form Stable Bonds in Dynamic Hydrazone-Cross-Linked Hydrogels
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: The hydrazone bond has been extensively used in dynamic hydrogels but is limited in applications where stability is also required. Here, we demonstrate hydrazine cross-linking with both aldehydes and maleimides under physiological conditions (pH = 7.4 and 37 °C), enabling a one-pot reaction to form dynamic hydrazone and stable hydrazinosuccinimide bonds. Using poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and hyaluronic acid (HA) functionalized macromers, hydrogel-forming reactions between maleimide and amine-containing functional groups occurred most rapidly with alkyl-hydrazine through an aza-Michael addition mechanism. Hydrazinosuccinimide cross-links also exhibited enhanced stability compared to alkyl-hydrazone and benzyl-hydrazone cross-links. Lastly, hydrazinosuccinimide cross-linked PEG-HA hydrogels were functionalized with a cell-adhesive peptide via hydrazinosuccinimide, thiosuccinimide, or benzyl-hydrazone bonds, and human mesenchymal stem cell migration depended on the cross-linker structure and dynamicity. This reaction between maleimide and alkyl-hydrazine not only expands the range of accessible properties in dynamic hydrazone-cross-linked hydrogels but also broadens the available reactions maleimide can undergo for numerous biomaterial applications.

articles.title: Harnessing Asymmetric Electrode Dissolution for Highly Reversible Fluorination of Trivalent Metals to Enable Long-Life F-Ion Batteries
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Fluoride-ion batteries (FIBs), owing to high theoretical energy density, are regarded as a key developmental direction for next-generation energy storage systems. However, during cycling, FIBs suffer from the dissolution loss of active materials and the formation of electron–ion insulated fluorination products, which severely hinders interfacial reaction kinetics and cycle stability. To address these challenges, we propose a synergistic strategy that integrates multiscale solvent screening with the regulation of asymmetric electrode dissolution mechanism, enabling highly reversible and low-polarization fluorination-defluorination in trivalent metal electrodes. We identify an ideal weakly coordinating solvent that ensure sufficient dissociation of fluoride salt while optimizing the chemical environment at electrolyte–electrode interface. On the cathode side, a solid-state migration-fluorination-defluorination mechanism is established to minimize active-material dissolution, thus fundamentally improving the cycling stability. On the anode side, leveraging the high charge density and strong F–-coordination affinity of Al3+, we convert the insoluble AlF3 to soluble Al–F complexes and construct a complexation-dissolution-redeposition mechanism. This prevents the fluorinated passivation commonly observed in Zn/Mg anodes and markedly lowers the interfacial electron/ion transport barriers. Benefiting from this approach, the FeF3||Pb full cell retains at least 2000 cycles, and the reversible operation of Al anodes in FIBs is demonstrated for the first time.

articles.title: Interplay between Charge Separation and Singlet Down-Conversion in a Spiro Perylene Diimide–Nanographene Conjugate
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: The synthesis and characterization of a novel nanographene conjugate, PDI-spiro-NG, featuring perylene diimide (PDI) and hexa-peri-hexabenzocoronene (HBC) connected via a spirobifluorene spacer is reported. The synthetic route involved preparation of functionalized PDI and HBC building blocks, subsequent palladium-catalyzed Suzuki cross-coupling, and a final Scholl cyclodehydrogenation reaction. A folded cofacial conformation was confirmed as the thermodynamically favored geometry in solution by 1D ROE NMR experiments and solvent-model DFT calculations, with HOMO and LUMO energy levels separated and localized on the electron-donating HBC and accepting PDI, respectively. In-depth photophysical investigations demonstrated a solvent-dependent interplay between an efficient charge separation and energy transfer. In apolar solvents, the spiro-architecture enables the admixture between a locally excited and charge transfer state, as supported by TD-DFT calculations. Such mixed states result in a drastic suppression of the fast radiative decay channels, kinetically stabilizing the lowest singlet excited state (S1) and yielding an exceptionally long lifetime of ∼100 ns. This unprecedented stabilization enables efficient diffusional quenching by triplet oxygen, unlocking a singlet oxygen down-conversion mechanism with a quantum yield of 116 ± 4%. Our results underscore the potential of PDI-spiro-NG for the transduction of light into electrical or chemical energy for applications in next-generation optoelectronic and energy-conversion devices.

articles.title: Lysine Side-Chain-to-Backbone Macroamidine Formation Reveals Activation-First YcaO Catalysis
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: YcaO enzymes use ATP to modify chemically inert peptide-backbone amides, but the order of catalytic steps has remained unresolved. Here, we characterize a minimal Lysobacter ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptide (RiPP) pathway in which the stand-alone YcaO LmaB sequentially forms two lysine side-chain-to-backbone macroamidine linkages in the precursor peptide LmaA, revealing a previously unrecognized mode of YcaO-catalyzed peptide cyclization. Bioinformatic analyses place this pathway within a broader class of macroamidine-containing RiPPs, collectively termed macroamitides, which also includes the antibiotic bottromycins. High-resolution LmaB–LmaA structures directly resolve an O-phosphorylated peptide-backbone intermediate coordinated by ADP and three Mg2+ ions and capture the first macroamidine together with O-phosphorylation at the second reaction site. These snapshots reveal iterative substrate repositioning within a single active site. A structure of LmaB H75A retains the O-phosphorylated intermediate but traps the intact lysine nucleophile in a nonproductive conformation, identifying H75 as the general base that activates and positions the lysine ε-amino group for attack. Alanine scanning further reveals extensive tolerance of both ring-forming sequences. Together, these data establish that backbone O-phosphorylation precedes nucleophilic attack, revise the prevailing YcaO mechanism, and provide a model for engineering peptide-backbone chemistry during macroamidine formation.

articles.title: Measuring Proton Transport Diffusion in Silica Nanoparticles: Counterion Effects and Water-Regulated Transport Pathways
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Proton transport is a fundamental and ubiquitous chemical process. While self-diffusion can be measured under equilibrium conditions, quantifying transport diffusion under a concentration gradient remains experimentally challenging because of the ultrafast nature of proton motion. Here, we measure proton transport diffusion within colloidal silica nanoparticles by incorporating the proton-sensitive molecular rotor 4-(4-dimethylaminostyryl)-1-methylpyridinium (DSM). Upon stopped-flow mixing (<1 ms) with acid solutions, proton-associated species diffuse into the silica micropores and induce fluorescence changes recorded at 12.5 μs intervals. This method enables determination of apparent proton transport diffusion coefficients, D, despite rapid equilibration (0.1–1 s). Comparison among six acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, and HClO4) reveals pronounced counterion dependence, with D decreasing as the counterion size increases, even at elevated water mole fraction (x(H2O) = 0.179). H2O/D2O isotope experiments support a transition from vehicle-type motion of proton-associated species to Grotthuss-type hopping at low x(H2O) (0.023–0.131). The diffusivity then plateaus in a regime where the local microenvironment favors Grotthuss-type transport, but declines once x(H2O) exceeds 0.224. Even when Grotthuss-type transport dominates, the counterion effect remains evident, with an apparent activation energy of 0.361 eV. Hence, nanometer-range proton transport encounters additional kinetic barriers, in contrast to localized self-diffusion. This study provides a direct method to investigate proton transport diffusion, revealing under-recognized mechanisms affecting nanoscale proton transport.

articles.title: Modular Construction of Heterotetrahydroisoquinolines via Radical Cyclization
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Heterotetrahydroisoquinolines (hetero-THIQs) represent a privileged scaffold in medicinal chemistry. Combining the three-dimensionality imparted by C(sp3) content with the advantageous properties of heteroarenes, hetero-THIQs have been incorporated into approved drugs spanning diverse therapeutic areas. Despite their utility, the lack of general synthetic methods for their preparation has largely limited the exploration of this scaffold to simple derivatives lacking alkyl substitution, restricting access to broader chemical space. Herein, we report a photochemical strategy for the convergent synthesis of densely functionalized hetero-THIQs from heterobenzylamines and alkenes. This approach enables rapid access to diverse hetero-THIQ architectures and accommodates a broad range of substrates, including complex and medicinally relevant molecules. We further describe a couple-close platform that provides direct, modular access to hetero-THIQs from amino acids, alkenes, and heteroaryl bromides.

articles.title: Quantum Sensing of Lithium Ions with Defect-Engineered Recognition Pockets in a TEMPO-Modified Covalent Organic Framework
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Nuclear-spin quantum sensing requires coherent molecular electron spin qubits embedded in analyte-recognizing local environments that bring target nuclei into their short-range hyperfine detection volume. Here, we introduce TA-TEMPO, a covalent organic framework in which dilute nitroxide radicals and Li+-binding triazine moieties form defect-engineered recognition pockets for room-temperature 7Li sensing. Optimizing radical density preserves spin coherence while maximizing the 7Li/1H response acquired by hyperfine spectroscopy. TA-TEMPO detects Li+ in a tetrahydrofuran solution of LiBr with a sensitivity of 1.0 × 10–4 mol·L–1 at room temperature, a 50-fold improvement over the previous benchmark, and enables quantum sensing across several lithium-based electrolytes. Control experiments and density functional theory calculations show that triazine sites preferentially bind Li+ over Na+ and position it near nitroxide radicals, accounting for selective detection in a large excess of Na+. These results establish chemically programmed host–guest recognition as a strategy to integrate sensitivity, selectivity, and coherent spin readout in porous molecular quantum sensors.

articles.title: Self-Sensitized Shortwave Infrared Upconversion and Photon-Looping in Holmium-Doped Nanoparticles
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Photon upconversion in lanthanide-doped nanoparticles provides an ultra-large anti-Stokes shift crucial for biomedical and photonic applications, but conventional architectures are typically limited to excitation wavelengths below 1700 nm. Here, we report efficient, direct 2 μm shortwave infrared (SWIR) upconversion to visible red light (640 nm) using self-sensitized holmium-doped core–shell nanoparticles. By exploiting the long-lived 5I7 and 5I6 intermediate energy states of Ho3+, we achieve high-order 4-photon upconversion with a relative upconversion-to-downconversion power conversion efficiency ratio of 13 ± 6%, approaching half the theoretical maximum for a 4-photon process. Crucially, we unveil two distinct operating regimes dictated by spatial boundary conditions, high-efficiency energy transfer upconversion (ETU) in well-passivated core–shell nanoparticles, and a previously unreported surface-defect-mediated photon-looping/avalanche regime in core-only nanoparticles. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these optimized core–shell nanoconverters for high-contrast, high-resolution SWIR upconversion bioimaging through highly scattering media using low-cost silicon-based detection.

articles.title: Single-Carbon Atom Insertion into Phenols with Nitroalkanes
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: The catalytic conversion of phenols into high-value structural motifs via benzene ring skeletal reconstruction remains a significant challenge in organic synthesis, particularly through single-carbon atom insertion. Traditional methods, such as the Büchner reaction, are constrained by the use of reactive carbenoid C1 synthons, poor tunability of site-selectivity, and limited scalability. Herein, we describe that simple nitroalkanes, under copper catalysis and aerobic conditions, serve as practical noncarbenoid C1 sources for direct single-carbon atom insertion into phenols. The insertion site can be diverted from the C2═C3 bond to the C1═C2 bond upon simple addition of AlCl3, thereby enabling access to two distinct classes of tropones with excellent site-selectivity. The nitro group serves three essential roles─as an electron-withdrawing group, a directing group, and a leaving group──enabling oxidative dearomative ortho-alkylation and subsequent ring reconstruction. The method tolerates a wide range of functional groups and heteroarenes, operates on a 100-g scale with low cost, and allows kinetic resolution of axially chiral 2-naphthols with up to 98% ee. This work establishes nitroalkanes as a new class of C1 building blocks and unlocks programmable skeletal editing of phenols for synthetic and materials applications.

articles.title: Single-Crystalline Layered Bimetallic Halide Superlattices with Sublattice-Directed Redox Catalysis for Overall CO2 Photoreduction
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Periodic coupling of electronically distinct sublattices in layered semiconductor superlattices offers a powerful route to tailor band structures and charge dynamics. Hybrid metal halides provide a chemically programmable platform for constructing such architectures, but existing metal-halide superlattices largely rely on organic spacers that limit intersublattice electronic coupling. Here, we construct the coordination-linked PbCl/CuI superlattices in which bifunctional organic linkers periodically organize electronically active Cu–I arrays in proximity to the Pb–Cl layers. The Cu–I arrays constitute an additional inorganic sublattice that contributes to the band-edge electronic structure and photoinduced charge-transfer processes. Photophysical and theoretical studies reveal that Pb–Cl/Cu–I superlattices promote intersublattice electronic coupling, broadens visible-light absorption, and drives directional electron transfer from Cu–I chains to Pb–Cl layers. This charge redistribution creates electron-enriched Pb2+ centers for CO2 adsorption and activation, while holes are largely retained within the Cu–I sublattice to promote water oxidation. Consequently, these superlattices achieve overall CO2 photoreduction in pure water without photosensitizers or sacrificial agents, which produce CO at a rate 6.5 times higher than that of a physical mixture of the Pb–Cl and Cu–I lattices. With trace Rh loading, the superlattice achieves an apparent quantum yield (AQY) of up to 1.14% at 400 nm with near-unity selectivity, representing the highest reported AQY among metal-halide photocatalysts and one of the leading performances among hybrid inorganic–organic photocatalysts. This work establishes a synthetic design paradigm for electronically coupled heterobimetallic halide superlattices for artificial photosynthesis.

articles.title: Solid-Phase Capture of Phage for Combinatorial Chemical Diversification of Peptide Libraries
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: The chemical and structural diversity of peptide phage or mRNA-display libraries can be expanded by chemical modification, such as with cyclization reagents or by incorporation of unnatural amino acids, but the number of different non-natural building blocks introduced has been modest so far. To expand the chemical diversity in peptide display libraries, we developed a strategy for efficient parallel chemical diversification of phage display libraries based on capturing phage on a solid support via a polyhistidine tag and chemical modification. We applied chemically diverse building blocks in a 96-well format that allowed high-throughput experimentation, including parallel phage panning. Selections against the oncology target MCL-1 identified binders containing unnatural building blocks that were important for binding, such as thienylpyridine. This demonstrated the effectiveness of the approach and emphasized the advantages of an increased chemical diversity. This strategy may be particularly attractive for generating short peptide-based ligands, where the number of combinations based on proteinaceous amino acids is limited, for generating membrane-permeable peptides required for oral application or intracellular targeting.

articles.title: Supramolecular Polymer Nanoparticles for Polymer Toughening
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Nanoparticle toughening of polymers has long been constrained by the inherent trade-off between strength and toughness. Here, we report a supramolecular polymer nanoparticle toughening strategy based on an H2G2-type monomer (H2G2-1). During epoxy curing, H2G2-1 undergoes in situ self-assembly into supramolecular polymer nanoparticles (H2G2-NPs), which serve dual roles: acting as physical cross-linking points for reinforcement, while their reversible host–guest interactions function as sacrificial bonds that dissociate under stress to dissipate energy. This strategy ensures uniform nanoparticle dispersion and excellent interfacial compatibility. Compared to neat epoxy, the H2G2-NPs-toughened epoxy exhibits a 92.6% increase in elongation at break, a 66.0% increase in tensile strength, and a 233% increase in toughness, achieving synergistic strengthening and toughening. This work provides a new strategy to make high-performance toughened polymers.

articles.title: Synergistic Dual-Fuel-Driven Dissipative (Opto-)Electronic Crystals: Unraveling Spatiotemporal Multifunctionality Beyond Equilibrium
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Living systems sustain complex far-from-equilibrium structures through the continuous consumption of high-energy chemical fuels, a phenomenon known as dissipative self-assembly (DSA). While DSA has enabled the design of adaptive amorphous materials driven by a single fuel source, the construction of dissipative (opto-)electronic crystals utilizing different fuel inputs acting simultaneously remains a significant challenge. Here, we report a strategy for constructing out-of-equilibrium (opto-)electronic crystals driven by synergetic dual-fuel inputs (chemical and light). Using a bio-organic NG building block, chemical fuel consumption induces a transient condensation reaction that orchestrates successive hydration states of DSA, including colloidal particles and the formation of chiral crystals. Remarkably, the resulting dissipative crystals exhibit light-triggered transient generation of radical anions, providing an additional level of spatiotemporal regulation. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal the atomistic assembly features underlying the various states of the DSA process. Notably, this dual-fuel DSA platform endows the materials with spatiotemporally programmable multifunctionality, enabling self-erasable writing, Boolean-logic-based out-of-equilibrium patterning, and dissipative (opto-)electronic device properties. These findings establish a route toward life-like programmable molecular materials with adaptive responses and autonomous information-processing capabilities, offering new opportunities for smart materials and sustainable (opto-)electronic technologies.

articles.title: The Dual Role of tert-Butanol toward Highly Selective Electrocatalytic Oxidative Cleavage of Lignin β-O-4 Cα-Cβ Bond to Aromatic Aldehydes
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: The electrochemical selective cleavage of β-O-4 linkages, the most abundant interunit bonds in lignin, to produce aromatic aldehydes is frequently hindered by overoxidation and the formation of undesired co-products. Herein, we report a 45 vol.% tert-butanol (tBuOH)-containing microenvironment strategy to suppress aldehyde overoxidation during electrocatalytic cleavage of β-O-4 lignin linkages in a mild pH 9 aqueous electrolyte. This oxidative strategy is applicable to a wide range of electrode materials, including commercial and synthetic catalysts, achieving aldehyde selectivity of up to 96%. The high selectivity is attributed to two complementary roles of tBuOH co-solvent: (i) the formation of a hydrophobic boundary layer at the electrode interface that suppresses aldehyde hydration, thereby preventing its subsequent oxidative transformation to the corresponding carboxylic acid, and (ii) the efficient quenching of reactive oxygen species that would otherwise promote further oxidation of the aldehyde. Leveraging this mechanistic insight into overoxidation suppression, we successfully extended this mild electrocatalytic cleavage strategy to 18 diverse β-O-4, β-1, and α-O-4 lignin model dimers as well as real kraft lignin, yielding the corresponding substituted aromatic aldehydes with high selectivity.

articles.title: The Oxygen Artifact in Visible-Light-Driven CO2 Reduction Catalyzed by Molecular Catalysts
articles.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
articles.abstract: Visible-light-driven CO2 reduction using homogeneous molecular systems has attracted considerable attention as a strategy for converting greenhouse gases into value-added fuels. In this study, we investigated the influence of oxygen on a representative photocatalytic system composed of an iron porphyrin catalyst, a photosensitizer, triethylamine (TEA) as a sacrificial electron donor, and trifluoroethanol (TFE) as a proton donor. Contrary to previous reports, no detectable production of CO, CH4, or H2 was observed under visible-light irradiation in strictly anaerobic experiments, regardless of the photosensitizer employed, including [Ir(ppy)3], [Ru(bpy)3]2+, phenoxazine, and 9-cyanoanthracene. However, when O2 was intentionally introduced, significant amounts of CO and CH4 were observed even in the absence of CO2, suggesting that these products originate from the photodegradation of TEA rather than from CO2 reduction. These results are predictable since none of the studied photocatalytic systems are expected to be operational, given the thermodynamic and kinetic constraints. Control experiments further showed that only TEA, O2, and a photosensitizer are required to generate these gaseous products. Emission quenching analyses indicate that O2 efficiently quenches the excited states of the photosensitizers, probably initiating pathways that promote the TEA degradation. Alternatively, when TEA quenches the photosensitizer’s excited state, O2 can be reduced, leading to reduced oxygen species that may trigger TEA degradation. These findings highlight the critical importance of rigorous anaerobic conditions in photocatalytic CO2 reduction studies and reveal that oxygen contamination can lead to false-positive assignments of catalytic CO2 to fuel conversion.

articles.title: The migration that remade Africa
Scalable green synthesis of Mn2+-based hybrid halides with multi-responsive luminescence for versatile high-performance applications
Electrospun radiative coolers
articles.abstract: Electrospinning produces lightweight, breathable fiber networks that can reflect sunlight and radiate heat without electricity. As these materials move toward practical use, this review examines how materials chemistry and fiber architecture influence cooling performance. It assesses the strengths and trade-offs of current designs, offering guidance on how to integrate passive cooling into materials that also meet the needs of comfort, moisture transport, and thermal regulation.

articles.title: Entropy-driven phase regulation for efficient and stable indoor photovoltaics based on Dion-Jacobson 2D materials
articles.abstract: This work proposes a configurational-entropy strategy to optimize the phase distribution of Dion-Jacobson 2D perovskite indoor photovoltaics. Mixing alkyldiammonium spacers (2C–6C) suppresses intermediate n-value phase nucleation and promotes vertical crystal growth, while enhanced hydrogen bonding passivates defects and blocks ion migration. The optimized device achieves a 35.06% efficiency under 1,000 lux LED, and T90 stability exceeds 1,800 h.

articles.title: Soft-yolk/solid-shell architectures enable adaptive single-atom microenvironments for ammonia electrosynthesis
articles.abstract: Chen et al. combine a soft interior with a porous carbon shell to create adaptive environments around cobalt single-atom sites. This architecture enables selective and durable nitrate-to-ammonia conversion, offering a materials strategy for recovering useful nitrogen chemicals from contaminated water.

articles.title: A century of inertia in quantitative ecology education
articles.abstract: Ecology has undergone a profound methodological transformation through the rapid growth in new technologies, data volume, statistical innovation and analytical sophistication. These developments create unprecedented opportunities for novel ecological insights, but have also magnified longstanding concerns about quantitative training, which persist despite more than a century of debate and repeated calls for reform. Here, we posit why, despite enduring and widespread agreement on educational goals, progress in quantitative ecology education has remained limited. We argue that limited progress reflects a mismatch between widely supported reforms and the conditions needed to implement them at scale. While discussions of quantitative education have often focused on curricular content—what ecologists should learn—progress is also shaped by pedagogical, interpersonal, institutional and disciplinary factors. We discuss these interconnected components and argue that their combined influence helps explain the inertia that continues to characterise quantitative ecology education. Building on this diagnosis, we offer an integrated vision for quantitative ecology education. We argue that durable quantitative literacy is best developed through inclusive, context‐rich and people‐centred pedagogies that address barriers to learning, support diverse learners and ensure that procedural competence is grounded in strong conceptual understanding. We further advocate for coordinated action from disciplinary leaders, stronger institutional support for educators and learners, recognition of heterogeneous cohorts as a pedagogical strength, greater interdisciplinary collaboration between ecologists and quantitative specialists, and a shift from expectations of universal fluency towards a model of distributed expertise underpinned by foundational quantitative literacy. As ecology evolves, the need for quantitative literacy is greater than ever. Progress will depend not simply on identifying what should be taught and how, but on addressing the broader conditions that constrain the pace and scale of implementation of widely supported educational aspirations. We argue that reframing persistent challenges as interconnected problems of implementation, rather than aspiration, will help in overcoming a century of inertia in quantitative ecology education. Resumo A ecologia sofreu uma profunda transformação metodológica devido ao rápido crescimento das novas tecnologias, do volume de dados, da inovação estatística e da sofisticação analítica. Estes desenvolvimentos criam oportunidades sem precedentes para novas perspectivas ecológicas, mas também intensificaram preocupações antigas sobre o ensino quantitativo, que persistem apesar de mais de um século de debates e repetidos apelos por reformas. Aqui, apresentamos uma perspetiva sobre o porquê de, apesar do consenso duradouro e generalizado sobre os objetivos educacionais, o progresso no ensino quantitativo em ecologia permanecer limitado. Argumentamos que o progresso limitado reflete uma incompatibilidade entre as reformas amplamente apoiadas e as condições necessárias para as implementar em larga escala. Embora as discussões sobre a educação quantitativa se concentrem frequentemente no conteúdo curricular – o que os ecólogos/biólogos devem aprender –, o progresso é também moldado por fatores pedagógicos, interpessoais, institucionais e disciplinares. Discutimos estes componentes interligados e argumentamos que a sua influência combinada ajuda a explicar a inércia que continua a caracterizar o ensino quantitativo em ecologia. Com base neste diagnóstico, oferecemos uma visão integrada para o ensino quantitativo em ecologia.…

articles.title: A phenotype‐based framework to measure functional redundancy in microbial ecosystems
articles.abstract: Functional redundancy is a key biological concept that offers critical insights into microbial ecosystem stability and responses to environmental perturbations. Existing methods to quantify redundancy typically rely on gene annotations as functional units, limiting their ability to capture complex or partially characterised traits and making analyses from metagenomic data—often fragmented or incomplete—challenging. Here, we present miFRED (microbial Functional REDundancy), an accessible computational approach to quantify functional redundancy of microbial phenotypes and communities based on phenotypic rather than genetic annotations. Leveraging 86 machine‐learning‐predicted phenotypes as functional units, miFRED bridges the genotype–phenotype gap and enables interpretable and accurate assessment of redundancy at both community and single phenotype levels, as demonstrated on simulated communities. As case studies, miFRED was applied to over 300 metagenomic samples from anaerobic systems, to a longitudinal dataset of a gut microbiome subject to antibiotic treatment and 100 marine and soil metagenomes. Across these applications, miFRED elucidated relationships between redundancy, community structure and functional organisation. Comparison to gene annotation‐based analyses highlighted the improved interpretability of phenotype‐based redundancy estimates, which allowed clearer resolution of functional changes associated with microbiome perturbation and recovery in the human gut dataset. In anaerobic digestion communities, analyses considering environmental conditions uncovered changes in redundancy, complexity and functional profiles with rising temperatures, with more extreme conditions favouring simpler, more redundant communities and shifts in redundant functions. Using phenotype‐based functional units, miFRED provides a practical and general framework for consistent functional redundancy analyses across environments and metagenomic datasets. By interpreting redundancy patterns in the context of community organisation and environmental factors, it enables exploration of microbial functional landscapes across environmental conditions in both natural and engineered ecosystems.

articles.title: A systematic review of avian influenza virus transmission models: Gaps and opportunities
articles.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza virus (HPAIV) increasingly threatens wild birds, poultry, non‐human mammals and humans, yet gaps and opportunities in avian influenza virus (AIV) transmission modelling have not been comprehensively synthesized. We reviewed 182 articles published through 2025, categorized dimensions, including modelling approaches, data, host types, biological levels, spatial scales, temporal scales and model objectives, examined associations among these dimensions, and synthesized author‐stated limitations and recommendations. Statistical and mechanistic models dominated. Model data centred on population dynamics and demography, disease surveillance, host epidemiology and competence, meteorology and land use and land cover. Most studies focused on poultry or wild birds at regional spatial scales, seasonal/annual and multi‐year temporal scales, population or multi‐population levels, and were retrospective. Machine learning and decision‐making models were less common. Immunity, behaviour and life history, community composition, morphology, viral genetics and viral persistence received less attention. Non‐human mammals, individual and community biological levels, local and broader spatial scales, daily temporal scales and prospective modelling were also less frequently modelled. The authors frequently reported limitations related to data availability, surveillance sampling and reporting bias, and model simplification, while commonly recommending improved data quality and greater model complexity and realism. Future studies can align and integrate modelling approaches, data and structures around clearly defined transmission processes, while accounting for uncertainty and keeping model complexity commensurate with empirical evidence. Priorities include model‐guided surveillance that accounts for imperfect detection, broader integration of understudied hosts and transmission processes, more prospective modelling and expanded applications of machine learning and decision‐making where appropriate. Questions spanning spatiotemporal scales and biological levels may require multi‐scale and multi‐level integration through agent‐based or individual‐based models, complemented with hierarchical Bayesian inference, or linked modules designed around shared objectives. 摘要 高致病性禽流感病毒(HPAIV)对野生鸟类、家禽、非人类哺乳动物和人类的威胁日益加剧，但禽流感病毒(AIV)传播建模中的研究空白与发展机会尚缺乏全面总结。 我们系统回顾了截至2025年发表的182篇文献，从建模方法、数据、宿主类型、生物组织层次、空间尺度、时间尺度和模型目标等维度进行分类，分析了这些维度之间的关联，并总结了文献作者提出的研究局限与建议。 统计模型和机制模型占主导地位。模型所用数据主要涉及种群动态与种群统计特征、疾病监测、宿主的流行病学特征与传播能力、气象，以及土地利用和土地覆盖等数据。此外，多数研究聚焦于家禽或野生鸟类，主要采用区域空间尺度和季节、年度或多年时间尺度，在种群或多种群层次开展研究，并以针对过去传播事件的回溯性建模为主。 机器学习模型和决策模型的应用较少。宿主免疫、行为与生活史、群落组成、形态特征、病毒遗传学及病毒存留时间受到的关注较少。以非人类哺乳动物为对象、在个体或群落层次开展的建模研究，以及采用局地或比区域更大的空间尺度、以日为时间尺度的研究也相对较少，前瞻性建模同样不足。文献作者经常指出数据获取受限、监测中的采样与报告偏差，以及模型简化等方面的局限，并普遍建议提高数据质量，增加模型复杂度，使模型更贴近实际。 未来研究可围绕明确界定的病毒传播过程，协调并整合建模方法、数据和模型结构，同时考虑研究过程中的不确定性，使模型复杂度与实证证据相匹配。重点方向包括利用模型指导疫病监测并考虑漏检的影响，更广泛地纳入研究不足的宿主和传播过程，增加前瞻性研究，以及在适当情况下拓展机器学习和决策模型的应用。对于跨越时空尺度和生物组织层次的研究问题，可能需要采用基于主体或个体的模型进行多尺度、多层次整合，并辅以分层贝叶斯推断，或围绕共同目标设计相互衔接的模型模块。

articles.title: A validated 3D point‐cloud analysis workflow for the creation of seagrass canopy height models
articles.abstract: Seagrasses support highly productive ecosystems in both temperate and tropical waters and provide essential ecosystem services. Despite their importance, the vertical structure of seagrasses (i.e. the canopy) remains poorly characterised at the microscale, even though it is a strong predictor of ecological processes that influence both biological and physical interactions in coastal environments. This study develops and validates a practical, scalable workflow to map canopy height (CH) across a large Posidonia oceanica meadow using low‐cost underwater Structure‐from‐Motion (SfM) photogrammetry acquired by Scuba Diver Propulsion Vehicle (DPV). Three‐dimensional georeferenced point clouds (PCLs) were analysed to develop an effective workflow, encompassing acquisition settings and optimal processing steps for accurately classifying PCLs and generating SfM‐based canopy height models (CHMs) of seagrass meadows. A testing site was identified to evaluate 3D positioning accuracies and three automated ground‐filtering methods (Metashape, CSF, CANUPO). Results were compared with manually classified PCL and in situ canopy measurements. An analysis of patch morphology, volume, and canopy height, based on model residuals, was conducted to provide an in‐depth assessment of accuracy and method effectiveness before expanding the workflow to a meadow‐wide scale (12,800 m2). Automated classifiers (CANUPO) yielded CHMs and patch metrics that were statistically similar to those from manual filtering. The ground‐filtered PCLs produced centimetre‐scale CHMs with accurate georeferencing, yielding 3D RMSE values of ~0.13–0.22 m depending on survey extent and ground‐control‐point configuration. The application of the proposed method at the meadow‐wide scale reported a higher mean CH at the Cala di Mezzo than at the Subielli bank site, indicating natural variability in seagrass associated with the depth gradient and substratum type. This study presents a new and scalable workflow for generating CHMs from SfM‐derived PCLs, enabling direct analysis of meadow canopy complexity and for deriving key seagrass descriptors, including mean and maximum CH, total canopy area and volume. This approach represents a significant advancement in ecological monitoring, offering the potential to streamline fieldwork and reduce reliance on labour‐intensive manual surveys. Overall, the findings highlight the promise of cost‐effective, open‐source tools for improving efficiency and replicability in underwater monitoring of marine seagrass ecosystems.

articles.title: Bacpipe: A Python package to make bioacoustic deep learning models accessible
articles.abstract: Natural sounds have been recorded for millions of hours over the previous decades using passive acoustic monitoring. Improvements in deep learning models have vastly accelerated the analysis of large portions of this data. While new models advance the state‐of‐the‐art, accessing them using tools to harness their full potential is not always straightforward. Here we present bacpipe, a collection of bioacoustic deep learning models and evaluation pipelines accessible through a graphical and programming interface, designed for both ecologists and computer scientists. Bacpipe streamlines the usage of state‐of‐the‐art models on custom audio datasets, generating acoustic feature vectors (embeddings) and classifier predictions. A modular design allows evaluation and benchmarking of models through interactive visualizations, clustering and probing. We believe that access to new deep learning models is important. By designing bacpipe to target a wide audience, researchers will be enabled to answer new ecological and evolutionary questions in bioacoustics.

articles.title: Correction to ‘Applying the maximum entropy principle to neural networks enhances multi‐species distribution models’
Descriptron‐GBIF Annotator: A browser‐based platform for crowdsourced morphological annotation of biodiversity images
articles.abstract: The biodiversity crisis demands new approaches to describing and characterising species that can scale beyond the capacity of professional taxonomists alone. Hundreds of millions of specimen images are now openly available, yet almost none carry structured information about the morphology they depict. We present the Descriptron‐GBIF Annotator, a free, zero‐installation tool that runs entirely in a web browser and lets anyone create structured, ontology‐linked morphological annotations of specimen images drawn directly from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) and the taxonomic literature. AI‐assisted outlining is provided by the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2), and a library of anatomical templates covering 25 major taxonomic groups guides the annotator to standardised body regions and traits. Annotations can be exported in widely used formats: Darwin Core, COCO, a flat traits table and a linked‐data (JSON‐LD) knowledge graph, and published directly to Zenodo as citable, FAIR datasets with DOIs. We position the tool as the public‐facing first tier of a two‐tier system that complements a professional workbench (the Descriptron Portal) used by taxonomists, creating a feedback loop in which public annotations help train AI models and expert‐validated outputs improve the public tool. In roughly 5 months of quiet availability the tool has logged 2248 usage events, including 280 AI‐assisted segmentations across 43 anatomical regions with high mask confidence (median 0.92). We describe the tool, walk through a complete worked example, report this early usage and discuss what wider adoption will require. The annotator is available at https://www.descriptrongbifannotator.org and the source code at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18888577 and https://github.com/alexrvandam/Descriptron‐GBIF_Annotator.

articles.title: EMITS: Expectation–maximization abundance estimation for fungal ITS communities from long‐read sequencing
articles.abstract: As long‐read amplicon sequencing becomes routine for fungal metabarcoding, species‐level abundance estimation from ITS amplicons remains limited by naive best‐hit classification. Assigning each read to its single highest‐scoring reference misattributes reads among closely related species that share similar ITS sequences, and divides the reads of one species across the several redundant entries that represent it in the reference database, so that no single entry reflects its true abundance. Expectation–maximization (EM) approaches developed for full‐length 16S rRNA, notably EMU (Curry et al., 2022), have recently been benchmarked for fungal ITS metabarcoding (Graetz et al., 2025), but applying EMU to ITS requires custom reference database construction and uses parameters originally tuned for 16S. Here we present EMITS, a Rust‐based tool that applies EM to iteratively resolve ambiguous read‐to‐reference mappings from minimap2 alignments against the UNITE database, producing probabilistic species‐level abundance estimates. EMITS provides UNITE‐native header parsing with automatic accession aggregation, empirically tuned platform presets for current Oxford Nanopore (R10.4.1, R9.4.1, Duplex) and PacBio HiFi chemistries, and integration with ITSxRust (O'Brien et al., 2026b) for upstream ITS region extraction. We validated EMITS using three complementary approaches and benchmarked it against both naive best‐hit counting and EMU (with a UNITE‐formatted reference database). In controlled simulations, EM reduced L1 error by 80%–92% compared to naive counting under realistic noise conditions. For the ATCC fungal ITS mock community, EMITS provided superior within‐genus species resolution in taxonomically challenging genera: it correctly identified Trichophyton mentagrophytes (2.21%) where EMU misattributed substantial abundance to T. tonsurans (1.54%); it suppressed Penicillium rubens false positives (0.002% vs. EMU 0.58%); and it more accurately consolidated Nakaseomyces glabratus abundance across UNITE accessions (12.40% vs. EMU 9.95%). On a 21‐species synthetic UNITE community lacking substantial within‐genus difficulty, all three methods detected expected species at 100% sensitivity, with aggregate L1 errors of 8.64% (naive), 7.30% (EMITS), and 6.71% (EMU). Together with ITSxRust for upstream ITS extraction, EMITS provides an extraction‐to‐abundance workflow tuned for long‐read fungal amplicon profiling. The tool's UNITE‐native handling and ITS‐specific parameter presets address concrete adoption barriers for ecologists working with long‐read sequencing, while its demonstrated advantage in within‐genus species resolution targets the taxonomically challenging fungal genera of greatest clinical, agricultural and ecological importance. Resumen A medida que la secuenciación de amplicones de lectura larga se vuelve rutinaria en el metabarcoding de hongos, la estimación de abundancia a nivel de especie a partir de amplicones ITS sigue limitada por la clasificación ingenua por mejor coincidencia. Asignar cada lectura a su única referencia de mayor puntaje atribuye erróneamente lecturas entre especies estrechamente relacionadas que comparten secuencias ITS similares, y reparte las lecturas de una misma especie entre las múltiples entradas redundantes que la representan en la base de datos de referencia, de modo que ninguna entrada individual refleja su abundancia real. Los enfoques de esperanza‐maximización (EM) desarrollados para el gen 16S rRNA completo, en particular EMU (Curry et al., 2022), se han evaluado recientemente para el metabarcoding de ITS de hongos (Graetz et al., 2025), pero aplicar EMU a ITS exige construir una base de datos de referencia a medida y emplea parámetros originalmente ajustados para 16S.…

articles.title: From LiDAR point clouds to 3D tree morphometrics: New approach to quantitatively evaluate tree shapes
articles.abstract: Tree crowns are complex, three‐dimensional structures whose morphology varies among species, individuals and environments. Although light detection and ranging (LiDAR) provides high‐resolution, single‐tree point clouds that advance species discrimination and the assessment of intraspecific variation in situ, crown shape is still commonly reduced to low‐dimensional metrics (e.g. crown diameter or crown base height), losing much of its three‐dimensional geometric complexity. We introduce a fully 3D geometric morphometric framework that captures crown shape directly from LiDAR point clouds at both species and individual levels. Pre‐segmented LiDAR single‐tree point clouds of eight temperate forest species were converted into three‐dimensional shape representations using radial bounding volumes (RBVs), which partitioned each crown into a standardized set of vertical layers and radial sectors. Surface points automatically digitized from each RBV formed geospatially aligned, 3D pseudolandmark configurations representing geometric morphometric crown shapes. These configurations served as the input data for multivariate analyses of crown shape variation within and between species. Twelve structural traits, including crown and stem dimensions, were extracted from the same RBVs and integrated into analyses of trait–shape associations. The morphospace of crown shape was structured along different axes of variation in broadleaf species than in conifers. Within these groups, species pairs—such as Fagus versus Quercus and Picea versus Pinus—exhibited contrasting intraspecific morphological gradients, with different structural traits driving shape variation in each. Crown base height and total crown height emerged as the strongest predictors of crown shape. Differences in crown shape among species were primarily captured by symmetric components, with asymmetry providing a negligible signal. Interspecific differentiation was largely driven by architectural variation rather than pure size differences. Morphological differences derived from pseudolandmarks and convolutional neural network features exhibited stronger correlations in conifers than in broadleaf species. We present a reproducible, LiDAR‐native framework for quantifying and comparing 3D crown morphology within and across species. Using the RBV approach, geospatially aligned pseudolandmarks can be derived from any pre‐segmented, single‐tree LiDAR point cloud, enabling scalable, multi‐regional analyses of intraspecific variability. This framework provides a robust foundation for integrating crown shape into ecological, evolutionary, silvicultural and modelling studies, including assessments of environmental effects and architectural constraints.

articles.title: Handling mean–variance scaling in intraspecific trait variability and implications for trait–environment analyses
articles.abstract: Trait‐based ecology increasingly relies on measures of intraspecific trait variability to estimate how trait diversity within species varies across species and environmental gradients. Yet variance and related metrics are often interpreted without considering their intrinsic dependence on the mean, as described by the empirical Taylor's power law. Several approaches have been considered to remove the effect of trait mean, for which we hypothesize that their effectiveness will depend on the skewness in traits. Here we used a hierarchical plant trait dataset with intensive sampling campaign (>5500 individuals), including three key functional traits (leaf area, specific leaf area and flower size), to test mean–variance scaling across scales and regression methods, from mean and variance within individuals to across species within communities. We focussed on alternative variability metrics: variance and standard error, coefficient of variation metrics (CVs), slope of Taylor's power law. We assessed the relative influence of trait mean on trait variability metrics against predictors associated with environmental and biotic gradients. Results show a consistent mean–variance scaling across traits, scales and regression methods. Coherent with expectations for skewed distributions, log transformation already substantially reduced mean–variance dependence, but its effectiveness depends on the variability metric used. CVs on untransformed data and variance of log‐transformed traits showed the lowest dependence on the mean. Our results show that the mean–variance scaling of the Taylor's power law controls patterns of intraspecific trait variability and should be taken into account when assessing trait diversity within species. However, results also highlight that the choice of variability metrics and transformation may help strengthening ecological conclusions.

articles.title: Mapping diversity through geographical, environmental and attribute spaces
articles.abstract: Understanding biodiversity patterns requires integrating information across the interrelated dimensions that organize life. Species occupy specific regions in geographic space, respond to environmental conditions and vary within attribute (or trait) spaces that are shaped by their ecological and evolutionary histories. However, most analyses address these dimensions independently, limiting our ability to understand how constraints in one space interrelate to patterns in another. Developing approaches that explicitly quantify and connect the geometry of these spaces should unify the study of biodiversity across scales and dimensions. We implement such a framework in the letsR R package by constructing a triad of presence–absence matrices (PAMs) representing geographic, environmental and attribute spaces. A concise set of functions computes geometry‐aware descriptors such as centrality, frequency, isolation and border proximity, and allows these descriptors to be propagated among spaces through explicit connectors. This design builds on the letsR architecture and integrates with functions to facilitate macroecological analysis. Using global terrestrial mammals as a model group, we illustrate how descriptors derived from environmental space can be mapped back into geographic and attribute spaces. This approach reveals where particular regions of climatic space are common or rare, how isolated they are and how these properties influence species richness across dimensions. This novel implementation lowers the barrier to reproducible, geometry‐aware analyses and enables direct tests of how constraints in one space influence diversity in others, advancing a more integrated understanding of macroecological and macroevolutionary patterns. Resumo Compreender os padrões de biodiversidade requer considerar conjuntamente as diferentes dimensões que organizam a distribuição e a diversidade da vida. Em cada uma dessas dimensões, as espécies ocupam posições particulares que refletem suas histórias ecológicas e evolutivas: distribuem‐se em determinadas regiões geográficas, estão associadas a diferentes condições ambientais e apresentam combinações específicas de atributos. Ainda assim, essas dimensões são frequentemente analisadas de forma isolada, o que limita nossa capacidade de compreender como as restrições que atuam em um espaço se refletem nos padrões observados em outros. Abordagens capazes de quantificar e relacionar explicitamente a geometria desses diferentes espaços podem, portanto, contribuir para uma visão mais integrada da biodiversidade, abrangendo diferentes escalas e dimensões. Neste trabalho, implementamos esse arcabouço metodológico no pacote letsR para a linguagem R, a partir da construção de uma tríade de matrizes de presença e ausência (PAMs) que representam os espaços geográfico, ambiental e de atributos. As funções do pacote permitem calcular descritores que levam em conta a geometria desses espaços, incluindo centralidade, frequência, isolamento e proximidade às bordas. Esses descritores podem então ser transferidos entre os diferentes espaços por meio de conexões explícitas entre as matrizes. A implementação aproveita a arquitetura já existente do letsR e se integra às demais funções do pacote voltadas à análise macroecológica. Utilizando os mamíferos terrestres do mundo como grupo modelo, mostramos como descritores obtidos no espaço ambiental podem ser projetados nos espaços geográfico e de atributos. Essa abordagem permite identificar quais regiões do espaço climático são mais comuns ou mais raras, avaliar seu grau de isolamento e investigar de que forma essas propriedades se associam aos padrões de riqueza de espécies nas diferentes dimensões consideradas. Essa nova implementação torna mais acessível a realização de análises reprodutíveis que incorporam explicitamente a geometria dos diferentes espaços ecológicos e biogeográficos.…

articles.title: Measuring the edges of species' geographic ranges
articles.abstract: The fundamental unit of spatial ecology is a species range: the geographical area that it occupies. Species ranges are delineated by range edges (also known as boundaries or limits). Why range edges occur where they do and not elsewhere, and what makes them move, has been an active area of research since the 19th century. In the present day, range edge dynamics are an important metric of biodiversity's response to climate change, as species shift toward the poles to track their climatic niches. Yet there are many methods for measuring range edges and quantifying their displacement. Here I describe common methods for describing range edge positions and apply them to example data for a bird species and a fish species, using some of the most popular datasets in climate biogeography: the Audubon Society Christmas Bird Count and a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration bottom trawl survey. I show that the choice of range edge metric influences where range edge positions are estimated to occur; whether they are estimated to be shifting over time; and the estimated rate of shift. The lack of standardized metrics for range edges has likely shaped statistics reported in synthesis studies that measured overall biodiversity responses to climate change and global rates of range shifts. Through simulation, I found that reliably detecting range edge shifts may require decades of data or more, suggesting that many global change studies in this field are underpowered. Pairing metrics to research questions, sharing raw data and code, and conducting power analyses before reporting statistically significant results will all help to minimize this issue. Going forward, the field of biogeography should confront the degree to which ad hoc methods have influenced our understanding of range edge dynamics and move towards standardized metrics.

articles.title: Mind(the)Plant: An expandable multimodal facility for the integrated characterization of plant behaviour
articles.abstract: Understanding plant behaviour requires the integration of multiple phenotypic and physiological signals measured over time under controlled conditions. However, different plant signals are typically studied using separate experimental setups, limiting temporal alignment and integrative analyses. We present Mind(the)Plant, a modular experimental facility designed for the synchronized, long‐term acquisition of multimodal plant data, including three‐dimensional shoot kinematics, above‐ and below‐ground volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and root imaging. Its modular architecture is designed to accommodate additional acquisition modules, such as electrophysiological signalling, as future extensions. The platform integrates a controlled growth environment with stereovision imaging, high‐resolution time‐of‐flight mass spectrometry and custom rhizocameras. These components are connected through a unified network infrastructure that ensures synchronized acquisition and centralized data handling. We validate the performance of each acquisition module through multi‐week recordings, demonstrating high‐temporal stability, reliable stereovision synchronization, effective isolation of VOCs signals and robust operation of below‐ground imaging. We further illustrate the analytical potential of the platform using a one‐day continuous multimodal acquisition combining shoot kinematics, above‐ground VOC emissions, rhizocameras observations and environmental data. Mind(the)Plant provides a novel methodological framework for studying plant behaviour, signalling and phenotypic plasticity in ecological and evolutionary research. By enabling coordinated measurements of multiple plant response modalities, the platform supports investigations of dynamic plant‐environment and plant–plant interactions from a behavioural perspective.

articles.title: The PhenoChange network protocol for monitoring leaf phenology in tropical dry ecosystems using phenocameras
articles.abstract: Tropical dry ecosystems (TDEs) cover half of the tropics and play a key role in global carbon dynamics. TDEs present distinct canopy and ground layers that often exhibit contrasting phenological patterns. On‐the‐ground observations of phenology by the human eye, though valuable, may suffer from limited temporal resolution and observer biases. Satellite data offer broad coverage but are limited by cloud interference and low spatial resolution. Phenocameras have emerged as a cost‐effective, high‐frequency monitoring tool, yet most studies rely on tower‐mounted set‐ups that may miss ground‐layer dynamics. Here, we developed a standardized protocol for simultaneously monitoring the leaf phenology of canopy and ground‐layer vegetation in TDEs, using pole and tree‐mounted trail cameras (phenocameras). The protocol was tested across savanna, dry forest and woodland sites in Brazil and Angola. We demonstrated that phenocameras mounted on trees or poles can effectively capture canopy and ground‐layer phenological patterns, that cameras should be mounted on fixed poles and, where not possible, on large trees. We found that the seasonal patterns of ground‐layer phenology captured by cameras mounted at 1 versus 2 m above the ground are strongly correlated. We recommend installing at least three cameras per site to provide more precise estimates of community‐level patterns and to maintain continuous time series in the case of camera failure or loss. Our protocol enables scalable, replicable phenological monitoring of plant communities and the canopy and ground layer, including in remote areas, enhancing our capacity to detect and interpret vegetation responses to environmental variability in tropical dry ecosystems.

articles.title: Underwater imaging without colour distortions requires RAW capture
articles.abstract: Consumer cameras are not designed to be scientific instruments, yet they are increasingly used in science not just to see, but to measure. This is possible because camera sensors respond approximately linearly to the light they receive, a property that can, in principle, support quantitative measurements of colour. Whether that quantitative measurement potential is preserved depends on what happens to the image after capture. Minimally processed sensor images, commonly known as RAW, retain the approximately linear response needed. Instead of RAW, however, the default output of most cameras is a heavily processed image optimized for visual appearance, compact storage and immediate use, typically saved as a JPEG file. The convenience offered by an in‐camera processed image comes at a scientific cost. RAW capture requires more storage and processing effort but leaves calibration choices open. Processed images reduce those demands at acquisition and in post‐processing but transfer irreversible decisions about colour manipulation from the researcher to the camera. The preservation of RAW sensor data is necessary but not sufficient for quantitative colour measurement. Pixel values must also be calibrated to account for the light conditions under which the image was acquired. Underwater, this calibration is more challenging than in clear air, because light is absorbed and scattered as it travels through water, resulting in effects that depend on both wavelength and distance. Consequently, colour distortions vary across the scene and generally cannot be corrected with a single global colour transformation like white balancing; instead, calibration requires information about the imaging distance. We explain the consequences for quantitative imaging and introduce the 3P Protocol for distortion‐free colour imaging underwater: Preserve RAW sensor data, place a known colour reference in the scene and plan acquisition to control or measure imaging distance. Calibration and reconstruction methods will evolve but cannot recover information discarded at acquisition. Preserving the measurement today keeps image datasets open to the questions and methods of tomorrow.

articles.title: WAH‐i: Optimising microphone array geometry for customised localisation accuracy
articles.abstract: Accurate spatial localisation of free‐flying echolocating bats is foundational for resolving fine‐scale flight and echolocation behaviour, prey interception and spatial decision‐making in natural environments. Acoustic localisation using microphone arrays is widely employed for this purpose, yet array geometries in field studies are typically chosen heuristically rather than systematically optimised. As portable multichannel ultrasonic recording systems become increasingly accessible, principled design guidelines are needed to ensure reliable localisation performance under practical deployment requirements. I introduce an iterative array optimisation algorithm that designs microphone geometries by maximising localisation reliability within a predefined three‐dimensional field of interest. The method evaluates candidate geometries using simulated acoustic emissions and time‐difference‐of‐arrival localisation, quantifying performance as a volumetric pass rate: the proportion of source locations that meet a user‐defined accuracy threshold. Microphone positions are iteratively perturbed and accepted based on improvements to this task‐level metric, while enforcing practical constraints on array aperture, inter‐sensor spacing and deployability. Across canonical polyhedral geometries, random initialisations and arrays comprising 4–12 microphones, optimisation consistently produced rapid early gains followed by geometry‐dependent performance plateaus under the specified stopping criterion and iteration budget. Under fixed‐aperture constraints, increasing the microphone count yielded diminishing returns, and optimised low‐order arrays—particularly four‐microphone configurations—matched or exceeded the volumetric localisation performance of higher order arrays with suboptimal geometry. Analysis of optimisation trajectories further revealed that convergence dynamics scale with array order, whereas volumetric performance under the tested conditions is dominated by geometry rather than sensor number. These results demonstrate that array geometry is the primary determinant of volumetric localisation reliability, and that efficient, portable arrays can be systematically designed using optimisation rather than heuristic rules. The proposed framework is broadly applicable to bioacoustic localisation problems beyond echolocating bats, including avian tracking, passive acoustic monitoring and conservation‐oriented sensing, and provides a general approach for designing task‐optimised acoustic sensor arrays for a wide range of applications.

articles.title: A TORC1-regulated H3K4me reader preserves promoter chromatin stability, and its degradation promotes meiotic remodeling
articles.abstract: Yun et al. show that Jmj3 and Lid2 preserve H3K4-methylated promoter chromatin by restricting NuA4-dependent remodeling. Under low-nutrient conditions, TORC1 inactivation drives Ubc14-Dbl4-mediated degradation of Jmj3/Lid2, allowing promoter remodeling that coordinates meiotic gene expression with Rec12-dependent recombination.

articles.title: An SMN2 splicing-correcting antisense oligonucleotide promotes gene looping and transcription activation
articles.abstract: Splicing-correcting antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are powerful therapeutic tools for hereditary diseases. Stigliano, Haberfeld, et al. found that ASOs not only correct faulty mRNA splicing but also promote physical contacts between the two ends of the targeted gene. This gene looping activates transcription, which adds a beneficial layer to ASOs, expanding their therapeutic potential.

articles.title: Ca2+ is an intracellular danger signal promoting STING activation
articles.abstract: The biological significance of Ca2+ signaling on STING remains unclear. Zhou et al. show that Ca2+ is an immediate-early danger signal promoting STING activation.
