An insight into molecular identification and DNA barcoding of bamboo: current status, challenges, and future prospects
articles.abstract: IntroductionBamboo exhibits a complex taxonomy due to polyploidy, hybridisation, and long flowering periods, which complicate species identification. Traditional morphological taxonomy often struggles with limited diagnostic traits and considerable phenotypic variability, leading to taxonomic ambiguities and misinterpretations. The convergence of similar traits among unrelated species further complicates phylogenetic classification. To address these challenges, integrative taxonomic approaches are needed to combine morphological, molecular, and ecological data for accurate bamboo classification. This review synthesises the current status, recent advances, and emerging trends in molecular identification and DNA barcoding of bamboo, highlighting their potential to improve taxonomy, conservation, and the sustainable utilisation of bamboo genetic resources.MethodTo provide a framework for the review, a scientometric analysis was performed using bibliographic records.ResultsThe review suggests that no single marker or combination of markers can currently serve as a universal barcode across bamboo. The performance of commonly used markers such as ITS, matK, rbcL, psbA-trnH, rps16-trnQ, and alternative plastid regions provides valuable insights into species identification. Comparative evidence indicates that barcode performance is strongly marker- and lineage-dependent. These markers have improved plant taxonomy by providing more reliable species identification than traditional morphological methods.DiscussionDNA barcoding has been effectively used to understand complex species relationships and identify cryptic species that are difficult to distinguish morphologically. Furthermore, next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies have transformed genomic data acquisition, enabling species discrimination. Integrating machine learning with DNA barcoding further improves species identification accuracy and shows promise for improving conventional methodologies in bamboo systematics. However, the application of ML and NGS in bamboo is still in its early stages and will require substantial work on bamboo databases to achieve greater accuracy.

articles.title: The intermediate social resilience hypothesis: a testable framework linking animal sociality to population resilience under environmental change
articles.abstract: Sociality can improve access to information, cooperation, collective defense, parental care, collective decision-making, and social buffering, but it can also intensify competition and pathogen transmission, spread outdated information, and create dependence on particular partners, roles, or traditions. In this article, we propose the Intermediate Social Resilience Hypothesis (ISRH), which predicts that, under specified conditions, population resilience may be greatest at an intermediate value of a defined social dimension. We do not rank all animal societies on a single universal scale. Instead, low, intermediate, and high values must be defined within a measurable dimension, such as group size, cohesion, network connectivity, cooperative effort, or reliance on social information, and within a biologically comparable system. Resilience must likewise be specified as resistance, recovery, temporal stability, or persistence under a defined form and scale of environmental change. The distinctive contribution of the ISRH is not simply the recognition that sociality can generate both benefits and costs, but the explicit prediction that their balance can, under identifiable conditions, produce a testable intermediate maximum in population resilience. An intermediate optimum is expected only when social benefits initially increase but eventually saturate, whereas one or more relevant social costs continue to rise. Environmental harshness, variability, unpredictability, and the flexibility, modularity, redundancy, or multilevel organization of social systems may shift, flatten, or eliminate this relationship. The hypothesis generates two falsifiable predictions that can be tested through comparative, longitudinal, experimental, phylogenetic, network, and population-monitoring approaches. By integrating behavioral ecology, social evolution, resilience theory, and conservation, the framework explicitly recognizes the multidimensional nature of animal social systems while providing explicit criteria for distinguishing support for the ISRH from monotonic, threshold, flat, or context-dependent alternative relationships.

articles.title: When wildlife damage threatens livelihoods: why national park residents consider a transition to tourism
articles.abstract: Wildlife damage is often expected to push national park residents toward new sources of income, but the appraisals that turn damage into a willingness to move into tourism remain unclear. Drawing on protection motivation theory and questionnaire data from 513 residents in and around the Wuyishan City section of Wuyishan National Park, China, this study distinguishes perceived tourism adaptive efficacy from tourism self-efficacy and examines how these two beliefs relate to intentions to shift household livelihoods toward tourism. Greater perceived wildlife damage was related to stronger threat appraisal of traditional livelihoods. Residents who perceived greater livelihood threat also reported stronger transition intentions and were more likely to view tourism as a workable livelihood alternative. However, no clear relationship emerged between livelihood threat and tourism self-efficacy, although both adaptive efficacy and self-efficacy were positively related to transition intention. As a moderator, perceived tourism development opportunity was more relevant to adaptive efficacy than to self-efficacy. When residents perceived greater tourism opportunities, the positive relationship between livelihood threat and adaptive efficacy was stronger, as was the corresponding indirect relationship with transition intention. In contrast, perceived opportunity made little difference to the relationship involving self-efficacy. These findings suggest that livelihood threat was associated with greater perceived usefulness and feasibility of tourism without a corresponding association with residents’ confidence in their own ability to engage in tourism activities. Policies aimed at encouraging livelihood diversification in national park communities may therefore need to combine the creation of tourism opportunities with training, skills development, and other forms of support that strengthen residents’ capacity to participate.

articles.title: Mitochondrial DNA abundance is a determinant of immunogenic cell death in cancer
articles.abstract: Mitochondrial stress can trigger either immunogenic or apoptotic cell death. Tanaka et al. find that mitochondrial DNA abundance, shaped by oncogenic KRAS signaling and mitophagy, determines the immunological outcome of mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, providing a mechanistic basis for targeting mitochondrial stress to augment antitumor immunity.

articles.title: Host seasonal trophic strategies linked to dietary‐microbiota coupling: A potential mechanism mediating the coexistence of sympatric small rodents
articles.abstract: This study reveals that host trophic strategy, not shared seasonality, drives gut microbiota plasticity in sympatric rodents. Herbivorous voles show tight diet–microbiome coupling; granivorous gerbils exhibit functional stability. This highlights gut microbiota as a potential key mechanism for niche differentiation and coexistence. Abstract The coexistence mechanisms of sympatric species have long attracted widespread research attention. However, it remains unclear whether sympatric species experiencing the same seasonal conditions exhibit convergent or host‐specific gut microbiota responses. We compared the herbivorous Brandt's vole (Lasiopodomys brandtii) and the granivorous Mongolian gerbil (Meriones unguiculatus), two sympatric rodent species with divergent trophic strategies inhabiting the grasslands of Inner Mongolia, China. By integrating plant DNA metabarcoding, gut microbiota profiling and microbial functional output analyses across seasons, we investigated seasonal dietary–microbiome associations. Our results revealed that although seasonal dietary variation affects the composition of the host gut microbiota, the taxonomic and functional plasticity of gut microbiota is strongly influenced by host trophic strategies. Brandt's voles maintained a fermentation‐oriented microbiota tightly coupled with seasonal shifts in Poaceae and Cyperaceae intake, exhibiting coordinated changes in microbial taxa, short‐chain fatty acid production and cellulase activity. In contrast, Mongolian gerbils exhibited substantial seasonal dietary turnover between Chenopodiaceae and Caragana plants, while maintaining comparatively stable microbial functional outputs, suggesting metabolic buffering. Host trophic strategy, rather than shared environmental seasonality, is related to the strength and functional consequences of the coupling between diet and microbiome. Our results emphasize the gut microbiome as a potential key mechanism underlying trophic niche differentiation and ecological coexistence in wild mammalian communities.

articles.title: Mechanistic insights and structure–reactivity relationships of Ru(II)–Imidazole complex catalysts for formic acid dehydrogenation: A combined DFT and machine learning study
Beyond Static Catalysts: Dynamic Interfaces for Adaptive Energy Conversion
articles.abstract: Catalytic interfaces in energy-conversion systems are rarely static under operating conditions. Applied potentials, reactive intermediates, electrolyte environments, chemical potentials, and transport fluxes can continuously reshape atomic structures, electronic states, adsorption...

articles.title: Crosslinked γ-polyglutamic acid gel polymer electrolyte for Hightemperature sodium metal battery with the high rate and long cycling
articles.abstract: Dendrites growth and unstable interface between Na metal anode and electrolyte have inhibited the large-scale applications of Na-metal batteries, which will be deteriorate further under high temperatures. In this work,...

articles.title: Dynamic polyphenol-reinforced CMC hydrogel with permanent-reversible network coupling for self-healing and multimodal sensing
articles.abstract: A polyphenol-reinforced dual-network hydrogel combines reversible hydrogen bonding and covalent crosslinking, enabling robust mechanics, self-healing, strong adhesion, and reliable multimodal sensing for wearable bioelectronics and electronic skin.

articles.title: Engineering interfacial oxophilicity through surface hydroxyl-regulated trimetallic Ni–Co–Al synergy for enhanced selectivity via electrocatalytic nitrate-to-ammonia conversion
articles.abstract: Surface hydroxyl-regulated trimetallic Ni–Co–Al synergy engineers interfacial oxophilicity, tuning NO x intermediate binding and facilitating the key hydrogenation step toward highly selective nitrate-to-ammonia electroreduction.

articles.title: Leakage-proof multifunctional phase change composites enabled by commercial activated carbon fiber felt for passive and active thermal management
articles.abstract: Commercial activated carbon fiber felt stabilized PEG with PDMS coating form flexible phase change composites with high latent heat storage, leakage resistance, and photothermal/electrothermal conversion for thermal management.

articles.title: Small-molecule structural regulators enable strain-adaptive molecular ordering in intrinsically stretchable organic photodetectors
Comparison between interfacial pyroelectric and transient interfacial photovoltaic effects
articles.abstract: Interfacial pyroelectricity and transient interfacial photovoltaic effects provide two distinct routes for converting thermal and optical fluctuations into transient electrical signals through interfacial charge redistribution. This review compares their mechanisms, output characteristics, evaluation metrics with particular emphasis on polarization-mediated lyroelectric responses, and potential in sensing, energy conversion, and event-driven optoelectronics.

articles.title: Structural basis for the non-canonical nucleosome remodeling by ATRX
articles.abstract: Wang et al. show that ATRX remodels chromatin through an unusual mechanism that favors nucleosome disassembly over repositioning. ATRX also captures histones and cooperates with ASF1 for tetrasome assembly, linking chromatin remodeling to histone chaperoning for reassembly and helping explain how ATRX functions at accessible chromatin regions.

articles.title: Asymmetric Migration Shapes Genetic Structure of the Invasive Avian Vampire Fly (Philornis downsi) Across the Galápagos Islands
articles.abstract: Biological invasions on islands provide a natural framework to study how dispersal and connectivity influence evolutionary and ecological processes. The avian nest parasitic fly, Philornis downsi—first recorded in Darwin's finch nests in 1997—causes high mortality in endemic land birds, yet its inter‐island and sex‐specific patterns of dispersal and genetic structure remain poorly understood. We use low‐coverage whole genome sequencing to investigate genome‐wide patterns of genetic diversity, directional migration and effective population size in P. downsi across five major Galápagos Islands and its native range in mainland Ecuador. We find evidence for a genetic bottleneck in the Galápagos, isolation by distance, and evidence that the island closest to the Ecuadorian mainland, San Cristóbal, is genetically divergent from the other four islands sampled, despite retaining the highest genetic diversity. No evidence was found for sex‐biased dispersal; however, sex‐biased genetic structure was detected using only markers from inferred autosomal scaffolds. We found asymmetric gene flow with higher migration rates from San Cristóbal westward to the other islands, matching the direction of both southeast trade winds and major cargo shipping routes. Our results suggest both natural and human‐mediated colonisation of P. downsi from the mainland through San Cristóbal to the other islands, followed by high inter‐island dispersal among closely situated sink islands. Our findings are critical for prioritising islands for control strategies that will reduce P. downsi impacts on vulnerable endemic birds and underscore the value of understanding directional migration patterns for managing invasive species in metapopulations.

articles.title: A cross-interface ion-sharing strategy for efficient perovskite solar cells
Chemically functionalized fullerene-based triboelectric nanogenerators for efficient mechanical heart energy harvesting
Tuning active layer film formation with fluorinated non-fused ring acceptors for high-performance organic solar cells
A Multicolor Electrochromic Device Enabled by Shared-Zn Energy Routing for Self-Powered Wearable Displays
articles.abstract: Wearable displays remain constrained by high energy consumption and a heavy reliance on external power during repeated refreshing. Here, we develop a multicolor electrochromic device based on shared-Zn energy routing for self-powered wearable displays. An intermediate Zn mesh couples an upper W/WO3 display electrode with a lower MnO2 energy-storage electrode, enabling self-driven coloration and internally powered bleaching through separate electrochemical circuits. The upper Nylon-66/W/WO3 optical cavity determines the visible color and optically shields the underlying storage electrode, decoupling display color from energy-storage chemistry. The device achieves coloration and bleaching within 10 s and sustains at least 500 consecutive refresh cycles. Integration with a microcontroller and heart-rate sensor demonstrates its potential for wearable physiological monitoring. This compact architecture combines display refreshing, optical memory, and electrical energy output, providing a route toward self-powered wearable displays with integrated sensing and energy functions.

articles.title: Dynamic Charge Gradients from Interfacial Electron Transfer Enable Self-Powered Gate-Controlled All-Metal-Nanoparticle Neuromorphic Systems
articles.abstract: Harvesting electricity from ambient moisture represents a transformative approach to power generation, a process traditionally ascribed solely to ion or proton diffusion. Here, we report a moisture-energy-harvesting mechanism that originates from interfacial electron transfer in a ligand-decorated metal nanoparticle film. Partially covering the film creates an asymmetric humidity gradient that triggers unbalanced electron transfer from adsorbed water to the metal nanoparticle core. This establishes a persistent dynamic charge separation and concentration gradient along the film that is sustained by continuous water evaporation from its exposed side, as supported by multiscale simulations. With this mechanism, we demonstrate that the electricity generated by these nanoparticle devices can not only power common microelectronic devices but also be directly integrated with a nanoparticle synaptic transistor to achieve a self-powered gate-controlled all-metal-nanoparticle neuromorphic system.

articles.title: A user’s guide to building the Universe
Rapid growth in a dual active galactic nucleus during a gas-rich merger at z ≈ 4.5
articles.abstract: Observations reveal two rapidly growing supermassive black holes in a gas-rich galaxy merger just 1.3 billion years after the Big Bang. Both already lie on the black hole–host mass relation, indicating a period of early co-evolution.

articles.title: ANO6-mediated trogocytosis of cancer-associated fibroblasts promotes pancreatic cancer cell growth and immune suppression
articles.abstract: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the fibroblastic stroma constitutes most of the tumor mass and is remarkably devoid of functional blood vessels, leaving unresolved how PDAC cells obtain essential metabolites and water-insoluble lipids. We find that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) acquire and transfer lipids from blood-borne particles to PDAC cells through trogocytosis of CAF plasma membranes, a process requiring the CAF-expressed phospholipid scramblase anoctamin 6 (ANO6) to promote PDAC cell survival. Cancer cells and CAFs form synapse-like contacts that induce cytosolic calcium influx in CAFs through Orai channels, activating ANO6 and driving phosphatidylserine exposure on CAF membranes, which initiates trogocytosis and transfer of membrane lipids, including cholesterol, to PDAC cells. This ANO6-dependent phosphatidylserine externalization also supports CAF-mediated immunosuppression of cytotoxic T cells through trogocytosis. Blockade of ANO6 antagonizes tumor growth, partly by disrupting cholesterol delivery to cancer cells, and attenuates immune suppression, identifying ANO6 as a candidate therapeutic target in PDAC. Ogier et al. uncover that cancer-associated fibroblasts fuel pancreatic tumor growth and immune suppression by transferring membrane lipids to cancer cells through anoctamin 6-dependent trogocytosis.

articles.title: BAZ2A-induced epigenetic states in cancer cells fuel palmitate accumulation in the tumor microenvironment driving CAR-T cell exhaustion
articles.abstract: Wang et al. reveal that epigenetic remodeling driven by BAZ2A in renal cancer cells induces the production of palmitate that is taken up by tumor-infiltrating cells, resulting in impaired metabolic fitness of CAR-T cells via PGC-1α palmitoylation.

articles.title: GALE is a tumor-intrinsic checkpoint of Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated killing
articles.abstract: Shan et al. identified UDP-galactose 4-epimerase as an immune checkpoint of Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated cancer cell killing by enhancing interaction of CD155 and CEACAM1 with their receptors TIGIT and TIM3, respectively, and simultaneously inhibiting CD155 binding to CD22.

articles.title: Targeting GALE harnesses γδ T cells for cancer immunotherapy
articles.abstract: Cancer cells can evade the immune system through mechanisms such as downregulation of MHC I molecules and expression of inhibitory ligands. Research now shows that targeting the metabolic enzyme GALE in tumor cells boosts the killing of these cells by γδ T cells through altering the glycosylation of key immune-checkpoint ligands.

articles.title: Photoenzymatic stereodivergent hydrophosphinylation enabled by nicotinamide-dependent imine reductases
articles.abstract: Stereocontrol of phosphorus-centred radicals remains a major challenge, limiting access to P-chiral organophosphorus compounds. Now a photoexcited imine reductase is reprogrammed to enable stereodivergent hydrophosphinylation, delivering C-, P- and C/P-chiral phosphine oxides with high selectivity.

articles.title: From poppies to pain relief
articles.abstract: Madison Sowden discusses the origin of morphine, how the structure and medical effects were first studied, and how the compound is produced today.

articles.title: How expansive and flexible is the matrix of life?
articles.abstract: All known life needs water, but its operative mechanisms are extraordinarily diverse. Bruce Gibb discusses the chemistry of some of Earth’s most extreme ecosystems and what they reveal about life beyond our planet.

articles.title: A combinatorial genetics approach reveals limits to redundancy within Plasmodium falciparum invasion ligand families
articles.abstract: The authors use a genetic approach to explore redundancy within two multigene families important for Plasmodium falciparum invasion of human red blood cells, revealing that not all family members function equivalently.

articles.title: A multilamellar organelle for chemosymbiosis in an aplacophoran mollusc adapted to anoxic cold seep sediment
articles.abstract: Animals living in the deep sea often form symbiotic partnerships with chemosynthetic bacteria. Here authors discover a multilamellar organelle in the worm-mollusc Chaetoderma shenloong containing bacteria and name it dracosphera (‘dragon ball’).

articles.title: Ancestry-specific and multi-ancestry genome-wide association studies of restless legs syndrome
articles.abstract: Restless legs syndrome is a neurological disorder that disrupts sleep and quality of life, but its genetics have mostly been studied in individuals of European ancestry. Here, we perform GWAS of restless legs syndrome using data from individuals of African, Latin American, and European ancestry, followed by a multi-ancestry meta-analysis. We leverage biobank-based cohorts that established RLS diagnosis using validated clinical criteria, allowing for precise phenotypic characterization. We perform ancestry-specific association studies and post-GWAS analyses to prioritize candidate genes. Our analyses reveal ancestry differences in the genetics of restless legs syndrome. At the MEIS1 and BTBD9 loci, lead variants showed lower allele frequencies and did not reach genome-wide significance in African ancestry. We identify ancestry-specific and shared risk loci, including novel associations near GYPC/TEX51 and PRIMA1 in African ancestry and ISX in Latin American ancestry. The European meta-analysis identifies 11 additional loci and replicates 50 previously reported associations. The combined multi-ancestry analysis finds ten new loci. This multi-ancestry study broadens the genetic understanding of restless legs syndrome, and the absence or reduced frequency of key European restless legs syndrome alleles in individuals of African ancestry provides insights into known epidemiological differences. The genetics of restless legs syndrome have mostly been studied in European populations. Here, the authors perform a multi-ancestry genetic study of the condition, revealing differences in genetic risk across populations with different ancestries.

articles.title: Genomic heterogeneity inflates the performance of variant pathogenicity predictions
articles.abstract: Recent studies have reported unprecedented accuracy predicting pathogenic variants across the genome, including in noncoding regions, using large deep-learning models trained on vast genomic data. To verify and understand the basis of these reports, we systematically evaluated the prediction accuracy of frontier models over single-nucleotide variants, focusing on general models capable of scoring multiple variant types across coding or noncoding regions. Our evaluations reveal that the performance of genome-wide predictions is severely inflated by mixing variant categories with different baseline prevalences of pathogenic variants. We constructed a benchmark stratified by variant type to identify the best-performing models for each genomic context, determine where reliable predictions remain out of reach, and establish rigorous standards to guide future evaluations. Evaluations of AI models predicting disease-causing single nucleotide variants reveal that the performance of genome-wide predictions is inflated by mixing variant types, e.g. canonical splice and 5’ UTR variants. The authors introduce a stratified benchmark to accurately identify the most robust models.

articles.title: Hydrogen-bond-mediated quasi-two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks for ultrahigh gold extraction
articles.abstract: Covalent organic frameworks are ideal for precious metal recovery but the confinement of binding sites within inner pores often leads to restricted mass transfer and limits extraction capacities. Here, the authors report a quasi-2D topology-directed strategy to construct exposed binding sites for highly efficient gold recovery.

articles.title: IDPForge: deep learning of proteins with global and local regions of disorder
articles.abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins and regions (IDPs/IDRs) are defined by diverse structural ensembles. We present IDPForge that exploits a transformer protein language diffusion model to create all-atom IDP and IDR ensembles that maintain folded domains with options to conform to experimental data.

articles.title: Intruding delta waves during REM sleep are associated with tau, amyloid, and forgetting in aging
articles.abstract: Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep degrades with age, and more severely in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). REM sleep comprises about twenty percent of adult sleep, alternates between phasic and tonic periods, and includes delta waves (1-4 Hz) in two forms: fast sawtooth waves and slower, NREM-like waves, whose expression dynamically varies across REM periods. Yet, the functional relevance of these REM sleep delta waves remains unknown. Here, using two independent cohorts, we show that aging is associated with a shift from fast sawtooth to slow NREM-like delta waves, particularly during phasic REM sleep - a period typically marked by high cortical activation. Beyond chronological age, this shift is associated with amyloid-β and tau burden, suggesting that AD pathology is associated with REM-specific oscillatory patterns. Furthermore, this shift in REM oscillations is linked to impaired overnight memory consolidation, independent of NREM sleep quality. Moreover, variation in APOE alleles, a major genetic risk factor for AD, was independently associated with a reduction in fast sawtooth wave density, thereby linking a genetic predisposition for AD to these specific REM microstructural changes. These findings identify a signature of memory decline in aging and implicate REM sleep as a distinct vulnerable substrate through which AD pathology may impair brain function. Desel et al. report that memory loss in aging is associated with a shift from fast sawtooth to slow delta waves during REM sleep. This shift correlates with amyloid and tau burden, marking a REM sleep signature of impaired memory consolidation.

articles.title: Process-dependent shifts in conspecific negative density dependence during boreal forest succession
articles.abstract: Conspecific negative density dependence may maintain diversity, but its role during succession is unclear. This study shows that changes depend on demographic processes and species abundance rather than following a uniform community-wide trend.

articles.title: Publisher Correction: Regional heterogeneity in phenotypic and genetic associations between bone and brain in humans
articles.abstract: Publisher Correction: Regional heterogeneity in phenotypic and genetic associations between bone and brain in humans

articles.title: Spatial patterning of hierarchical lamellar-cellular structured hydrogels for programmable deformation-coupled information encryption
articles.abstract: Inspired by organisms capable of adaptive morphological regulation, hydrogel actuators with softness and large deformability are attractive for biomedical devices and information encryption, yet remain limited by the lack of hierarchically oriented structures simultaneously enabling rapid actuation and high-order complex deformation. Here, we report a multiscale lamellar-confined assembly polymerization strategy for fabricating synchronous programmable shape-morphing and information-encoding hydrogels with hierarchically periodic lamellar-cellular structure. Owing to the periodic asymmetric stresses that amplify deformation and hierarchical porous channels that accelerate water transport, the obtained hydrogel exhibits large three-dimensional deformation with the rapidest recovery speed of 112.5°/s among the reported thermo-responsive hydrogels, facilitating programmable shape morphing by orchestrating localized curvature. Furthermore, a spatial orientation-patterning strategy is developed to precisely regulate the site-specific arrangement of lamellar-cellular structures for diverse cooperative sophisticated deformations at high speed. Importantly, the highly oriented architecture endows the hydrogel with tunable birefringence, enabling a dynamic encryption platform that couples programmable deformation with information encoding. This work provides a flexible structural strategy for preparing hydrogels with biomimetic dynamic information encryption. Hydrogel actuators have potential in a range of applications, but combining rapid actuation and complex deformation is challenging. Here, the authors report a lamellar confined assembly polymerisation strategy for preparing programmable shape-morphing and information-encoding hydrogels.

articles.title: An extra beat every minute
articles.abstract: Small deviations in the power system frequency are routinely attributed to stochastic fluctuations in load and generation. New research reveals a disturbance recurring precisely every minute in grids worldwide, caused by clock-synchronized self-tests in battery-based uninterruptible power supplies that inadvertently act in unison.

articles.title: Caloric cooling devices and systems
articles.abstract: Caloric cooling offers a promising solid-state alternative to conventional refrigeration, but system-level challenges continue to limit practical deployment. This Review evaluates the state of the art, identifies the key barriers to scalable devices and outlines a roadmap for sustainable cooling.

articles.title: Durable reactive CO2 capture exceeding 1,000 h via self-reinforcing molecular catalysts
articles.abstract: Reactive CO2 capture integrates carbon capture and electrochemical conversion in a single process, but poor catalyst durability remains a major challenge. Here the authors show that pH-swing-driven acidification accelerates catalyst demetallation and develop a cobalt phthalocyanine catalyst that suppresses metal loss, sustaining efficient CO production for 1,000 h.

articles.title: Ironing out oxygen instability
articles.abstract: Oxygen redox in layered-oxide cathodes could facilitate the development of high-energy sodium-ion batteries, but poor reversibility has limited its practical application. Now, an iron-mediated redox strategy offers a pathway to substantially improving oxygen-redox reversibility.

articles.title: One-minute frequency disturbances from unintended synchronization in cyber–physical power systems
articles.abstract: Power grids on five continents show frequency oscillations with a period of exactly 1 min. The authors trace this to clock-synchronized software in devices such as uninterruptible power supplies that creates coherent, repeating demand peaks.

articles.title: Autophagy limits steady-state IL-1α expression to restrain innate immunity
articles.abstract: Autophagy controls pulmonary innate immunity at the steady-state by restraining IL-1α expression by alveolar macrophages. Disrupting this regulatory pathway primes lung innate immunity and enhances resistance to distinct respiratory infections, identifying an unexpected role for autophagy in determining host immune readiness.

articles.title: Linda J. Miller (1958–2026)
Climate change threatens malaria elimination in the Asia Pacific
articles.abstract: A multidisciplinary group of policymakers and researchers discusses the impacts of climate change on malaria in the Asia Pacific, identifies gaps in national adaptation strategies and outlines five priority actions for the region.

articles.title: Continuous mass measurement of single proteins
articles.abstract: We developed an approach to monitor the mass of individual proteins and the complexes they form for up to an hour by mass photometry. The ability to follow the mass of individual species enables the detection and characterization of interactions as a function of time — the essence of biomolecular mechanisms.

articles.title: Foundation models unlock robust phenotypic representations from Cell Painting images
articles.abstract: We pretrained and systematically benchmarked a suite of self-supervised foundation models on the largest public Cell Painting dataset, enabling robust morphological feature extraction directly from multichannel high-content images without cell segmentation or feature engineering. These models outperformed classical methods and demonstrated generalizability across cell types.

articles.title: Multivalent ADAR1 recruitment for precise RNA editing
articles.abstract: Current ADAR-recruiting RNA editing systems suffer from limited efficacy and bystander editing. We developed a system in which the multivalent recruitment of endogenous ADAR1 p150 through its Zα domain enables up to 100% A-to-I editing in vitro and 84% in vivo, enabling precise correction of disease-associated mutations at the transcript level.

articles.title: Spatial single-cell mapping of transcriptional differences across genetic backgrounds in mouse brains
articles.abstract: Genetic variation can alter organ structure and function. Comparative statistical analysis of organs across genetic backgrounds requires spatial, single-cell, atlas-scale data in replicates. Here we introduce atlas-scale transcriptome localization using aggregate signatures (ATLAS), a scalable tissue mapping method that learns transcriptional signatures from single-cell RNA sequencing data, encodes them in situ with tens of thousands of oligonucleotide probes and decodes them to infer cell types and imputed transcriptomes. We validated ATLAS against direct MERFISH measurements of marker genes and through quantitative comparisons to four other technologies. We profiled 40 million cells across more than 400 coronal sections from central brains of five male and five female C57BL/6J mice and five male BTBR T+tf/J mice, an idiopathic autism model. Our analysis revealed more than 40 significant differences in cell-type distributions and identified 16 regional composition changes across male–female and B6–BTBR comparisons. ATLAS thus enables systematic comparative studies, facilitating organ-level structure–function analysis of disease models. ATLAS is a highly scalable tissue profiling method that leverages existing atlas data and in silico decoding to generate imputed cell maps.

articles.title: Automated inverse design of metainterfaces with tailored friction laws
articles.abstract: Providing dry solid contacts with on-demand macroscale frictional behaviour remains a formidable challenge in tribology, haptics and robotics. It has been shown that metainterfaces created from surfaces with engineered asperity-based topographies can achieve such friction control. However, only a few types of friction behaviour were demonstrated because suitable topographies were identified on the basis of human intuition. Here we introduce a numerical-optimization-based inverse design framework to automatically discover new metainterfaces that satisfy specified friction laws—relationships between friction and the normal force. To illustrate the framework’s versatility, we first expand the range of achievable friction coefficients for a given pair of materials. We next unlock friction laws showing power-law variation of frictional force with normal force, with exponents ranging between 2/3 and 1.35. We then achieve bilinear variation when the range of normal force is divided into segments, including cases for a smaller slope in the second segment than in the first. We validate relevant cases experimentally. Our automated framework enables systematic exploration of large parameter spaces, not limited to topography but potentially incorporating the individual asperities’ bulk material or surface physicochemistry. It offers design solutions for different friction laws and provides insights into the relationship between local interfacial properties and macroscopic friction. Understanding friction between contacting surfaces is important to improve device performance. Now a method is shown to discover materials that offer on-demand frictional behaviour using inverse design based on genetic algorithms.

articles.title: Motors use biased diffusion to shepherd diffusible proteins on microtubules
articles.abstract: Far-from-equilibrium mixtures of active and passive molecules self-organize, but the principles remain unclear. Microtubules are cytoskeletal polymers composed of 13 protofilaments bound by mixtures of actively moving motors and passively diffusing microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs). They can serve as a model system for self-organization on a multi-lane lattice. Here we show that motors can shepherd diffusive MAPs along the lattice by rectifying Brownian motion into net directional drift without motor–MAP binding. Our model reveals that biased movement increases when fewer protofilaments are accessible or when lateral diffusion between protofilaments is limited, and identifies local dimensionality and diffusion as key parameters governing spatial patterning. In particular, shepherding depends on the total number of motors bound to the microtubules, and not on the individual motor processivity. We experimentally recapitulate micrometre-scale shepherding with a kinesin-1 motor (K401) and a diffusive MAP (PRC1), which show no detectable binding. These findings suggest shepherding is an emergent mechanism by which ensembles of motors generate micrometre-scale spatial patterning and transport of MAPs without direct binding interactions. Microtubules are bound by active motors and passively diffusing proteins. Now it is shown that this mixture of active and passive molecules is a realization of rectified Brownian motion in active matter.

articles.title: Multiparticle quantum walks in a dipole-conserving Bose–Hubbard model
articles.abstract: A strong potential gradient can localize individual particles in a crystal or optical lattice by making ordinary hopping energetically costly. Interactions can nevertheless enable correlated hopping processes that preserve the system’s centre of mass or, equivalently, its dipole moment. This constraint gives rise to fractonic behaviour, in which isolated excitations are immobile but their bound states can move. Here we realize individual mobile bound states of fractons in a dipole-conserving Bose–Hubbard model and observe their coherent quantum dynamics. Starting from a one-dimensional chain of ultracold bosonic atoms in an optical lattice, we use site-resolved optical potentials to deterministically generate localized dipole and antidipole excitations, which represent mobile bound states of a hole and a doublon. We track their individual quantum walks and characterize their strongly interacting scattering dynamics. Our study provides a bottom-up investigation of a Hamiltonian with kinetic constraints and offers an approach to exploring low-energy phases of fractonic matter. Strong potential gradients can localize individual particles, but interactions can still generate collective motion. An experiment with ultracold atoms in a tilted lattice now shows this collective motion by tracking mobile bound states of fractons.

articles.title: The challenge of recognition in large scientific collaborations
articles.abstract: The authorship practices of large collaborations can hide individual contributions. A recognition programme developed by the LIGO Scientific Collaboration publicly documents verified contributions to research, infrastructure and community service.

articles.title: Thermodynamic demonstration of tetracriticality and multicomponent superconductivity in UTe2
articles.abstract: The candidate topological superconductor UTe2 exhibits a complex phase diagram with multiple superconducting states, and the nature of their coexistence is not yet resolved. In particular, the apparent observation of two intersecting second-order phase boundaries at a triple point in the pressure–temperature phase diagram is thermodynamically forbidden. This suggests either a hidden phase transition or a fundamental misunderstanding of the superconductivity in this material. Here we observe an additional phase boundary that is characterized by an upward jump in the sound velocity. This is direct thermodynamic evidence for a phase transition in which superconducting order is lost on cooling. Our results establish a tetracritical point beyond which the ambient and pressure-induced superconducting order parameters form a multicomponent state. We use the measured phase diagram to demonstrate that strong competition between the two superconducting order parameters drives the loss of order when cooling, and leads to phase locking that suppresses superconducting fluctuations. These findings provide the definitive magnetic field–pressure–temperature phase diagram of UTe2 and establish a thermodynamic foundation for multicomponent superconductivity. Prior measurements of the phase diagram of UTe2 contain a triple point that is forbidden by thermodynamics. Now, an additional phase boundary is discovered that resolves this problem and confirms multicomponent superconductivity in this material.

articles.title: Enhanced neutral seawater photoelectrolysis by fast hydrogen pumping at subnanometre triple interfaces
articles.abstract: Atomically dispersed Cr(OH)x on Pt/GaN creates subnanometre triple interfaces that couple water activation, hydrogen transfer and Pt–H formation across adjacent interfaces for fast hydrogen pumping in photoelectrochemical seawater splitting. This overcomes hydrogen-utilization limitations in single-interface catalysis and enables high-current outputs under neutral seawater photoelectrolysis in low-bias and bias-free devices.

articles.title: Expanding atropisomerism to C–P bonds
A beneficial root endophyte buffers natural variation in pathogen susceptibility across Arabidopsis accessions
articles.abstract: Beneficial symbionts act as ecological stabilizers that mitigate differential pathogen susceptibility within natural plant populations. Summary Host genetic diversity shapes pathogen susceptibility within plant populations, raising the question of whether beneficial root microbes can buffer these differences. The fungal root endophyte Serendipita indica (Si) promotes plant growth and can mitigate disease caused by the pathogen Bipolaris sorokiniana (Bs). Here, we assessed how natural host genetic variation influences Si‐mediated protection against Bs in Arabidopsis thaliana. We screened 47 A. thaliana accessions for susceptibility to Bs with and without Si colonization and performed phenotypic, transcriptomic, and comparative genomic analyses of two genetically and geographically proximate Swedish accessions, T510 and T530, that differed strongly in Bs colonization. Si conferred consistent protection against Bs across all accessions, despite variation in baseline susceptibility and immune‐gene content. T510 and T530 differed in Bs colonization, disease symptoms, transcriptional responses, and immune‐gene repertoires, including presence–absence variation of the TIR‐NLR gene ISI. T530 lacks ISI, and mutation of ISI in Col‐0 increased Bs susceptibility, demonstrating that ISI contributes to root immunity. However, Si‐mediated protection was retained in the absence of ISI, demonstrating that ISI is not required for this protective effect. Beneficial fungal endophytes can thus buffer phenotypic consequences of natural variation in pathogen susceptibility, stabilizing disease outcomes across genetically diverse plant populations.

articles.title: Decomposition and mycorrhizal suppression of saprotrophs remain stable after wildfire and clearcut disturbance in boreal forests
articles.abstract: Boreal forests store a large portion of global terrestrial carbon, primarily in soils, yet their sensitivity to environmental changes remains uncertain. Disturbance is one major agent of change, with dominance shifting from wildfire to forest management over the past century. Mycorrhizal suppression of saprotrophic decomposition may be an important control on boreal soil carbon storage, but its occurrence and magnitude remain uncertain. Additionally, the distinct impacts of wildfire and clearcutting on decomposition and soil microbial communities remain largely unexplored. We quantified mycorrhizal suppression of saprotrophs and decomposition in needle and humus litter through a root‐exclusion experiment in 31 sites across wildfire (4–375 yr since disturbance) and clearcut chronosequences (1–109 yr since disturbance) in northern Sweden. Mycorrhizas suppressed decomposition by 15.5 ± 5.9% overall, with no consistent change over time after disturbance. This pattern was linked to absolute fungal abundance but not to other microbial community shifts, soil temperature or soil moisture. Decomposition rates were stable across time since disturbance for all substrates and disturbance types. Our findings improve understanding of mycorrhizal‐decomposition interactions and highlight the need to further explore key fungal traits and compositional changes, especially at the soil surface, that regulate carbon storage dynamics in boreal soils.

articles.title: RCD1 nuclear shuttling releases WRKY47 to trigger bHLH105/bHLH115‐dependent iron acquisition
articles.abstract: WRKY47 functions upstream of bHLH105 and bHLH115 to mediate iron (Fe) deficiency stress responses in Arabidopsis. Summary Iron (Fe) deficiency limits plant growth, yet its upstream regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identify WRKY47 as a positive regulator of Fe‐deficiency responses in Arabidopsis. WRKY47 directly binds and activates bHLH105 and bHLH115, key IVc bHLH factors that trigger the Fe uptake cascade. We further show that RCD1 interacts with WRKY47 and suppresses its DNA‐binding and transcriptional activity. Fe deficiency also promotes the redistribution of RCD1 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, suggesting a potential mechanism for modulating WRKY47 activity during the response. Our findings uncover a previously uncharacterized regulatory mechanism linking WRKY transcription factors and the bHLH cascade through RCD1‐mediated modulation, providing a conceptual framework for engineering crops with enhanced Fe acquisition and stress resilience.

articles.title: Water stable isotopes reveal the ecohydrological importance of stemflow infiltration for mature and juvenile European beech
articles.abstract: Field site and experimental set‐up with stemflow‐labelled European beech trees. Summary Stemflow of forest trees can contribute a significant fraction of water to forest's water fluxes; however, it is still unclear whether and to what extent trees and their neighbours use stemflow for water uptake and supply. We applied deuterium‐enriched stemflow equivalent to a 23‐mm throughfall event to adult Fagus sylvatica trees to trace stemflow through the soil and trees. We continuously measured in situ water stable isotopes in soil and xylem water and destructively sampled xylem water in the crowns of adult labelled, nonlabelled F. sylvatica and nonlabelled Picea abies, complemented by destructive xylem water sampling of neighbouring juvenile F. sylvatica. Stemflow water supported up to 5.7 ± 2.1% of daily sap flux of adult F. sylvatica trees labelled at the stem base and was detectable in xylem water for several weeks. In the soil, deuterium‐enriched stemflow was present at a maximum distance of 0.40 m from the labelled tree. Moreover, nonlabelled juvenile trees within a distance of 2 m showed uptake of labelled water, indicating rooting into soil compartments affected by stemflow. We demonstrate the importance of stemflow as a water source for both adult and neighbouring juvenile F. sylvatica, even when soil water is not limiting.

articles.title: AR signaling context and the apparent lack of synergy between AR-targeted therapy and PARP inhibition

Deep mutational scanning of the GPCR rhodopsin reveals pleiotropic mutational effects and their roles in modulating receptor signaling
articles.abstract: Biophysical pleiotropy, the phenomenon in which a mutation affects multiple protein properties, underlies many genetic diseases and shapes protein evolution, yet remains poorly understood, limiting synthetic biology and therapeutic development. Although extensively studied in soluble proteins, little is known about how pleiotropic effects shaped the evolution of receptor protein functions. Here, we developed a cell-based assay designed to assess pleiotropic effects in G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest receptor class in eukaryotes. Because our assay allows for multiple GPCR molecular phenotypes (basal activity, ligand-dependent signaling, and cellular receptor abundance) to be simultaneously assessed, we applied it to study rhodopsin, a visual GPCR that evolved for high phototransduction capabilities by maximizing light-driven responses while minimizing noise. To investigate this, we integrated our assay with deep mutational scanning to test the impacts of ~2,000 single-residue substitutions in rhodopsin across all three molecular phenotypes (~6,000 measurements). By analyzing these data in the context of rhodopsin’s protein structures, we found complex pleiotropic effects that act asymmetrically to impose joint constraints, restricting mutational tolerance in rhodopsin’s retinal binding pocket and G protein interaction interface. A dose–response analysis of rhodopsin signaling revealed that these pleiotropic constraints arise from the dual functions of its chromophore, which acts as an agonist upon light-driven isomerization but also an inverse agonist in darkness. Because these constraints reflect mechanistically driven limitations in the evolution of receptor signaling, these findings reveal a role for biophysical pleiotropy in shaping the signaling capabilities of receptor proteins.

articles.title: Evidence and gaps in the proposed ALDH9A1–carnitine–acetyl-CoA–IL-1β axis
HAR1 receptor kinase links nodule autoregulation with repression of auxin signaling and lateral root development
articles.abstract: Nitrogen-fixing root nodules develop as lateral organs on legume roots and their formation is restricted by autoregulation of nodulation (AON), a systemic mechanism with unclear evolutionary origins. We identify Lotus japonicus NUCLEAR FACTOR Y subunit A4 ( NF-YA4 ) gene as a central target of the leucine-rich repeat receptor kinase HAR1, which controls both AON and root system architecture. Under nonsymbiotic conditions, HAR1 suppresses expression of NF-YA4 and its close paralog NF-YA1 , at least in part through a miR169-dependent mechanism, mirroring the Arabidopsis CLAVATA1/2-miR169- NF-YA module. Loss of HAR1 leads to NF-YA4 overexpression, broad transcriptional reprogramming, and induction of LATERAL ORGAN BOUNDARIES DOMAIN , STYLISH , and YUCCA auxin biosynthesis genes, enhancing auxin signaling and lateral root development. Grafting experiments show that HAR1 constrains NF-YA4 -mediated branching both locally in roots and systemically from shoots. Because NF-YA4 functions partly redundantly with NF-YA1 to mediate nodule emergence, our results suggest a model in which duplication and neofunctionalization of an ancestral NF-YA-dependent pathway controlling lateral root development facilitated its recruitment to the nodulation program. They also raise the possibility that AON could have evolved, at least in part, through the co-option of a LRR-RK/miR169/ NF-YA regulatory module that limited lateral root development.

articles.title: In-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling
articles.abstract: Constitutive modeling is fundamental to computational solid mechanics, yet most existing approaches remain material-specific and require retraining or recalibration when materials change. Here we introduce In-Context Modeling (ICM), a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling that infers constitutive behavior from physical context rather than material-specific optimization. Using hyperelasticity as a testbed, we demonstrate that ICM can be trained once on equilibrium deformation fields spanning diverse materials, geometries, and boundary conditions, enforcing physical equilibrium without stress labels. After training, the same model can be directly deployed on previously unseen hyperelastic materials without retraining. At inference, ICM treats a small set of nonuniform strain fields as physical context to generate constitutive response in a single forward pass. Numerical benchmarks and experimental validation demonstrate accurate stress prediction across out-of-distribution materials and boundary-value problems, together with substantial reductions in deployment cost compared with per-material learning approaches. These results establish in-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling, particularly valuable for heterogeneous biological tissues such as the brain, and suggest a pathway toward foundation models for computational mechanics.

articles.title: Mark A. Ratner (1942–2026): Founded molecular electronics while spearheading the growth of science at Northwestern University
articles.abstract: Recently, we lost one of the original developers of the field of molecular electronics. Mark A. Ratner wrote a famous paper in 1974 that developed the theoretical framework for making a molecule act as a rectifier. This idea, and a host of further ideas that were stimulated by this and other papers, led to a huge amount of experimental and theoretical studies that continue to this day. But Mark’s career was much more than that, with leadership at Northwestern University and beyond that continues to shape the scientific enterprise.

articles.title: Mechanism of catalytic regulation by an allosteric hot spot in dihydrofolate reductase
articles.abstract: Allostery is central to catalysis and regulation, yet how distal perturbations control enzyme activity remains unresolved. Here we elucidate how a distal allosteric hot spot regulates catalysis in dihydrofolate reductase, a benchmark enzyme exhibiting latent allostery. We combine enhanced conformational sampling, reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step, and perturbation-induced nonequilibrium molecular dynamics with evolutionary analysis and experimental kinetics to obtain a comprehensive molecular description of conformational landscapes, catalytic activity, and allosteric communication. We show that a mutational perturbation at the hot spot redistributes the populations of two globally similar conformations with a subtle but critical structural difference that makes one catalytically competent and the other not. Nonequilibrium relaxation simulations further reveal that the transition between these two states in the mutant proceeds through a stepwise sequence of local structural rearrangements rather than a concerted global motion. Guided by this mechanism, we rationally engineer a compensatory second-site mutation that partially restores activity. These results provide a unified thermodynamic and kinetic view of allostery and establish a general, mechanistically guided framework for engineering allosteric regulation in enzymes.

articles.title: Multiscale Brownian dynamics simulations reveal effects of macromolecular crowding on protein–ligand association
articles.abstract: Macromolecular crowding is known to influence the diffusive, binding, kinetic, and equilibrium properties of proteins in a range of environments such as occur inside biological cells or in highly concentrated solutions of protein therapeutics. However a quantitative understanding of the effects of macromolecular crowding on the rates of protein-small molecule binding is lacking. Here, we present an adaptive model to simulate the association of two solutes in a macromolecularly crowded environment using Brownian dynamics and to compute the corresponding bimolecular association rate constant. The adaptive model represents interactions with atomistic detail for short-range crowder–noncrowder interactions, while using a coarse-grained approach for long-range crowder–noncrowder interactions and all crowder–crowder interactions. This multiscale approach is integrated in the Simulation of Diffusional Association (SDA) software for Brownian dynamics simulation of biomolecular diffusion. We applied this model to compute the rates of association for two contrasting protein-small molecule inhibitor complexes in environments varying in macromolecular crowder type and density, and we used Markov State modeling of the encounter trajectories to analyze the binding pathways. The results reveal competing effects: While the presence of the crowders can hinder ligand binding by reducing the translational diffusion rates of the solutes and obstructing the protein binding sites, crowders can also enhance the bimolecular association rate by other mechanisms, including channeling and the caging effect.

articles.title: Origami state machine with time-varying magnetic fields
articles.abstract: Achieving reliable, remote control over multiple stable states in modular systems remains a challenge due to the coupling between modules and history-dependent transitions. Here, we present magnetic origami state machines that enable deterministic navigation from any unknown initial state to any target state under magnetic actuation. By assuming mutually distinct energy barriers in modular Kresling origami assemblies, we realize fully accessible transition graphs with scalable state spaces. Guided by the graph associated to the state machine, a rotating magnetic field induces a universal reset that autonomously drives the system to a known equilibrium state from arbitrary states without sensing or feedback, while pulsed magnetic inputs further enable programmable transitions to any target state via prescribed actuation sequences. A reduced-order Lagrangian mechanics model predicts snap-through dynamics across reset, stepwise programming (between graph nodes), and shortcuts (by adapting pulse magnitude and orientation) where inertia triggers simultaneous multicell transitions with a single pulse. These results establish a general framework for programmable magneto-mechanical state machines with autonomous state reset and full state-space control.

Structural basis of glycoprotein recognition by the human folding sensor UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase
articles.abstract: UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) plays a central role in quality control of glycoprotein folding within the early secretory pathway, yet the molecular basis of UGGT1 substrate recognition remains poorly understood. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human full-length multidomain UGGT1. Monomeric UGGT1 structures reveal two conformational states corresponding to “open” and “closed” architectures. Three-dimensional variability and molecular dynamics simulations suggest the existence of intermediate conformations, leading to a model in which a continuum of structural transitions underlies UGGT1 function. Notably, in the open state, the EM-maps reveal at the top of the U-shaped protein a density that bridges the sensory TRXL2 and the glucosyltransferase catalytic domains, consistent with substrate association. This observation supports a mode of binding that places the substrate near the catalytic domain. A dimeric form of UGGT1 was observed in which the glycoprotein substrate binding sites are occluded, suggesting that dimerization may regulate UGGT1 activity. To better understand the spatial relationship between the site of misfolding and that of UGGT-mediated N-glycan reglucosylation, we identified N-glycosylation sites on endogenous glycoprotein substrates by glycoproteomics. No consensus sequence was found flanking modified sites, indicating that substrate recognition relies on mechanisms beyond primary sequence. Mutations in the UGGT1 gene cause a novel congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, and the human UGGT1 structure helps explain how disease-associated missense and deletion variants disrupt function. Together, our data provide insight into the relationship between UGGT1 structure and function, integrating enzyme conformational states with client glycoprotein interaction and processing.

articles.title: Where intention goes, responsibility flows: Grounding AI accountability in the machine learning paradigm
articles.abstract: An opening salvo of lawsuits in US courts has begun holding AI companies accountable through independent doctrinal routes: Product liability and agency law cut as swords, while the shields of Section 230 immunity and First Amendment doctrine begin to crack. This Perspective points out that these converging paths share a unifying principle, built on the very engineering architecture of machine learning (ML) itself. Every ML system, across all variants, is constituted by a human-specified objective function before learning begins. Training data, deployment context, user interaction, and postdeployment oversight add further layers of deliberate human intention traceable to identifiable actors. AI output is therefore not the expression of a single speaker but a composite of layered human intents. It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care. This transforms AI accountability from a philosophical puzzle into a tractable legal inquiry: Trace the chain of intentional design decisions across the ML pipeline, grade each actor’s responsibility by their intent’s specificity and foreseeability, and apportion liability accordingly, following the standard three doctrine-neutral questions (attribution, causation, apportionment). Sufficient for most cases, four gaps remain: who owes what share when many hands build one system, proving fault inside an opaque model, harms that surface only after deployment, and remedies that match the technology’s pace. Targeted reforms drawing on environmental, vaccine, and financial regulatory precedents can close these gaps without requiring new legal categories, AI speech rights, AI legal personhood, or defining AI consciousness.
