articles.title: Healthwatch: Plans to abolish patient watchdog are scrapped in government U turn
articles.abstract: Ministers have scrapped plans to abolish Healthwatch England and local Healthwatch groups, after pushback from health leaders and organisations.Launched in 2012, Healthwatch functions as a statutory independent voice for patients, helping the public hold the NHS accountable and push for patient centred improvements.Plans to abolish the Healthwatch network, consisting of 153 local groups and the national body Healthwatch England, were introduced as part of the Health Bill in May,1 amid wider governmental efforts to “simplify the patient safety landscape” of the NHS.It was proposed that the functions of the local Healthwatch organisations would be transferred to NHS integrated care boards, while the role of Healthwatch England would be transferred to the Department of Health and Social Care.2 This would mean an increased reliance on the NHS App for patient feedback. But critics warned that a loss of independence would have led to “health and care services marking their own homework.”Now,...

articles.title: Rama Shanker Singh
articles.abstract: bmj;395/oct30_11/e101174/F1F1f1Rama (known to many of his UK colleagues as “Ron”) was born in Bihar, India, in 1949. His father was an acclaimed general surgeon and, after Rama’s mother died suddenly, he was raised by his beloved second mother, a nurse. The eldest of four siblings, he was raised in Patna, a historic city on the banks of the Ganges. There he attended St Xavier School before transferring to Darbhanga for further college. In his teens he developed a lifelong passion for cinema and at one stage was keen to be an actor himself, before deciding to devote his life to medicine.He graduated from Darbhanga Medical College, Bihar, in 1972. He obtained his masters in general surgery in 1976 and moved to the UK in 1979. He worked in various hospitals and was subsequently appointed as a consultant in emergency medicine at Withybush General Hospital in Wales. From there he moved...

articles.title: Thousands of patients automatically deleted from electronic referral service, watchdog warns
articles.abstract: Patients waiting for specialist care were dropped off the electronic referral service (e-RS) without warning, a national safety watchdog has warned.A Health Services Safety Investigations Body (HSSIB) report earlier this month found that from February to July 2026 over 120 000 referrals, including advice and guidance requests and referrals for review, disappeared from the e-RS.1The watchdog warned that these disappearances came to light only after GPs raised the alarm that patients had not heard from a provider about their referrals and otherwise might have been missed.The HSSIB’s report found no evidence of patients being harmed because of these referral disappearances. However, it acknowledged concerns that some patients could have avoided invasive treatment had they been seen earlier.The e-RS is a web based digital platform supplied by NHS England for referring patients to specialist providers.Responding to the HSSIB’s report, NHS England said that the e-RS was not designed for current referral...

articles.title: [Comment] Governing artificial intelligence for reliable research
articles.abstract: The report, Open Science and the Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Scientific Exchange: Policy Options for Reliable Research,1 published in October, 2026, was commissioned by the European Parliament's Panel for the Future of Science and Technology at a crucial moment for research. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how knowledge is created2 as AI systems are increasingly integrated across many stages of the research lifecycle.3 These methodological and epistemological challenges are leading to AI capabilities that now outpace human verification, transforming scientific disciplines faster than researchers or current governance can respond.

articles.title: 2026 ESMO Congress
Brazil improves access to cancer screening and care
India caps price of 137 cancer drugs
WHO releases framework for expanding access to early breast cancer care
A roadmap for quantifying metabolism in patients with cancer
articles.abstract: Advancements in in vivo stable isotope tracing have revolutionized our understanding of cancer metabolism, transitioning the field from static metabolomic snapshots to dynamic metabolic pathway activities. However, interpreting raw fractional enrichment data presents significant biological and analytical challenges. This review systematically examines the methodological landscape of in vivo tracing, addressing the interpretive gap created by clinical constraints, such as single-timepoint surgical sampling. We dissect how secondary circulating tracers and the inherent heterogeneity of the tumor microenvironment can confound metabolic signals. We highlight the critical transition to metabolic flux analysis as the requisite computational step to overcome these challenges and to identify targetable metabolic vulnerabilities in precision oncology.

articles.title: Navigating clinical decisions through cancer cartography
articles.abstract: Multiplexed spatial profiling has shown that tumor architecture influences therapy response, yet few spatial phenotypes are in clinical use. We opine that the immediate priority is simplification and validation of complex spatial features. We draw a parallel to cartography: maps are useful because they carry a limited set of named features whose meaning is agreed. Tumor maps could be built the same way: from the presence of a defined cell type, its proximity to another, its location within a tissue compartment, its state of activation, or combinations of these. Such features may have more clinical applicability than variable, unsupervised two-dimensional ‘neighborhoods’. We propose cancer cartography as the process of assembling such validated features into tumor maps that guide treatment selection.

articles.title: Trends at 50: a mission that matters
articles.abstract: What makes a great review article in your field? As more research is published every day, it has become increasingly difficult to keep up with the latest developments and to ensure that you are hearing from the leading scientists driving these innovations and advances. How do you know what is new and what is valuable?

articles.title: Ultrastructure of multiciliated cell basal bodies revealed by expansion microscopy
articles.abstract: van Grinsven et al. combine tenfold expansion microscopy with a volumetric fluorescence averaging tool to map the human airway basal body at nanoscale resolution. They resolve the 3D organization of more than 20 proteins and assess the function of a subset of proteins in the organization of the apical microtubule network.

articles.title: Hydrogen bonds in electrocatalytic CO2 reduction
articles.abstract: The electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) can convert CO2 into value-added chemicals, but its efficiency and selectivity are limited by the thermodynamic stability of CO2 and competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). hydrogen bonding offers a design strategy beyond direct metal-site modification by stabilizing CO2-derived intermediates and mediating proton transfer. In homogeneous catalysts, hydrogen bonding units in the molecular outer sphere stabilize metal-bound intermediates and guide protonation pathways. In heterogeneous systems, analogous functions are implemented at solid–liquid interfaces, where catalyst-surface modification alters the stability of surface-bound intermediates and regulates proton transport pathways. This review highlights hydrogen bonding as a shared design element that bridges molecular precision and interfacial regulation in CO2RR catalysis, identifying common design requirements for balancing intermediate stabilization, proton delivery, and HER suppression.

articles.title: How do we know when invasive species control strategies work?
articles.abstract: Controlling invasive species is costly and difficult but can have major ecological, economic, and health benefits. Researchers commonly compare the efficacy of specific control methods. However, invasive species control programs vary greatly in overarching goals and often occur over large areas, long timeframes, and varied environmental and social contexts. The success of these programs likely hinges on factors including organizational structures, concurrent restoration activities, geographic and temporal scope of control, and the invasive species’ biology. To enable assessment of the relative influence of these common features, we propose clearer definitions of success in invasive species control and explicit comparisons among control programs. Post hoc assessment of existing programs’ success will complement system-specific studies to guide strategies that work in real-world situations.

articles.title: A Hybrid Message-Passing and Electric-Field Representation for Electrostatic QM/MM Embedding with Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
articles.abstract: Within a hybrid quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics approach a small region of a large atomistic system is described quantum mechanically, while the rest of the system is represented by a classical force field. Despite this, the computational cost of the quantum calculation severely limits the accessible simulation and sampling time. Replacing the quantum calculation with a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) trained on quantum reference data can greatly increase the accessible simulation time. However, the accuracy and efficiency strongly depend on the specific way in which the MLIP incorporates information about the classical (electrostatic) environment. Here, we demonstrate that existing strategies based purely on features derived from an external electric field fail to distinguish certain environments, ultimately limiting their accuracy. As a solution, we propose an extension to the equivariant TensorNet architecture that mitigates this shortcoming by incorporating classical atoms close to the quantum region into the message-passing scheme, combined with features derived from the electric field for describing the environment farther away. We show that this combination achieves higher accuracy than either approach alone.

articles.title: Atomistic Emergence of Vibrational Polariton Condensation
articles.abstract: Nonequilibrium polariton condensation is a macroscopic quantum phenomenon in which overwhelming population accumulation is observed at the band edge of the lower polariton (LP) dispersion curve under incoherent material pumping. As a promising route toward nonequilibrium Bose--Einstein condensates, its description, however, remains predominantly limited to models with phenomenological material parameters. Herein, a fully atomistic description of vibrational polariton condensation is developed by employing mesoscale cavity molecular dynamics simulations, a method which self-consistently propagates classical electromagnetic dynamics coupled to realistic molecules in a multimode Fabry--Pérot cavity. Under continuous-wave pumping, a lower polariton condensate forms when the infrared cavity is coupled to harmonic, homogeneously broadened molecular vibrations, such as the bending modes of liquid CO2 and CS2, whereas anharmonic stretching modes and liquids with fast intramolecular relaxation hardly condense. The role of libration-bending coupling for facilitating the LP condensation is further discussed. GPU-accelerated mesoscale simulations involving approximately 50 million atoms additionally provide direct two-dimensional real-space imaging of fluid-like polariton patterns during the condensation formation. Overall, this study provides key design insights into vibrational polariton condensation as a novel approach for controlling liquid-phase chemistry.

articles.title: Dysfunctional Functionals and their Therapies in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory
articles.abstract: The exchange-correlation functional in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory (TDDFT) is known to have dependence on past densities and initial states, and yet this memory-dependence is ignored in practical calculations which almost always use an adiabatic approximation. We discuss the dysfunction that arises due to this deficiency and point to therapies that go beyond the adiabatic approximation. Still, adiabatic TDDFT has had success in a wide range of systems for response properties and for fully non-equilibrium dynamics, and why this is so is only partially understood. This, together with the rigorous foundation of the exact theory and its favorable system-size scaling, provides tremendous impetus for continuing to strive towards improved approximations to the exact functionals, and a deeper understanding of the impact of approximations in applications.

articles.title: Estimating Irving-Kirkwood pressure profiles from per-atom virial and density profiles: a closure for the contour-dependent term in planar liquid films
articles.abstract: The local pressure tensor of an inhomogeneous fluid is not unique. Two tangential profiles are in common use in planar simulations: the Irving-Kirkwood (IK) profile, which requires a dedicated pass over every pair of atoms for every slab, and the per-atom virial (PAV) profile, which molecular-dynamics codes produce at negligible cost and coincides with the Harasima contour. The two differ by the derivative of a pair quantity, P_T^IK - P_T^PAV = dQ/dz. We show that, for Lennard-Jones free-standing films, Q(z) can be predicted from the density profile and the bulk radial distribution function of the coexisting liquid: under the closure rho2(r1,r2) ~ rho(z1) rho(z2) g(r12), with a pair-local interpolation of g between its liquid and dilute limits, Q is a double integral of rho(z) against a kernel built from u'(r) g(r). The estimator P_T^IK,est = P_T^PAV + dQ/dz is tested against IK profiles measured on the same trajectories for 20 films (thicknesses 7-25 sigma, three cutoff radii, two temperatures): the root-mean-square residual is 0.001-0.002 epsilon/sigma^3, against 0.010-0.021 for the uncorrected profile, and Q, the amount that the contour choice transfers between the two interfaces of a film with non-equivalent surfaces, is recovered to within 0.6% of the surface tension. Applied to the normal component, the same closure removes 83-92% of the spurious structure of the per-atom zz profile, a test that needs no IK run. Its mixture form is validated on three two-component films with an adsorbate unequally distributed between their faces, where it resolves the tension of each face; a clean face recovers the tension of the pure film.

articles.title: General-purpose foundation models surpass specialized ones on chemical property prediction tasks
articles.abstract: Foundation models (FMs) learn reusable representations from large collections of unlabeled data. In chemistry the corresponding data mainly consists of molecular structures, which are abundant, whereas experimental measurements are scarce. Chemical FMs such as ChemBERTa and MoLFormer were therefore trained on diverse molecular structures to enable fine-tuning on small experimental datasets (less than 100 datapoints in most realistic scenarios) and subsequent property prediction. At the same time, general-purpose FMs such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were trained on virtually all publicly available data, including knowledge of the humankind on molecular properties and laws governing them. Here we compare accuracies of chemical and general-purpose FMs on tasks from various areas of chemistry. Strikingly, general-purpose GPT-6 Astra outperforms the currently eligible chemical FMs on five physicochemical and quantum-chemical regression tasks when only 60 experimental datapoints are available. Only when provided 10x datapoints do the best chemical FMs reach performance of GPT-6 Astra: on 1,000 and 10,000 points they show performance on par with Astra on 60 and 1,000 points, respectively. Thus, counterintuitively, frontier general-purpose FMs are better suited for guiding chemical research in data-scarce areas than specialized chemical FMs, suggesting that learning relevant primitives (e.g. chemical structures) does not substitute training on relevant humankind knowledge.

articles.title: Impact of Surface Preparation on the Propulsion of Catalytic Janus Colloids and Implications for Reproducibility
articles.abstract: Platinum-coated polystyrene (PS) Janus particles (JPs) propelled by the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) are a widely used model system for active matter, yet reported speeds for similar particles and fuel concentrations differ by more than an order of magnitude. Broad adoption of these materials requires increasing consistency in the preparation and achieving improved repeatability in their behavior. Herein, we focused on two routine, but rarely reported, preparation steps that we found to alter the particle speed. First, we found that pre-exposing the platinum cap to H2O2 before cell assembly increased the mean speed by a factor of 2.4. The size of this effect depended on batch history, where an aged batch responded strongly, while a freshly prepared batch sped up by only 16%. Second, we found that plasma cleaning of the glass substrate decreased the speed 2.7 times. In a 120 $μ$m cell the suppression was the same at both walls even when only one wall was treated. The suppression grew with the treated glass area per unit fluid volume, which pointed to species released into the bulk solution rather than to a change at the wall. Plasma-cleaned glass released more ions into water than untreated glass, and XPS detected an ionic metal fluoride on the plasma-cleaned surface. A model in which the released ions lower the speed through the solution conductivity reproduced the measured speeds in all four cell geometries. Of the 17 published studies compared here, pre-activation is reported in only four studies and substrate cleaning in only six studies. We propose a minimum reporting standard for the preparation and associated speed measurements of catalytic Janus particles.

articles.title: Intermolecular and Interfacial Origins of Layering in a Near-Isotropic Organic Glass Former
articles.abstract: Physical vapor deposition can produce organic glasses with enhanced stability and pronounced structural anisotropy (layering) even when the constituent molecules are nearly spherical. However, the microscopic origin of the layering in spherical molecular glass formers remains unclear. We investigated vapor-deposited films of 9-(3,5-di(naphthalen-1-yl)phenyl)anthracene (α,α-A) by grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering, atomistic molecular dynamics, and coarse-grained simulations. Experimentally, the layering signal varies nonmonotonically with deposition temperature and is strongest near 0.8T_g. Simulated scattering calculations reproduce the principal experimental features and show that the layering peak does not originate from shifts in single molecule degrees of freedom. In fact, the simulated deposited and bulk glasses show largely the same single-molecule conformations. Interestingly, a one-site coarse-grained liquid with isotropic interactions develops a comparable interfacial layering signature. These results indicate that layering in α,α-A arises primarily from collective density correlations generated at the free surface during deposition rather than from conformational bias or orientational ordering. The findings connect structural anisotropy in vapor-deposited molecular glasses to the generic interfacial organization of simple liquids.

articles.title: Molecular conical intersections with odd electron number are realizations of the topological Yang monopole
articles.abstract: The two-level conical intersection of a molecule with odd electron number in the absence of magnetic field obeys time-reversal symmetry $T^{2}=-1$ (referred to as the $T^{2}=-1$ conical intersection), and has a five-dimensional branching space due to the Kramer degeneracy. Similar to how the conical intersection of a molecule in a magnetic field ($T^{2}=0$) behaves as the Dirac monopole, the $T^{2}=-1$ conical intersection behaves as the Yang monopole, an mathematical generalization of Dirac monopole with SU(2) gauge field and SO(5) symmetry. This implies that we can study topological properties of $T^{2}=-1$ conical intersections in chemistry based on what is known about Yang monopole in high energy physics. In this work, we present a few mathematical tools to study this connection. First, we show that geometric algebra and quaternion numbers together provides a natural way to utilize the $T^{2}=-1$ time reversal symmetry and the SO(5) symmetry in scaled coordinates, making it simple to derive eigenfunctions, Berry connection and Berry curvature of $T^{2}=-1$ conical intersection. In particular, this approach provides a simple proof that when viewed from the upper or lower states, the $T^{2}=-1$ conical intersection behaves as the self-dual or self-antidual Yang monopole with second Chern number $C_{2}=+\frac{1}{4}$ or $-\frac{1}{4}$ respectively. In addition, we propose a visualization method for the SU(2) Berry connection of $T^{2}=-1$ conical intersection. This is achieved by showing that the nonzero part of the Berry connection induces Hopf-fibration on the $S^{3}$ longitude space, and is further visualized through stereographic projection.

articles.title: Second-order Bethe-Salpeter kernels: the interplay of vertex-corrected quasiparticle energies and the screened interaction
articles.abstract: We study second-order Bethe-Salpeter kernels generated by truncating an iterative formulation of Hedin's equations after the second cycle. Starting from the Hartree-Fock or the $GW$ self-energy, whose first cycles correspond to TDHF and $GW$+BSE, we obtain the second-cycle kernel by differentiating the first-cycle correlation self-energy with the interacting correlation function replaced by the non-interacting one, and evaluate it in the static limit of the effective kernel. Using fixed restricted Hartree-Fock orbitals, we benchmark 30 singlet and 28 triplet excitation energies for seven small molecules (six for the triplets) against the theoretical best estimates from QUEST v1.2. The second cycle lowers the mean absolute error (MAE) in both sequences. For the $GW$ sequence, the MAE decreases from 0.63 to 0.29 eV (singlets), on par with ADC(2) (0.30 eV), and from 0.43 to 0.38 eV (triplets). BSE$^{(2)}$@HF removes the triplet instabilities of TDHF and yields MAEs of 0.43 and 0.38 eV, or 0.31 and 0.30 eV when the Tamm-Dancoff approximation is applied in all cycles. Assigning the statically screened interaction $W_0$ to the exchange part of the $GW$ self-energy counts second-order screening twice in the second-cycle kernel and strongly blueshifts valence excitations. Without this double counting, dressing the exchange-type terms with $W_0$ lowers the singlet MAE from 0.37 to 0.29 eV but leaves the triplets nearly unchanged. Replacing second-order Green's function (GF2) quasiparticle energies by vertex-corrected ones in the same kernel raises excitation energies by about 0.7 eV, improving Rydberg but degrading valence excitations. A perturbative dynamical correction of the kernel blueshifts valence excitations by 0.3-0.4 eV and increases the errors of all full-matrix BSE$^{(2)}$ variants. The consistent improvement over the first cycle suggests that higher cycles are worth pursuing.

articles.title: Simple algorithm for evaluating SU(2) non-abelian geometric phase in the vicinity of molecular conical intersection of odd electron number
articles.abstract: Molecular conical intersection of odd-electron number are known to give arise to non-abelian geometric phases. In this work, we present a simple algorithm for evaluating the SU(2) geometric phases given a trajectory represented as a discrete set of coordinates in the 5-dimensional branching space. Motivated by the special property that such conical intersection behaves as abelian ones in 3-dimensional subspace, we take two steps to establish the algorithm. We first prove that it is possible to construct an augmented trajectory consisting of spherical triangles that has the same geometric phases as the original trajectory. We then prove that the geometric phase contribution from each spherical triangle can be evaluated from its properties using Stokes' theorem in a way that closely resembles abelian conical intersections. The total geometric phases are thus evaluated by path-ordered products of contributions from each spherical triangle. Based on the augmented trajectory, we further show that the geometric phases of the upper and lower states will switch under inversion transformation of the trajectory. This relation is further generalized to show that the Wilson loop, defined as the trace of the geometric phases, will switch between the two states under any 5-dimensional improper isometric transformation. Example calculations of geometric phases for trajectories generated on 5-dimensional polytopes are also presented and discussed.

articles.title: Streptavidin-Biotin Binding is Intrinsically Non-Cooperative, but Experimental Artefacts Can Induce Apparent Positive Cooperativity
articles.abstract: The biotin-streptavidin interaction is a key component of nanobiotechnology, yet the nature of its cooperativity remains a debated question. Here, we introduce a label-free spectroscopy approach based on confocal UV autofluorescence microscopy to probe the binding cooperativity of this high-affinity system. By leveraging the intrinsic autofluorescence of tryptophan residues, we avoid artefacts associated with extrinsic fluorescent labels, enabling precise measurements of fully biotin-saturated streptavidin across a wide range of molar ratios. Our experimental results, supported by Monte Carlo simulations, provide conclusive evidence for the absence of cooperativity. However, we show that false signs of apparent positive cooperativity can emerge from local concentration inhomogeneities occurring when rapid reaction kinetics outpace mixing. By establishing the non-cooperative nature of biotin-streptavidin binding and identifying the key conditions to avoid cooperativity artefacts, these insights resolve a longstanding debate and offer critical implications for streptavidin-based biotechnological applications.

articles.title: Surface Hopping Dynamics on Adiabatic States Propagated with Real-Time TDDFT
articles.abstract: Real-time time-dependent density functional theory (RT-TDDFT) is widely used to simulate ultrafast electron dynamics, but it is usually coupled to the nuclei through the mean-field Ehrenfest approximation, which cannot describe wavepacket branching and violates detailed balance. Surface hopping avoids these problems, but has not previously been combined with RT-TDDFT because real-time propagation does not directly provide the necessary adiabatic states. In this work we introduce an energy-scaled time-dependent Kohn--Sham (TDKS) propagation scheme, motivated by the quantum adiabatic theorem. Scaling widens the separation between electronic and nuclear timescales, so that each propagated state follows the adiabatic surface selected by its initial condition: either the ground state or a non-Aufbau self-consistent-field ($Δ$SCF) solution. The propagation thereby avoids the convergence failures of static SCF solvers in regions of strong nonadiabatic coupling. Because the independently propagated states are complex-valued and not mutually orthogonal, we reformulate the mapping approach to surface hopping (MASH) in a complex adiabatic basis and introduce a dynamical transition orbital (DTO) gauge that restores a well-defined particle--hole representation for evaluating time-derivative couplings and nonadiabatic coupling vectors. Applied to the photoisomerization of \textit{trans}-diimide, the scheme converges systematically as the scaling factor is increased and yields an excited-state lifetime in good agreement with previous nonadiabatic simulations based on static SCF.\@ These results establish real-time propagation as an efficient and numerically stable route to the adiabatic states and couplings required for first-principles surface hopping.

articles.title: Surface chemistry as data for level-set simulation of etching and deposition
articles.abstract: Level-set simulators of etching and deposition move the surface with a velocity that depends on adsorbate coverages. These coverages are usually computed from balances solved and coded by hand for each chemistry, whereas voxel-based Monte Carlo profile simulators read the reaction mechanism as data. For the open-source level-set simulator ViennaPS, this work presents a surface model whose rate laws, Jacobian and velocity are derived from a reaction file and evaluated with ray-traced fluxes. Steady-state coverages are obtained with Newton's method and transient coverages with a conservative integrator. One compiled model is applied to eight chemistries for chemical vapour deposition, selective epitaxy, plasma etching, sputtering and atomic layer deposition. It reproduces a hand-written silicon etch model to seven significant digits at a single point and within the Monte Carlo noise in a masked trench. In a high-aspect-ratio cavity, alumina conformality is determined by a trimethylaluminium reaction probability within the measured range.

articles.title: The Role of Electron-Nuclear Coupling on Chemical and Physical Processes
articles.abstract: Over the last few decades, Born-Oppenheimer (BO) and Born-Oppenheimer-Huang (BOH) treatments for electron-nuclear equation of motion have been considered as the cornerstone for qualitative as well as quantitative exploration and understanding of chemical and physical processes. The BO approximation due to the large mass difference between electrons and nuclei as well as the energy separation among the electronic states could able to predict some of the processes (chemical and physical) satisfactorily at lower energy regime. Such approximation (BO) quite often fails for those cases with the involvement of excited electronic states, in particular, due to the coupling among the states. On the other hand, the BO treatment provides two important quantities, namely, the adiabatic potential energy surfaces (PESs) and the nonadiabatic coupling terms (NACTs) determining the forces, which control the motion of the nuclei in a molecule. The NACTs play a major role in photoexcitation spectra, charge transfer chemical reactions, ferroelectric property and other processes, where significant anomalies are observed between single and multiple PES(s) results. Since the NACTs often exhibit singularity at the close vicinity of degenerate states forming conical intersections (CIs), such coupling terms could break the symmetry of the molecular processes changing the observables qualitatively.

articles.title: Towards Out-of-Distribution Uncertainty Quantification for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials via Pre-Training
articles.abstract: Informative uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for the practical deployment of machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), as it provides insight into their reliability across chemical space. Although numerous post-hoc uncertainty estimation methods for MLIPs have recently been proposed, most have been trained in low-data regimes, restricting their applicability to narrow domains of interest. Inspired by the emergence of foundational MLIPs, we propose pre-training uncertainty estimators on large, diverse datasets to enable broader applicability. We pre-train several UQ models on large materials science datasets to quantify the uncertainty of different MLIPs, and evaluate their performance on both in-distribution and out-of-domain (OOD) adsorption-energy predictions. We find that pre-trained uncertainty estimators provide viable zero-shot uncertainty estimates across multiple datasets, while fine-tuning consistently yields positive correlations between predicted uncertainty and prediction error, even on the most challenging datasets. These results lay the groundwork for foundational UQ models for MLIPs, ultimately facilitating their deployment in practical settings by providing users with a priori information about model reliability and applicability.

articles.title: VESPER: Online Learning of Free Energies with a Multi-Tempered Variational Objective
articles.abstract: Computing molecular free-energy landscapes over collective variables (CVs) is central to understanding molecular mechanisms, but poses a difficult learning problem without training data available a priori. Samples of the marginal CV distribution must be generated by molecular dynamics (MD), whose trajectories can remain trapped in metastable states and rarely cross the free-energy barriers governing conformational changes or chemical reactions. We introduce VESPER, which couples the generation of these samples to neural-network-driven free-energy learning: MD supplies configurations for learning, while the evolving model biases the MD to accelerate exploration and generate further training data. VESPER minimizes a single variational objective that is convex in the free energy and can combine several tempering levels, each flattening the free-energy landscape to promote barrier crossing. Every level has the same physical free energy as its minimizer, allowing data from all levels to train one shared model without reweighting. Learning uses the difference in mean parameter gradients between biased MD configurations and auxiliary walkers that explore the flattened model in CV space. We prove conditional convergence of the coupled overdamped population dynamics without replica exchange under log-Sobolev and Polyak-Lojasiewicz assumptions. VESPER matches or improves on established enhanced-sampling methods on alanine dipeptide and yields self-consistent free-energy reconstructions from three to six CVs on alanine tetrapeptide. For methane dehydrogenation on Ni(511) with a machine-learned interatomic potential, it recovers two-CV Boltzmann marginals and a reactant-to-saddle free-energy difference along a three-CV path, both qualitatively consistent with the lower-dimensional reference. It also samples RMSD-defined folded and unfolded regions of chignolin while biasing seventeen CVs.

articles.title: eCAS: An Orbital Embedding Method for Quantum Computing
articles.abstract: Future fault-tolerant quantum computers will allow us to calculate electronic structures of atomistic systems. However, these systems will be intrinsically limited in size, requiring embedding theories for many systems because of the unfavorable scaling of the number of terms describing the electron-electron interaction in the second-quantized electronic Hamiltonian. Quantum embedding theories address this challenge by partitioning a quantum system into a region of interest, the impurity, and its (larger) complement, the environment. However, currently available quantum embedding methods place restrictive demands on near-future quantum computers, such as the need to measure reduced density matrices or the need for repeated evaluations. Here, we introduce the new orbital embedding method eCAS that steers clear of these pitfalls by constructing a multi-CAS problem, the active spaces of which are localized and can be solved independently of each other with any quantum algorithm. This also allows for the development of comparatively simple gradient expressions. eCAS leverages the Schmidt decomposition to construct initial impurity and bath orbitals and augments them with localized environment orbitals, based on a mutual correlation criterion. The mutual correlation criterion makes eCAS systematically improvable without the need for any iteratively determined quantities.

articles.title: Compensation of hyperexcitability with simulation-based inference
articles.abstract: The activity of healthy neuronal networks is tightly regulated, and a shift toward hyperexcitability can cause various problems, such as epilepsies, memory deficits, and motor disorders. Numerous cellular, synaptic, and intrinsic mechanisms of hyperexcitability and compensatory mechanisms to restore healthy activity have been proposed. However, quantifying multiple compensatory mechanisms and their dependence on specific pathophysiological mechanisms has proven challenging, even in computational models. We use simulation-based inference to quantify the interactions of putative compensatory mechanisms in a spiking neuronal network model. Various parameters of the model can compensate for the changes in other parameters to maintain baseline activity, and we estimated their compensatory potential. Furthermore, specific causes of hyperexcitability – interneuron loss, excitatory recurrent synapses, and principal cell depolarization – have distinct compensatory mechanisms that can restore normal excitability. Our results show that spiking neuronal network simulators could generate hypotheses about the mechanisms of pathophysiological network mechanisms.

articles.title: Distinct gradients of cortical architecture capture visual representations and behavior across the lifespan
articles.abstract: The microstructure of cells within the human cerebral cortex varies across the cortical ribbon, where changes in cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture are thought to endow each region of the cortex with its unique function. While fine-scale relative to a cell, these changes at the population level impact architectural properties of the cortex measurable in vivo by noninvasive MRI, such as the thickness and myelin content of the cortex. This raises the question of whether or not we can use these in vivo architectural measures to understand cortical organization, function, and development more broadly. Using the human visual cortex as a test bed, we demonstrated two architectural gradients, one in which cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture converge and another in which they diverge. These two gradients underlie the structural and functional topography of the visual cortex, even predicting the presence of new visual representations. Moreover, the two gradients show distinct visual behavior relevance and lifespan trajectory. These findings provide a more general framework for understanding the human cortex, showing that architectural gradients are a measurable fingerprint of functional organization and ontogenetic routines in the human brain.

articles.title: Fitness level, but not sex, affects exercise-induced pain modulation
articles.abstract: In a previous study by our group (Nold et al., 2025), we investigated exercise-induced pain modulation after high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise in a heterogeneous sample of diverse fitness levels. Exploratory analyses suggested an interaction of sex, fitness level, and drug treatment, indicating that males showed increasing hypoalgesia after high- compared to low-intensity exercise with increasing fitness levels, which was diminished when naloxone was administered. In contrast, these effects were not evident in females. These exploratory findings warranted further investigation to determine if and to what extent exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level and/or sex. In this current study, we investigated an all-female sample (N=21) of high fitness levels using a similar paradigm as in the previous study, comparing heat and pressure pain ratings after high-intensity and low-intensity exercise. Our data show an interaction of exercise intensity and stimulus intensity in heat pain, with greater pain relief following high-intensity exercise, especially at the highest stimulus intensity. Despite results for pressure pain not reaching significance, a similar trend was evident. These results suggest that females at a high fitness level also show exercise-induced pain modulation for high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise. Furthermore, we pooled the data of the current and previous study, providing evidence for fitness level but not sex to moderate exercise-induced pain modulation in heat pain. These findings suggest that exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level but not on sex.

articles.title: Glutamate receptor composition at Drosophila neuromuscular junctions depends on developmental stage and muscle identity
articles.abstract: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of larval Drosophila is widely used for studying synaptic transmission. Larval body wall muscles express five ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) subunits that assemble into two tetrameric complexes, with subunit composition determining the strength and plasticity of synaptic transmission. Because NMJ function has been extensively characterized in larvae, it has commonly been assumed that adult fly NMJs share this molecular composition, despite substantial differences between life stages. Here, we systematically compare glutamate receptor expression across larval and adult Drosophila muscles. We find that adult leg and flight muscles exhibit different iGluR expression than larvae, lacking expression of several receptors previously considered essential. Adjacent muscles within the adult femur express distinct iGluRs, suggesting specialization of flexor and extensor muscles. Finally, the glutamate-gated chloride channel (GluClα) is expressed extrasynaptically in adult but not larval muscle fibers. Our results reveal unexpected heterogeneity in glutamate receptor expression across muscles and developmental stages, demonstrating the need for muscle-specific analyses in flies and other animals.

articles.title: Oxytocin neurons signal state-dependent transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal
articles.abstract: Core body temperature (Tb) is defended within narrow limits through thermoregulatory behaviors like huddling, nesting, and physical activity, as well as autonomic responses like brown fat thermogenesis. While Tb displays regulated fluctuations across different behavioral states and rest/arousal cycles, the neural control of these transitions remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the relationship between oxytocin neurons of the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVNOT) and behavioral and autonomic thermoeffector pathways across physiological states in mice. First, we show that PVNOT neurons are activated during social thermoregulation. We then demonstrate that in vivo PVNOT calcium dynamics align with transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal. Counter to our initial hypothesis, these dynamics were observed in both social and non-social contexts. Using a computer vision model to track thermoeffector pathways, we demonstrate that precisely timed stimulation of PVNOT neurons during low-Tb resting states increases thermogenesis followed by behavioral arousal. We therefore suggest a model in which PVNOT neurons facilitate homeostatic state-dependent transitions in thermo-behavioral states.

articles.title: SVEP1 enables efficient binding of angiopoietin-2 to the TIE1 receptor, allowing receptor phosphorylation and downstream signaling
articles.abstract: The molecular mechanisms that drive (lymph-)angiogenesis are crucial to understanding diseases, such as lymphedema, that are caused due to malformations of the lymphatic vasculature. Recently, an interaction between the secreted protein Svep1, a key regulator in lymphangiogenesis, and the transmembrane receptor Tie1 was shown in zebrafish, humans, and mice. Here, guided by in silico AlphaFold-multimer structure predictions of SVEP1 complexes, we assert with protein binding studies that the human CCP20 domain is the primary binding site for TIE1. We further demonstrate that SVEP1 mediates strong binding of ANG2 and TIE1, and that combined stimulation of hdLECs with SVEP1 and ANG2 leads to phosphorylation of TIE1. TIE1 activation by SVEP1 and ANG2 enables downstream signaling and, in turn, potentiates nuclear exclusion of FOXO1 and phosphorylation of AKT compared to SVEP1 or ANG2 alone. We present a model in which ANG1/2 dimers bind to both SVEP1 and TIE1, resulting in the recruitment of multiple TIE1 receptor molecules to a multimeric complex at the cell membrane, potentially amplifying its signaling capacity.

articles.title: ARCADE: Automated and Interpretable Design of Complex Catalysts
articles.abstract: The rational design of high-performance catalysts is pivotal for modern industry but is often hindered by the time-consuming nature of trial-and-error methods. While computational and data-driven approaches have accelerated materials discovery, significant challenges remain, especially for complex systems like multielement disordered nanoparticles. These challenges include immense computational costs, difficulties in modeling stability and heterogeneous active sites, and a lack of interpretability in “black-box” AI models. To address these multifaceted challenges, herein, we introduce ARCADE (Automated Rational Catalyst Design), a generalizable and transferable framework for the automated and interpretable design of complex catalysts. This highly cohesive pipeline introduces key methodological innovations in realistic structure generation, autonomous active-site processing, and short-range order guided interpretability, seamlessly coupled with state-of-the-art pH-dependent microkinetic modeling. Notably, ARCADE streamlines the structural modeling of irregular nanoparticles by transforming intractable combinatorial enumeration into a targeted iterative search; robustly identifies active sites and subsequently resolves ubiquitous adsorbate drift issues arising during structural relaxations; and employs geometric short-range order descriptors derived contribution scores to rapidly decode catalytic mechanisms, thereby efficiently unraveling the complex synergistic effects inherent in multielement catalysts. Using the challenging design of multielement nanoparticle catalysts for CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) as a representative system, we demonstrate that ARCADE can systematically navigate the design process, from evaluating material stability to identifying site-specific activity and selectivity. Our results show that this methodology substantially accelerates the development cycle for complex catalysts, confirming its feasibility and broad applicability. Crucially, this work establishes a fully integrated paradigm for the rational design and discovery of complex materials for challenging chemical reactions.

articles.title: Achieving Low-Temperature High-Efficient Ammonia Decomposition Over sub-nm Ru Cluster with CeO2– x Support via Photopromoted Hydrogen Spillover and Nitrogen Recombination
articles.abstract: The low-temperature high-efficient decomposition of ammonia, a carbon-free hydrogen carrier, is essential to the promising hydrogen energy storage. However, the decomposition is hindered by slow reaction kinetics due to dynamically hydrogen poisoning and thermodynamically high nitrogen recombination barrier in ordinary thermocatalysis. Herein, we propose a photothermocatalytic strategy to resolve these kinetic issues and achieve enhanced hydrogen production. Under full-spectrum light irradiance of 20 kW m–2, a hydrogen production rate of 4.2 mmol g–1 min–1 at 300 °C has been achieved over the Ru/CeO2–x catalyst, significantly outperforming conventional thermocatalysis. Insights from in situ characterizations and density functional theory calculations indicate that the enhanced performance is ascribed to photopromoted hydrogen spillover and nitrogen recombination, which are mediated by the strong metal–support interaction. On one hand, the photogenerated electrons promote the H dissociation over sub-nm Ru clusters and migration across the metal–support interface, and the photoinduced oxygen-vacancy-rich CeO2–x surface favors to spread the active H· species. On the other hand, the photogenerated electrons reduce the activation energy for Ru–N bond cleavage, which is beneficial for N–N recombination. This study has demonstrated the distinct advantage of photothermocatalytic hydrogen production as an energy-saving, high-efficient, and carbon-free route.

articles.title: Anionic Photocatalyst as Excited-State Super-Reductants in Organic Synthesis
articles.abstract: Organic chromophores have emerged as powerful photoreductants in modern photocatalysis, enabling a wide range of synthetically valuable transformations under mild conditions. Among these, anionic chromophores constitute a particularly distinctive class owing to their extreme reducing power in the photoexcited state. Deprotonation-driven generation of anionic species frequently induces a bathochromic shift in the absorption profile of the parent neutral chromophore, thereby extending light harvesting into the visible region. More importantly, localization of negative charge on a heteroatom or π-conjugated framework can promote intramolecular charge-transfer transitions when an appropriate electron-accepting motif is present. Such excited states often exhibit prolonged lifetimes, facilitating diffusion-controlled electron transfer with substrates. Collectively, these features endow photoexcited anions with extraordinary reducing power, enabling the activation of some of the most reductively recalcitrant chemical bonds that remain inaccessible to conventional photocatalysts. In recent years, the rapid expansion of anion-mediated photochemistry has established photoexcited anions—many of which are generated in situ—as versatile super-reductants for addressing longstanding challenges in synthetic chemistry. This review highlights the fundamental design principles governing anionic photocatalysts, their photophysical and photochemical properties, and the mechanistic features that underpin their reactivity. We further provide a comprehensive overview of the diverse classes of anionic chromophores and their emerging applications, and discuss future opportunities to advance anion-based organophotocatalysis.

articles.title: Correction to “Boosting Benzene Hydroxylation via Hydroxyl-Migration-Mediated Synergy of Spatially Isolated Cu and La Single Atoms”
Entropy–Enthalpy Compensation in Electrocatalytic Rates
articles.abstract: Measuring the temperature dependence of electrocatalytic reaction rates is a powerful, yet underexplored, way of investigating the underlying kinetics. In this study, we develop the understanding behind such kinetic measurements. Through a very simple model of the surface kinetics for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), we explore how extracted Arrhenius parameters depend on potential and rationalize a series of entropy-enthalpy correlations in experimental HER rates. We find that the entropy-dependent prefactor can change alongside the apparent activation energy, thus signaling deviations from the established Butler-Volmer kinetics that have so far mostly been attributed to potential-driven solvent dynamics. Distinct kinetic fingerprints emerge for different groups of metal catalysts that are in qualitative agreement with recent experiments. We elucidate these characteristic fingerprints in terms of shifting kinetic regimes and generalize our findings to other electrocatalytic reactions and setups. Our analysis overall suggests the entropy loss/gain due to species’ adsorption/desorption as the main driver behind measured changes in the Arrhenius prefactor.

articles.title: Light-Reconfigured Adsorption over Zeolite-Confined Amorphous Multicomponent Alloy Nanoparticles Enables Photothermal Dry Reforming of Methane
articles.abstract: High-temperature dry reforming of methane (DRM) over Ni-based catalysts is limited by sintering and coking, while competitive adsorption can further restrict efficient utilization of CH4 and CO2. Here, we report a one-step hydrothermal strategy to encapsulate amorphous NiCoCuZnMn multicomponent alloy nanoparticles with partially oxidized Zn/Mn-containing surface domains within a TS-1 zeolite matrix, affording a structurally confined photothermal catalyst (denoted MA@TS-1). Under illumination, MA@TS-1 reaches a CO production rate of 21.85 mmol g–1 h–1 at 450 °C and sustains continuous operation for 500 h. Kinetic analysis, pulse-response experiments, in situ DRIFTS, and illumination-dependent XPS collectively show that irradiation changes both the adsorption response and the surface electronic state of the catalyst. CO2 pre-adsorption strongly suppresses subsequent CH4 net retention in the dark, whereas the corresponding CO2-induced pulse-response loss is markedly attenuated under illumination. Concurrently, opposite XPS shifts of Ni and the Zn/Mn-associated species are consistent with illumination-induced interfacial electronic redistribution accompanied by relative electron enrichment of Ni-rich sites. Control catalysts and qualitative DFT calculations further support a model in which CH4 activation preferentially involves Zn/Mn oxide-associated interfacial regions, whereas CO2 activation is favored at Ni-rich sites. These results show that light-responsive electronic and adsorption modulation can accompany photothermal heating and provide a route to regulating competitive adsorption in multicomponent DRM catalysts.

articles.title: Ring-Expansion/Cross-Coupling Cascade of Ketones via Radical Sorting
articles.abstract: Ring-expansion/cross-coupling cascade of saturated carbocycles remains an underdeveloped strategy, despite its immense potential to provide rapid access to molecular architectures that are challenging to synthesize in a single operation. Herein, we report a dual photoredox/nickel catalyzed ring-expansion/cross-coupling cascade of ketones through radical sorting, employing carboxylic acid derivatives as C(sp3) coupling partners. This protocol is broadly applicable to the one-carbon ring-expansion and concomitant functionalization of diverse 5-, 6-, 7-, 8-, 12-, 13-, 14-, and 16-membered ketones using various redox-active esters that bear a wide range of functional groups. Remarkably, the strategy can also be extended to three-carbon ring-expansion, enabling remote functionalization of ketone frameworks. Furthermore, the methodology is applicable to acyclic ketones, enabling a chain-extension/cross-coupling cascade. The synthetic utility of the methodology is demonstrated through late-stage scaffold remodeling of drugs and natural products, as well as the synthesis of 3-methylmuscone. Mechanistic investigations, supported by DFT calculations, shed light on selectivity in the coupling step and provide compelling evidence for a homolytic bimolecular substitution (SH2) pathway.

articles.title: Ruthenium Single Atom Switches the Interfacial Mechanism to Mars–van Krevelen for Coking-Resistant Photothermocatalytic Reforming of (Micro)Plastics with CO2
articles.abstract: Photothermal dry reforming of polyethylene (PE) with carbon dioxide (CO2) is a promising route for waste plastic and greenhouse gas valorization, but mismatched PE cracking and CO2 activation kinetics cause coke deposition and limit reforming stability. Here, we develop a photothermal catalyst, Ru1Cun/TiO2–x, that enables efficient and stable conversion of PE and CO2 into syngas under simulated and natural sunlight across diverse plastic feedstocks. Mechanistic studies show that Ru single atoms reconstruct the Cu-TiO2–x interface, shifting the reaction from a Langmuir–Hinshelwood mechanism to a Mars–van Krevelen (MvK) pathway that strengthens CO2 activation and lattice oxygen cycling, thereby directing PE-derived intermediates through sequential oxidation before dehydrogenation and suppressing coke formation. Life-cycle assessment and scale-up simulations show that solar-driven photothermal co-reforming has a lower carbon footprint than conventional plastic upcycling, supporting its feasibility and scalability for solar-driven plastic waste remediation and greenhouse gas utilization.

articles.title: Visible-Light-Driven Dehydrogenative Ketone Synthesis from Unprotected Primary Alcohols and Aryl Bromides
articles.abstract: Owing to their widespread natural abundance, alcohols are regarded as highly attractive coupling partners in organic synthesis. Although O–H or C–O activating cross-couplings of alcohols have been well-established in distinct contexts, the direct C–H oxidative coupling of alcohols to form ketones remains rare. Herein, we disclose a visible-light-driven, bromine-radical-mediated hydrogen-atom-transfer/nickel relay that enables the direct conversion of unprotected primary alcohols and aryl bromides to aryl alkyl ketones under ambient conditions. The transformation merges selective α-C–H arylation of alcohols with in situ dehydrogenation of the resulting secondary alcohol intermediates, thereby accomplishing C–C bond formation and ketone formation in one catalytic manifold without an exogenous stoichiometric oxidant or hydrogen acceptor. The protocol is compatible with simple and functionalized primary alcohols, aryl and heteroaryl bromides, as well as complex fragments relevant to late-stage diversification, delivering 80 ketone products in up to 91% yield. Combined mechanistic experiments and density functional theory calculations support a pathway initiated by bromine-radical-mediated hydrogen-atom transfer to generate ketyl radicals, followed by nickel-catalyzed arylation and dehydrogenation of the resulting secondary alcohol intermediates to furnish the ketone products. This work establishes native primary alcohols as practical ketone-building partners in metallaphotoredox catalysis and offers a mild and efficient cross-coupling strategy for the direct transformation of alcohols to ketones.

articles.title: Predictive Design Principles for Plasma-Catalysis
articles.abstract: Centralized production of fuels and commodity chemicals emits 1.4–2 Gt CO2 yr–1 and depends on fossil-fuel supply chains that prevent distributed deployment. Nonthermal plasmas offer a path to decentralized, electrified production by generating vibrationally excited molecules, radicals, and ions without bulk heating of gas. Despite this potential, plasma-catalysis remains difficult to design because plasma excitation, surface reaction energetics, and intermediate removal are treated separately, and activity trends do not transfer across chemistries. This perspective develops a quantitative framework connecting nonequilibrium excitation, surface binding energetics, coreactant chemistry, and surface temperature to reaction rates, selectivity, and catalyst stability. Reactions are classified into three kinetic regimes by the balance between intermediate supply and removal rates, each with distinct rate-controlling steps and deactivation modes. Design tools and principles derived from this classification are applied to four example case studies that transfer across chemistries without reparameterization and provide a basis for reactor design at scale.

articles.title: Carrier-Induced and Coherent-Phonon-Controlled Band Renormalization in Quasi-One-Dimensional α-Bi4Br4
articles.abstract: Directional control of band structures at ultrafast time scales is a key requirement for nanoscale optoelectronics. Here, we realize cooperative band engineering in the quasi-one-dimensional (quasi-1D) van der Waals topological insulator α-Bi4Br4 through joint carrier-phonon band renormalization. Femtosecond excitation drives quasi-1D carrier accumulation, generating a strongly nonlinear many-body band renormalization that redshifts an optical transition by up to ∼25 meV, with >90% polarization anisotropy. Superimposed Ag coherent phonons further modulate the same transition by ∼1 meV on intrinsic lattice time scales. By implementing phase-controlled dual-pump excitation, we achieve deterministic and reversible positioning of the renormalized band edge with ∼100 μeV precision within a ∼1.5 meV tuning window. First-principles calculations with charge-neutral photoexcitation constraints qualitatively reproduce the carrier-induced narrowing of the relevant interband transition, while phonon-mode analysis reveals that coherent Ag phonons modulate the same transition through interchain hopping and orbital polarization. These results establish cooperative carrier-phonon band renormalization as a scalable, all-optical mechanism for ultrafast, polarization-sensitive band engineering in quasi-1D van der Waals nanomaterials, enabling dynamically reconfigurable optoelectronic functionality.

articles.title: Colloidal Atomic Layer Deposition on Plasmonic Metal Oxide Nanocrystals
articles.abstract: Colloidal atomic layer deposition (c-ALD) has emerged as a powerful technique for enhancing the functional properties of nanocrystals (NCs) while preserving their solution dispersibility. Previous studies have shown that the deposition of amorphous metal oxide shells via c-ALD can passivate surface states in NCs, resulting in improved stability, photoluminescence, conductivity, and energy transfer. However, its application to doped metal oxide NCs, such as tin-doped indium oxide (ITO), which exhibit surface depletion due to surface hydroxyls, remains unexplored. In this work, we implement a c-ALD strategy using ligand-modified precursors to grow amorphous Al2O3, TiO2, and Ga2O3 shells on ITO NCs. We reveal how these coatings influence the plasmonic response and mitigate surface depletion, which we ascribe to surface state passivation. Energy-dependent X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) reveals a reduction in band bending, indicating a modification of the near-surface electronic structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that control over shell thickness enables tunability of the collective plasmonic resonances in assembled ITO NC superlattices. This work expands the scope of c-ALD and establishes a versatile approach for tailoring the optoelectronic properties of doped metal oxide NCs in solution-processable systems.

articles.title: Halide Exchange Reactions in Large Halide Perovskite Nanocrystals
articles.abstract: We have studied halide exchange reactions in large colloidal nanocrystals of lead halide perovskites, with sizes (∼40–60 nm) that are intermediate between those of typical nanocrystals synthesized and studied by the community (5–10 nm) and those of microcrystals or thin films. This size regime still allows an investigation of the nanocrystals with techniques used for colloidal nanocrystals while enabling the observation of phenomena such as phase segregation, generation of planar defects, strain accumulation and relaxation, which are harder to identify in smaller nanocrystals, also given their high instability under the electron beam. We compare nanocubes with hollow nanocubes, and highlight how the presence of the hollow region can influence structural and morphological changes during the reactions. Notably, we report core–shell epitaxial CsPbI3/CsPbCl3 heterostructures by partial I– to Cl– exchange on CsPbI3 nanocrystals. Transient absorption spectroscopy provides evidence consistent with electronic coupling and exciton transfer between the Cl-rich shell and I-rich core in these heterostructures, evidenced by the accelerated bleach decay of the CsPbCl3 component and the delayed population of the CsPbI3 band edge.

articles.title: Highly Emissive NIR-II Unimolecular Micelles via a Core–Cap Synthetic Strategy for Deep-Tissue Imaging and Image-Guided Surgery
articles.abstract: High-performance fluorescence imaging in the second near-infrared (NIR-II, 1000–1700 nm) window holds promise for deep-tissue optical diagnostics. However, simultaneously achieving high fluorescence quantum yields (QYs) and ultrasmall dimensions in physiological aqueous environments remains a fundamental challenge. Here, we report a de novo core–cap synthetic strategy to construct highly emissive, renal-clearable NIR-II fluorophores based on a unimolecular micelle architecture. By integrating a rigid, donor–acceptor–donor (D–A–D) hydrophobic core containing orthogonal axial and lateral steric shielding networks with a hydrophilic polyethylene glycol (PEG) outer cap, we successfully suppress water-induced nonradiative decay and intermolecular aggregation-induced quenching without compromising lateral conjugation. Molecular dynamics simulations and experimental characterizations reveal that these amphiphilic structures self-assemble into highly monodisperse unimolecular micelles featuring an ultrasmall hydrodynamic diameter of ∼5 nm. The optimized fluorophore exhibits a peak NIR-II emission centered at 1034 nm with a high aqueous QY of 4.6%. Owing to their sub-5 nm dimensions, unimolecular micelles undergo dual renal and hepatic clearance pathways, circumventing the biosafety concerns of prolonged tissue retention typical of conventional nanoparticles. Capitalizing on their high brightness, we demonstrate high-resolution, contrast-enhanced in vivo imaging of systemic and cerebral vasculatures, allowing the quantitative morphometric visualization of structural abnormalities in transgenic brain tumors. Furthermore, these fluorophores enable high-contrast, intraoperative fluorescence-guided tumor resection with clearly defined margins. This work provides a promising strategy for the rational design of bright, fast-clearing organic NIR-II probes for advanced biomedical diagnostics.

articles.title: Morphology-Tunable Nanoparticles of Aspartic Acid Paclitaxel Conjugates for Breast Cancer Treatment
articles.abstract: The structural morphologies of nanomaterials serve as vital determinants in their biological interactions and efficacy in vivo. Achieving programmable control over the assembly morphology solely through molecular design remains challenging. Herein, a supramolecular strategy to control the assembly morphology of prodrugs for the orchestration of drug delivery in vivo is reported. A paclitaxel prodrug (PCA) was synthesized by conjugating aspartic acid with paclitaxel through a succinyl linker. PCA can spontaneously self-assemble into nanofibers. Incorporating the diacylphosphatidylethanolamine-PEG2k (DSPE-PEG2k) induces a morphological transition from fibers to rods and ultimately to spheres. Molecular dynamics simulations show that intermolecular hydrogen bonds fall from approximately 50 in DP1 NFs to fewer than 5 in DP3 NPs, and carboxyl-related atoms in aspartic acid account for 53.24% of the total hydrogen bonds, proving that the carboxyl-mediated hydrogen-bond network dominates anisotropic assembly. Although fibrous and spherical assemblies exhibit the fastest release rate and optimized cellular delivery of paclitaxel in vitro, respectively, the rod-shaped assemblies achieve an optimal combination of prolonged blood circulation, enhanced tumor accumulation, and facilitated cellular internalization, resulting in superior antitumor efficacy in vivo, compared to fibrous and spherical counterparts and Abraxane. This study elucidates how supramolecular interactions regulate the macroscopic morphology of prodrug assemblies at the molecular level, establishing a design paradigm for engineering anisotropic nanomedicines with tailored in vivo fate.

articles.title: NanoBlocks: Creating Genetically Encoded Protein Switches Using Competitive Binding
articles.abstract: Many regulatory mechanisms function by changing a molecule’s conformation such that it is switched between active and inactive states. Engineering macromolecules such as proteins to show robust conformational changes in response to arbitrary, well-defined molecular stimuli is of great interest in fields such as synthetic biology and nanoscale engineering, because it allows the development of “smart” molecular tools. We present a strategy that can convert “simple” affinity binders such as nanobodies into protein switches that undergo clear structural rearrangements in response to their innate targets, by introducing a peptide that competes for the binding site. We demonstrate proof-of-concept implementations of this “NanoBlock” design by developing genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors based on two entirely different binder frameworks, the ALFA nanobody and the PDZ domain of Erbin. We show that our design allows the construction of well-performing protein switches that can reliably detect their targets in vitro, in mammalian cells, as part of fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) experiments, and that also generalizes to the creation of stimulus-responsive enzymes via the integration of a bioluminescent readout. We furthermore develop a theoretical model that rationalizes the observations and provides insight into the underlying molecular mechanisms. Overall, our strategy expands the possibilities to create “smart” protein-based molecules and effectors.
